title: Understanding the variable-length path in graph databases
text:
A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum. It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Consider a social network model built from Person, Post, Group. To work out who are the friends of friends of a user, you rely directly on the variable-length path.

A frequent problem: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

It is closely related to the query parameter. A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Recommended practice: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Asha and Elena are connected in the social network graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Asha and Elena are connected in the social network graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Person {name: 'Asha'})-[*..6]-(b:Person {name: 'Elena'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 ACTED_IN hops of a Person called Lena Park
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 2 ACTED_IN hops of a Person called Lena Park.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Lena Park'})-[:ACTED_IN*1..2]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Questions and answers: path, query parameter, index
text:
Q: What is a path?
A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: Why does the path matter?
A: Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Q: What is good practice for the query parameter?
A: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 CONTAINS hops of a Order called ORD-1002
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 2 CONTAINS hops of a Order called ORD-1002.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Order {name: 'ORD-1002'})-[:CONTAINS*1..2]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Account named ACC-204 is linked to a Transaction named TX-9004, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Account named ACC-204 is linked to a Transaction named TX-9004, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Account {name: 'ACC-204'})
MERGE (b:Transaction {name: 'TX-9004'})
MERGE (a)-[:SENT]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Cypher example: add a new Author and connect it to a Article with a WROTE relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Author and connect it to a Article with a WROTE relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Author {name: 'M. Costa'})-[:WROTE]->(b:Article {name: 'Backup guide'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Understanding the query parameter in graph databases
text:
A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text. Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

A team modeling knowledge base data with Article, Topic, Author will meet the query parameter as soon as they need to know which topics an author covers.

A frequent problem: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

It is closely related to the index. An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Recommended practice: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

title: Questions and answers: pattern matching, query plan, community detection
text:
Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the pattern matching?
A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

Q: What is a community detection?
A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Q: Why does the community detection matter?
A: It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the community detection?
A: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: What is good practice for the relationship?
A: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Service named reports is linked to a Server named srv-app-02, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Service named reports is linked to a Server named srv-app-02, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Service {name: 'reports'})
MERGE (b:Server {name: 'srv-app-02'})
MERGE (a)-[:RUNS_ON]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Understanding the community detection in graph databases
text:
Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest. It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

In a e-commerce graph with Customer, Product, Order nodes, the idea of a community detection appears when you ask which products are often bought together.

A frequent problem: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

It is closely related to the MERGE. MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Recommended practice: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Understanding the path in graph databases
text:
A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node. Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

In a social network graph with Person, Post, Group nodes, the idea of a path appears when you ask which groups a user's friends have joined.

A frequent problem: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

It is closely related to the variable-length path. A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Recommended practice: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

title: Questions and answers: pattern matching, uniqueness constraint, relationship
text:
Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the pattern matching matter?
A: It lets you express a multi-hop question in a single line instead of a chain of joins.

Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?
A: A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Q: Why does the uniqueness constraint matter?
A: It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the uniqueness constraint?
A: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: What is good practice for the relationship?
A: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query parameter?
A: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

Q: What is good practice for the query parameter?
A: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: What is good practice for the graph projection?
A: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

title: Understanding the selectivity in graph databases
text:
Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few. The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

In a e-commerce graph with Customer, Product, Order nodes, the idea of a selectivity appears when you ask which categories drive the most repeat orders.

A frequent problem: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

Recommended practice: Anchor queries on unique or nearly unique properties.

title: Questions and answers: shortest path, LOAD CSV, MERGE
text:
Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is a LOAD CSV?
A: LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the LOAD CSV matter?
A: It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

Q: What is good practice for the LOAD CSV?
A: Create constraints first and process the file in batches.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the MERGE?
A: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query plan?
A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the supernode?
A: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

title: Understanding the PageRank in graph databases
text:
PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them. It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

A team modeling supply chain data with Factory, Warehouse, Shipment will meet the PageRank as soon as they need to know which shipments carry parts from several factories.

A frequent problem: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

It is closely related to the pattern matching. Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Recommended practice: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases
text:
A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels. Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

Consider an IT infrastructure model built from Server, Service, Database. To work out which services are affected if a server fails, you rely directly on the label.

A frequent problem: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

Recommended practice: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

title: Cypher example: show the Author nodes whose posts is above 50 in the knowledge base graph, highest first
text:

title: Cypher example: list every Group connected to a given Person through MEMBER_OF in the social network graph
text:
Task: List every Group connected to a given Person through MEMBER_OF in the social network graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: $name})-[:MEMBER_OF]->(b:Group)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Person found by name, follows outgoing MEMBER_OF relationships, and returns the name of each Group reached. The value of $name, for example 'Asha', is passed as a parameter.

title: Understanding the aggregation in graph databases
text:

title: Understanding the pattern matching in graph databases

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

Likely cause: the first step scans every node of a label because no index supports the filter. This is easy to hit when queries start from Service nodes and follow OWNS relationships from Team to Service.

How to fix it: create an index on the filtered property and confirm with PROFILE that the scan is gone.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Questions and answers: pattern matching, variable-length path, full-text index
text:
Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the pattern matching matter?
A: It lets you express a multi-hop question in a single line instead of a chain of joins.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the pattern matching?
A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

Q: What is good practice for the pattern matching?
A: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Q: What is good practice for the variable-length path?
A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: Why does the full-text index matter?
A: It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

Q: What is good practice for the full-text index?
A: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query parameter?
A: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Q: Why does the node matter?
A: Nodes are the anchor points of every query, so a clear choice of what becomes a node shapes the whole model.

Q: What is good practice for the node?
A: Give every node at least one label and a stable identifying property.

MATCH (n:Post)
WHERE n.likes > 100
RETURN n.name AS name, n.likes AS likes
ORDER BY n.likes DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Post nodes above the threshold. An index on Post(likes) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Understanding the MERGE in graph databases

title: Questions and answers: variable-length path, traversal, graph projection
text:
Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Q: What is good practice for the variable-length path?
A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: Why does the traversal matter?
A: Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the traversal?
A: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: Why does the transaction matter?
A: It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the transaction?
A: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: Why does the shortest path matter?
A: It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is good practice for the shortest path?
A: Set a maximum depth and check that both endpoints are indexed.

title: Cypher example: show the Merchant nodes whose risk is above 250 in the fraud detection graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Merchant nodes whose risk is above 250 in the fraud detection graph, highest first.

MATCH (n:Merchant)
WHERE n.risk > 250
RETURN n.name AS name, n.risk AS risk
ORDER BY n.risk DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Merchant nodes above the threshold. An index on Merchant(risk) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases
text:

A team modeling supply chain data with Factory, Warehouse, Shipment will meet the label as soon as they need to know which shipments carry parts from several factories.

title: Questions and answers: MERGE, query plan, relationship
text:

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship?
A: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In a movies graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

Likely cause: a large transaction holds locks on nodes that other writers need. This is easy to hit when queries start from Person nodes and follow ACTED_IN relationships from Person to Movie.

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

Likely cause: the first step scans every node of a label because no index supports the filter. This is easy to hit when queries start from Database nodes and follow DEPENDS_ON relationships from Service to Service.

How to fix it: create an index on the filtered property and confirm with PROFILE that the scan is gone.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the community detection in graph databases
text:
Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest. It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

Consider a movies model built from Person, Movie, Genre. To work out which genres a given actor appears in most, you rely directly on the community detection.

A frequent problem: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

Recommended practice: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Cypher example: show the Customer nodes whose age is above 10 in the e-commerce graph, highest first
text:

title: Understanding the aggregation in graph databases

title: Understanding the pattern matching in graph databases

text:

title: Troubleshooting: an algorithm run fails to start
text:
Symptom: In a knowledge base graph, an algorithm run fails to start.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases

title: Cypher example: find how closely Data modeling 101 and Index tuning are connected in the knowledge base graph
text:

MATCH p = shortestPath(

)

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Troubleshooting: the planner reports a cartesian product warning
text:
Symptom: In a knowledge base graph, the planner reports a cartesian product warning.

Likely cause: two patterns in the same MATCH are not connected to each other. This is easy to hit when queries start from Topic nodes and follow TAGGED relationships from Article to Tag.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Product named Notebook set is linked to a Category named Kitchen, without creating duplicates
text:

title: Cypher example: find how closely Espresso maker and Trail shoes are connected in the e-commerce graph
text:

A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query parameter?
A: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

Q: What is good practice for the query parameter?
A: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: Why does the shortest path matter?
A: It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is good practice for the shortest path?
A: Set a maximum depth and check that both endpoints are indexed.

Q: What is a selectivity?
A: Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Q: Why does the selectivity matter?
A: The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the selectivity?
A: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

Q: What is good practice for the selectivity?
A: Anchor queries on unique or nearly unique properties.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

title: Understanding the graph projection in graph databases
text:
A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms. It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

Consider a knowledge base model built from Article, Topic, Author. To work out which tags appear together on the same article, you rely directly on the graph projection.

A frequent problem: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

It is closely related to the variable-length path. A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Recommended practice: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

title: Understanding the LOAD CSV in graph databases
text:
LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships. It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

In a movies graph with Person, Movie, Genre nodes, the idea of a LOAD CSV appears when you ask which actors worked with the same director.

A frequent problem: Running it without a constraint and without batching makes the import slow and error-prone.

Recommended practice: Create constraints first and process the file in batches.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 PRODUCES hops of a Factory called Gdansk Site
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 3 PRODUCES hops of a Factory called Gdansk Site.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Factory {name: 'Gdansk Site'})-[:PRODUCES*1..3]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..3 allows paths of one to 3 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Questions and answers: path, variable-length path, pattern matching
text:

A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

A: Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

A: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What is good practice for the variable-length path?
A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?
A: A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Q: Why does the uniqueness constraint matter?
A: It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the transaction?
A: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

Q: What is good practice for the transaction?
A: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

title: Cypher example: list every Order connected to a given Customer through PLACED in the e-commerce graph
text:

MATCH (a:Customer {name: $name})-[:PLACED]->(b:Order)

title: Cypher example: find how closely Jonas and Carla are connected in the social network graph
text:

MATCH p = shortestPath(

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In a knowledge base graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

Likely cause: a large transaction holds locks on nodes that other writers need. This is easy to hit when queries start from Topic nodes and follow ABOUT relationships from Article to Topic.

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find every Device that can be reached from a Transaction in two steps, first through RECEIVED_BY and then through USED_DEVICE

title: Cypher example: make sure a Service named billing is linked to a Service named reports, without creating duplicates

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Understanding the PageRank in graph databases
text:
PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them. It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

A team modeling IT infrastructure data with Server, Service, Database will meet the PageRank as soon as they need to know which team owns the services that depend on a given database.

A frequent problem: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

It is closely related to the aggregation. Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Recommended practice: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

title: Understanding the variable-length path in graph databases
text:
A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum. It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

In a movies graph with Person, Movie, Genre nodes, the idea of a variable-length path appears when you ask which actors worked with the same director.

A frequent problem: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

It is closely related to the shortest path. A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Recommended practice: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

title: Questions and answers: query plan, relationship direction, shortest path
text:
Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What is a relationship direction?
A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Q: What is good practice for the relationship direction?
A: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is a path?
A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: Why does the path matter?
A: Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the path?
A: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

title: Questions and answers: full-text index, community detection, relationship
text:
Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: Why does the full-text index matter?
A: It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the full-text index?
A: Using a regular index for substring search gives poor results and slow scans.

Q: What is good practice for the full-text index?
A: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

Q: What is a community detection?
A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the community detection?
A: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

Q: What is good practice for the community detection?
A: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship?
A: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the node?
A: A common mistake is storing a repeating group of values inside one node instead of giving each its own node.

Q: What is good practice for the node?
A: Give every node at least one label and a stable identifying property.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Person named Sara Cole is linked to a Movie named Blue Meridian, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Person named Sara Cole is linked to a Movie named Blue Meridian, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Person {name: 'Sara Cole'})
MERGE (b:Movie {name: 'Blue Meridian'})
MERGE (a)-[:DIRECTED]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:
An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning. Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

A team modeling knowledge base data with Article, Topic, Author will meet the index as soon as they need to know which tags appear together on the same article.

A frequent problem: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

It is closely related to the variable-length path. A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Recommended practice: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

title: Understanding the selectivity in graph databases
text:
Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few. The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

In a fraud detection graph with Account, Transaction, Device nodes, the idea of a selectivity appears when you ask which accounts share a device.

A frequent problem: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

It is closely related to the query parameter. A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Recommended practice: Anchor queries on unique or nearly unique properties.

title: Troubleshooting: one query is much slower for some start nodes than others
text:
Symptom: In a movies graph, one query is much slower for some start nodes than others.

Likely cause: a few nodes have a huge number of relationships. This is easy to hit when queries start from Genre nodes and follow DIRECTED relationships from Person to Movie.

How to fix it: avoid traversing through hub nodes or filter on a relationship property before expanding.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the uniqueness constraint in graph databases
text:
A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property. It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

Consider an IT infrastructure model built from Server, Service, Database. To work out which team owns the services that depend on a given database, you rely directly on the uniqueness constraint.

A frequent problem: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

It is closely related to the node. A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Recommended practice: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

title: Understanding the MERGE in graph databases
text:
MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat. It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

A team modeling IT infrastructure data with Server, Service, Database will meet the MERGE as soon as they need to know which team owns the services that depend on a given database.

A frequent problem: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

It is closely related to the pattern matching. Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Recommended practice: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

text:

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 RUNS_ON hops of a Service called gateway
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 2 RUNS_ON hops of a Service called gateway.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Service {name: 'gateway'})-[:RUNS_ON*1..2]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:
Symptom: In a social network graph, a query runs out of memory.

Likely cause: a variable-length pattern has no upper bound and expands through most of the graph. This is easy to hit when queries start from Person nodes and follow MEMBER_OF relationships from Person to Group.

How to fix it: set a maximum depth, filter early and return only the properties you need.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: list every Movie connected to a given Person through DIRECTED in the movies graph
text:
Task: List every Movie connected to a given Person through DIRECTED in the movies graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: $name})-[:DIRECTED]->(b:Movie)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Person found by name, follows outgoing DIRECTED relationships, and returns the name of each Movie reached. The value of $name, for example 'Maya Lin', is passed as a parameter.

title: Troubleshooting: the planner reports a cartesian product warning
text:

How to fix it: connect the patterns with a relationship or split them into separate clauses on purpose.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find how closely ORD-1005 and ORD-1002 are connected in the e-commerce graph

title: Understanding the relationship in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: find every Post that can be reached from a Person in two steps, first through FRIENDS_WITH and then through POSTED
text:

title: Understanding the path in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: make sure a Warehouse named East Yard is linked to a Part named Sensor T4, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Warehouse named East Yard is linked to a Part named Sensor T4, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Warehouse {name: 'East Yard'})

```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:
A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph. Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

A frequent problem: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

It is closely related to the transaction. A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Recommended practice: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In a social network graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

Likely cause: a large transaction holds locks on nodes that other writers need. This is easy to hit when queries start from Group nodes and follow FRIENDS_WITH relationships from Person to Person.

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:
Symptom: In a social network graph, a query runs out of memory.

Likely cause: a variable-length pattern has no upper bound and expands through most of the graph. This is easy to hit when queries start from Post nodes and follow MEMBER_OF relationships from Person to Group.

How to fix it: set a maximum depth, filter early and return only the properties you need.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Questions and answers: property, node, graph projection
text:
Q: What is a property?
A: A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Q: Why does the property matter?
A: Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the property?
A: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

Q: What is good practice for the property?
A: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: Why does the graph projection matter?
A: It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the graph projection?
A: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

title: Understanding the query parameter in graph databases
text:
A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text. Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

A team modeling social network data with Person, Post, Group will meet the query parameter as soon as they need to know which groups a user's friends have joined.

A frequent problem: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

Recommended practice: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

title: Understanding the aggregation in graph databases
text:
Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists. It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

A team modeling supply chain data with Factory, Warehouse, Shipment will meet the aggregation as soon as they need to know how a delay at one warehouse affects shipments.

A frequent problem: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

Recommended practice: Aggregate as late as possible and limit the size of collected lists.

title: Questions and answers: uniqueness constraint, query plan, shortest path
text:
Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?
A: A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the uniqueness constraint?
A: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: Why does the shortest path matter?
A: It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is good practice for the shortest path?
A: Set a maximum depth and check that both endpoints are indexed.

title: Questions and answers: path, query plan, LOAD CSV
text:
Q: What is a path?
A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: Why does the path matter?
A: Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

A: It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

A: It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

title: Questions and answers: variable-length path, label, full-text index
text:

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Q: What is a label?

A: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

title: Understanding the node in graph databases
text:
A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product. Nodes are the anchor points of every query, so a clear choice of what becomes a node shapes the whole model.

In an IT infrastructure graph with Server, Service, Database nodes, the idea of a node appears when you ask which team owns the services that depend on a given database.

A frequent problem: A common mistake is storing a repeating group of values inside one node instead of giving each its own node.

It is closely related to the property. A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Recommended practice: Give every node at least one label and a stable identifying property.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

Likely cause: the first step scans every node of a label because no index supports the filter. This is easy to hit when queries start from Service nodes and follow USES relationships from Service to Database.

How to fix it: create an index on the filtered property and confirm with PROFILE that the scan is gone.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find every Topic that can be reached from a Article in two steps, first through REFERENCES and then through ABOUT
text:
Task: Find every Topic that can be reached from a Article in two steps, first through REFERENCES and then through ABOUT.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Article {name: $name})-[:REFERENCES]->(:Article)-[:ABOUT]->(c:Topic)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Topic nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'Data modeling 101' could be passed as $name.

title: Cypher example: show the Post nodes whose likes is above 250 in the social network graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Post nodes whose likes is above 250 in the social network graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Post)
WHERE n.likes > 250
RETURN n.name AS name, n.likes AS likes
ORDER BY n.likes DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Post nodes above the threshold. An index on Post(likes) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Cypher example: find how closely ACC-206 and ACC-204 are connected in the fraud detection graph
text:
Task: Find how closely ACC-206 and ACC-204 are connected in the fraud detection graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Account {name: 'ACC-206'})-[*..6]-(b:Account {name: 'ACC-204'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Questions and answers: PageRank, supernode, transaction
text:
Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: Why does the transaction matter?
A: It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the transaction?
A: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

Q: What is good practice for the transaction?
A: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 ABOUT hops of a Article called Backup guide
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 4 ABOUT hops of a Article called Backup guide.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Article {name: 'Backup guide'})-[:ABOUT*1..4]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..4 allows paths of one to 4 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: Why does the traversal matter?
A: Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Account named ACC-202 is linked to a Device named DEV-D4, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Account named ACC-202 is linked to a Device named DEV-D4, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Account {name: 'ACC-202'})
MERGE (b:Device {name: 'DEV-D4'})
MERGE (a)-[:USED_DEVICE]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

title: Cypher example: guarantee that every Post has a unique name
text:
Task: Guarantee that every Post has a unique name.

```cypher
CREATE CONSTRAINT post_name_unique IF NOT EXISTS
FOR (n:Post) REQUIRE n.name IS UNIQUE
```

The constraint rejects a second Post with the same name and also provides an index for lookups.

title: Questions and answers: variable-length path, LOAD CSV, pattern matching

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:
Symptom: In a supply chain graph, a query runs out of memory.

Likely cause: a variable-length pattern has no upper bound and expands through most of the graph. This is easy to hit when queries start from Shipment nodes and follow CONTAINS_PART relationships from Shipment to Part.

How to fix it: set a maximum depth, filter early and return only the properties you need.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Backup guide and Security basics are connected in the knowledge base graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Backup guide and Security basics are connected in the knowledge base graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Article {name: 'Backup guide'})-[*..5]-(b:Article {name: 'Security basics'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Understanding the path in graph databases
text:

A frequent problem: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

It is closely related to the index. An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Recommended practice: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 ACTED_IN hops of a Person called Victor Hale
text:

title: Understanding the node in graph databases
text:

title: Understanding the graph projection in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: find every Category that can be reached from a Customer in two steps, first through REVIEWED and then through IN_CATEGORY
text:
Task: Find every Category that can be reached from a Customer in two steps, first through REVIEWED and then through IN_CATEGORY.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Customer {name: $name})-[:REVIEWED]->(:Product)-[:IN_CATEGORY]->(c:Category)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Category nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'Desk lamp' could be passed as $name.

title: Questions and answers: node, shortest path, uniqueness constraint
text:

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the node?

Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?

title: Understanding the aggregation in graph databases
text:
Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists. It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

Consider a e-commerce model built from Customer, Product, Order. To work out which categories drive the most repeat orders, you rely directly on the aggregation.

A frequent problem: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

Recommended practice: Aggregate as late as possible and limit the size of collected lists.

title: Questions and answers: relationship, aggregation, relationship direction
text:

A: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

Q: What is a relationship direction?
A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

A: A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

A: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

A: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

Q: What is a variable-length path?

A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Q: What is good practice for the PageRank?
A: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

title: Cypher example: show the Merchant nodes whose risk is above 10 in the fraud detection graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Merchant nodes whose risk is above 10 in the fraud detection graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Merchant)
WHERE n.risk > 10
RETURN n.name AS name, n.risk AS risk
ORDER BY n.risk DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Merchant nodes above the threshold. An index on Merchant(risk) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In a social network graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

Likely cause: a large transaction holds locks on nodes that other writers need. This is easy to hit when queries start from Post nodes and follow FRIENDS_WITH relationships from Person to Person.

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find how closely notifier and search are connected in the IT infrastructure graph

title: Understanding the full-text index in graph databases
text:
A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking. It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

A team modeling movies data with Person, Movie, Genre will meet the full-text index as soon as they need to know how many movies two people have in common.

A frequent problem: Using a regular index for substring search gives poor results and slow scans.

It is closely related to the selectivity. Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Recommended practice: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

title: Understanding the shortest path in graph databases
text:
A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships. It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

Consider a knowledge base model built from Article, Topic, Author. To work out which topics an author covers, you rely directly on the shortest path.

A frequent problem: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Recommended practice: Set a maximum depth and check that both endpoints are indexed.

title: Cypher example: add a new Article and connect it to a Topic with a ABOUT relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Article and connect it to a Topic with a ABOUT relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Article {name: 'Security basics'})-[:ABOUT]->(b:Topic {name: 'Security'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Understanding the PageRank in graph databases
text:
PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them. It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

In a fraud detection graph with Account, Transaction, Device nodes, the idea of a PageRank appears when you ask which accounts share a device.

A frequent problem: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

It is closely related to the aggregation. Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Recommended practice: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

title: Understanding the community detection in graph databases
text:
Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest. It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

A team modeling knowledge base data with Article, Topic, Author will meet the community detection as soon as they need to know which topics an author covers.

A frequent problem: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

It is closely related to the variable-length path. A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Recommended practice: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Questions and answers: path, pattern matching, community detection
text:
Q: What is a path?
A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: Why does the path matter?
A: Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the path?
A: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the pattern matching?
A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

Q: What is good practice for the pattern matching?
A: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

Q: What is a community detection?
A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: Why does the full-text index matter?
A: It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

Q: What is good practice for the full-text index?
A: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

title: Cypher example: add a new Warehouse and connect it to a Part with a STORES relationship

```cypher
CREATE (a:Warehouse {name: 'Central Store'})-[:STORES]->(b:Part {name: 'Bracket M2'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:
A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph. Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

In a e-commerce graph with Customer, Product, Order nodes, the idea of a supernode appears when you ask which products are often bought together.

A frequent problem: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

It is closely related to the shortest path. A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Recommended practice: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Understanding the aggregation in graph databases
text:
Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists. It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

In a fraud detection graph with Account, Transaction, Device nodes, the idea of a aggregation appears when you ask which merchants receive money from many new accounts.

A frequent problem: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

Recommended practice: Aggregate as late as possible and limit the size of collected lists.

title: Troubleshooting: an import fails with a constraint violation
text:
Symptom: In a e-commerce graph, an import fails with a constraint violation.

Likely cause: the file contains two rows with the same value for a unique property. This is easy to hit when queries start from Customer nodes and follow REVIEWED relationships from Customer to Product.

How to fix it: deduplicate the input or use MERGE on the unique key.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Questions and answers: variable-length path, graph projection, aggregation
text:
Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What is good practice for the variable-length path?
A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the graph projection?
A: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

Q: What is a aggregation?
A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Q: What is a property?
A: A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Q: Why does the property matter?
A: Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

Q: What is good practice for the property?
A: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

title: Understanding the uniqueness constraint in graph databases
text:
A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property. It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

A team modeling knowledge base data with Article, Topic, Author will meet the uniqueness constraint as soon as they need to know which articles are most referenced by others.

A frequent problem: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

It is closely related to the LOAD CSV. LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Recommended practice: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In a supply chain graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

Likely cause: the first step scans every node of a label because no index supports the filter. This is easy to hit when queries start from Factory nodes and follow CONTAINS_PART relationships from Shipment to Part.

How to fix it: create an index on the filtered property and confirm with PROFILE that the scan is gone.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

title: Understanding the MERGE in graph databases
text:
MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat. It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

A team modeling knowledge base data with Article, Topic, Author will meet the MERGE as soon as they need to know which tags appear together on the same article.

A frequent problem: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

It is closely related to the index. An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Recommended practice: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

title: Cypher example: find how closely ACC-203 and ACC-204 are connected in the fraud detection graph
text:
Task: Find how closely ACC-203 and ACC-204 are connected in the fraud detection graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Account {name: 'ACC-203'})-[*..6]-(b:Account {name: 'ACC-204'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 DEPENDS_ON hops of a Service called search
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 3 DEPENDS_ON hops of a Service called search.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Service {name: 'search'})-[:DEPENDS_ON*1..3]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..3 allows paths of one to 3 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Questions and answers: query plan, selectivity, query parameter
text:
Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query plan?
A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

Q: What is a selectivity?
A: Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the selectivity?
A: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query parameter?
A: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

Q: What is good practice for the query parameter?
A: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

Q: What is a label?
A: A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Q: Why does the label matter?
A: Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Shipment named SHP-33 is linked to a Part named Valve K7, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Shipment named SHP-33 is linked to a Part named Valve K7, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Shipment {name: 'SHP-33'})
MERGE (b:Part {name: 'Valve K7'})

```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Cypher example: show the Team nodes whose people is above 20 in the IT infrastructure graph, highest first
text:

WHERE n.people > 20
RETURN n.name AS name, n.people AS people
ORDER BY n.people DESC
LIMIT 10

The WHERE clause keeps only Team nodes above the threshold. An index on Team(people) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Questions and answers: shortest path, variable-length path, query plan
text:

title: Understanding the relationship in graph databases
text:

title: Questions and answers: transaction, LOAD CSV, label
text:
Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: Why does the transaction matter?
A: It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the transaction?
A: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

Q: What is good practice for the transaction?
A: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

Q: What is a LOAD CSV?
A: LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the LOAD CSV matter?
A: It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

Q: What is a label?
A: A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Q: Why does the label matter?
A: Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the label?
A: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

Q: What is good practice for the label?
A: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship?
A: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:

title: Understanding the path in graph databases
text:

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 REFERENCES hops of a Article called Index tuning
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 3 REFERENCES hops of a Article called Index tuning.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Article {name: 'Index tuning'})-[:REFERENCES*1..3]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..3 allows paths of one to 3 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:

A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: Why does the graph projection matter?
A: It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

A: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

Q: What is a selectivity?
A: Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

A: The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the selectivity?
