title: Understanding the full-text index in graph databases
text:
A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking. It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

A team modeling knowledge base data with Article, Topic, Author will meet the full-text index as soon as they need to know which tags appear together on the same article.

A frequent problem: Using a regular index for substring search gives poor results and slow scans.

It is closely related to the traversal. A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Recommended practice: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

title: Cypher example: guarantee that every Group has a unique name
text:
Task: Guarantee that every Group has a unique name.

```cypher
CREATE CONSTRAINT group_name_unique IF NOT EXISTS
FOR (n:Group) REQUIRE n.name IS UNIQUE
```

The constraint rejects a second Group with the same name and also provides an index for lookups.

title: Understanding the community detection in graph databases
text:
Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest. It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

A team modeling fraud detection data with Account, Transaction, Device will meet the community detection as soon as they need to know which chains of transfers return to the starting account.

A frequent problem: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

It is closely related to the aggregation. Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Recommended practice: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Understanding the query plan in graph databases
text:
A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query. Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

In a social network graph with Person, Post, Group nodes, the idea of a query plan appears when you ask who are the friends of friends of a user.

A frequent problem: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

It is closely related to the property. A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Recommended practice: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

title: Troubleshooting: the planner reports a cartesian product warning
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, the planner reports a cartesian product warning.

Likely cause: two patterns in the same MATCH are not connected to each other. This is easy to hit when queries start from Account nodes and follow SENT relationships from Account to Transaction.

How to fix it: connect the patterns with a relationship or split them into separate clauses on purpose.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Questions and answers: LOAD CSV, supernode, query parameter
text:
Q: What is a LOAD CSV?
A: LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the LOAD CSV matter?
A: It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the LOAD CSV?
A: Running it without a constraint and without batching makes the import slow and error-prone.

Q: What is good practice for the LOAD CSV?
A: Create constraints first and process the file in batches.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Q: What is good practice for the query parameter?
A: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: Why does the full-text index matter?
A: It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

Q: What is good practice for the full-text index?
A: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

title: Cypher example: find how closely SHP-32 and SHP-33 are connected in the supply chain graph
text:
Task: Find how closely SHP-32 and SHP-33 are connected in the supply chain graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Shipment {name: 'SHP-32'})-[*..4]-(b:Shipment {name: 'SHP-33'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..4 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Troubleshooting: an import fails with a constraint violation
text:
Symptom: In a knowledge base graph, an import fails with a constraint violation.

Likely cause: the file contains two rows with the same value for a unique property. This is easy to hit when queries start from Topic nodes and follow TAGGED relationships from Article to Tag.

How to fix it: deduplicate the input or use MERGE on the unique key.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: show the Team nodes whose people is above 100 in the IT infrastructure graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Team nodes whose people is above 100 in the IT infrastructure graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Team)
WHERE n.people > 100
RETURN n.name AS name, n.people AS people
ORDER BY n.people DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Team nodes above the threshold. An index on Team(people) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Elena and Jonas are connected in the social network graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Elena and Jonas are connected in the social network graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Person {name: 'Elena'})-[*..4]-(b:Person {name: 'Jonas'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..4 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Questions and answers: traversal, query parameter, aggregation
text:
Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the traversal?
A: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Q: What is good practice for the traversal?
A: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: What is good practice for the query parameter?
A: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

Q: What is a aggregation?
A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Q: Why does the aggregation matter?
A: It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the aggregation?
A: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

Q: What is good practice for the aggregation?
A: Aggregate as late as possible and limit the size of collected lists.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Q: What is a LOAD CSV?
A: LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the LOAD CSV matter?
A: It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the LOAD CSV?
A: Running it without a constraint and without batching makes the import slow and error-prone.

title: Questions and answers: path, relationship direction, pattern matching
text:
Q: What is a path?
A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: Why does the path matter?
A: Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the path?
A: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

Q: What is good practice for the path?
A: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

Q: What is a relationship direction?
A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Q: Why does the relationship direction matter?
A: A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship direction?
A: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the pattern matching matter?
A: It lets you express a multi-hop question in a single line instead of a chain of joins.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the pattern matching?
A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Q: What is good practice for the query parameter?
A: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Shipment named SHP-32 is linked to a Part named Sensor T4, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Shipment named SHP-32 is linked to a Part named Sensor T4, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Shipment {name: 'SHP-32'})
MERGE (b:Part {name: 'Sensor T4'})
MERGE (a)-[:CONTAINS_PART]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Questions and answers: MERGE, PageRank, property
text:
Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: Why does the MERGE matter?
A: It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What is good practice for the PageRank?
A: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

Q: What is a property?
A: A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Q: Why does the property matter?
A: Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the property?
A: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases
text:
A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels. Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

Consider a movies model built from Person, Movie, Genre. To work out which actors worked with the same director, you rely directly on the label.

A frequent problem: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

It is closely related to the selectivity. Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Recommended practice: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

title: Questions and answers: query parameter, uniqueness constraint, selectivity
text:

Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?
A: A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Q: Why does the uniqueness constraint matter?
A: It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

A: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

A: It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the transaction?
A: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

text:

Q: What is a index?

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 LIKES hops of a Person called Ben
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 2 LIKES hops of a Person called Ben.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Ben'})-[:LIKES*1..2]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Cypher example: add a new Team and connect it to a Service with a OWNS relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Team and connect it to a Service with a OWNS relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Team {name: 'Platform'})-[:OWNS]->(b:Service {name: 'auth-api'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Troubleshooting: an algorithm run fails to start
text:
Symptom: In a social network graph, an algorithm run fails to start.

Likely cause: the projected graph does not fit in the memory that is available. This is easy to hit when queries start from Group nodes and follow POSTED relationships from Person to Post.

How to fix it: project only the needed labels and relationship types, or estimate memory before running.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In a knowledge base graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

Likely cause: the first step scans every node of a label because no index supports the filter. This is easy to hit when queries start from Author nodes and follow ABOUT relationships from Article to Topic.

How to fix it: create an index on the filtered property and confirm with PROFILE that the scan is gone.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find every Category that can be reached from a Customer in two steps, first through REVIEWED and then through IN_CATEGORY
text:
Task: Find every Category that can be reached from a Customer in two steps, first through REVIEWED and then through IN_CATEGORY.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Customer {name: $name})-[:REVIEWED]->(:Product)-[:IN_CATEGORY]->(c:Category)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Category nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'Espresso maker' could be passed as $name.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: list every Topic connected to a given Article through ABOUT in the knowledge base graph
text:
Task: List every Topic connected to a given Article through ABOUT in the knowledge base graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Article {name: $name})-[:ABOUT]->(b:Topic)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Article found by name, follows outgoing ABOUT relationships, and returns the name of each Topic reached. The value of $name, for example 'Backup guide', is passed as a parameter.

title: Troubleshooting: an import fails with a constraint violation
text:

title: Understanding the community detection in graph databases
text:
Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest. It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 SENT hops of a Account called ACC-201

Task: Find all nodes within 2 SENT hops of a Account called ACC-201.

text:

text:

A: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

A: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Order named ORD-1003 is linked to a Product named Wireless mouse, without creating duplicates
text:

title: Questions and answers: aggregation, node, PageRank
text:

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the node?

Q: What is a PageRank?

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?

Q: What is good practice for the PageRank?

text:

title: Questions and answers: index, uniqueness constraint, query plan
text:

A: It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:
A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes. Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

In an IT infrastructure graph with Server, Service, Database nodes, the idea of a traversal appears when you ask which services have the longest dependency chains.

A frequent problem: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

It is closely related to the supernode. A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Recommended practice: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Understanding the relationship direction in graph databases
text:

A frequent problem: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

It is closely related to the path. A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Recommended practice: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

text:

title: Cypher example: find how closely Cold Harbor and Paper Moon are connected in the movies graph


shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

text:
A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum. It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

In a knowledge base graph with Article, Topic, Author nodes, the idea of a variable-length path appears when you ask which topics an author covers.

A frequent problem: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Recommended practice: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

title: Cypher example: show the Service nodes whose replicas is above 10 in the IT infrastructure graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Service nodes whose replicas is above 10 in the IT infrastructure graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Service)
WHERE n.replicas > 10
RETURN n.name AS name, n.replicas AS replicas
ORDER BY n.replicas DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Service nodes above the threshold. An index on Service(replicas) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Understanding the query plan in graph databases
text:
A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query. Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

A team modeling IT infrastructure data with Server, Service, Database will meet the query plan as soon as they need to know which team owns the services that depend on a given database.

A frequent problem: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

It is closely related to the graph projection. A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Recommended practice: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:
A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes. Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

Consider a social network model built from Person, Post, Group. To work out which groups a user's friends have joined, you rely directly on the traversal.

A frequent problem: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Recommended practice: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Questions and answers: supernode, PageRank, MERGE
text:
Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the supernode?
A: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

Q: What is good practice for the supernode?
A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: Why does the MERGE matter?
A: It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the MERGE?
A: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

Q: What is good practice for the MERGE?
A: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

Q: What is a path?
A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the path?
A: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

Q: What is good practice for the path?
A: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 POSTED hops of a Person called Carla

```cypher
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

Likely cause: a large transaction holds locks on nodes that other writers need. This is easy to hit when queries start from Team nodes and follow RUNS_ON relationships from Service to Server.

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

text:

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 DIRECTED hops of a Person called Tom Reyes
text:

title: Cypher example: list every Transaction connected to a given Account through SENT in the fraud detection graph
text:
Task: List every Transaction connected to a given Account through SENT in the fraud detection graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Account {name: $name})-[:SENT]->(b:Transaction)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Account found by name, follows outgoing SENT relationships, and returns the name of each Transaction reached. The value of $name, for example 'ACC-204', is passed as a parameter.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Person named Asha is linked to a Person named Dev, without creating duplicates


Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

text:

text:

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:
Symptom: In a e-commerce graph, results differ every time the import is repeated.

Likely cause: CREATE was used where MERGE was needed, so duplicates accumulate. This is easy to hit when queries start from Product nodes and follow IN_CATEGORY relationships from Product to Category.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Transaction named TX-9001 is linked to a Account named ACC-201, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Transaction named TX-9001 is linked to a Account named ACC-201, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Transaction {name: 'TX-9001'})
MERGE (b:Account {name: 'ACC-201'})
MERGE (a)-[:RECEIVED_BY]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the path?
A: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the pattern matching matter?
A: It lets you express a multi-hop question in a single line instead of a chain of joins.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the pattern matching?
A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

Q: What is good practice for the pattern matching?
A: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

title: Questions and answers: PageRank, supernode, relationship
text:
Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What is good practice for the PageRank?
A: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the supernode?
A: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

Q: What is good practice for the supernode?
A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: Why does the relationship matter?
A: Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship?
A: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

Q: What is good practice for the relationship?
A: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: Why does the transaction matter?
A: It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

Q: What is good practice for the transaction?
A: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

title: Cypher example: speed up lookups of Server nodes by name
text:
Task: Speed up lookups of Server nodes by name.

```cypher
CREATE INDEX server_name IF NOT EXISTS
FOR (n:Server) ON (n.name)
```

The index lets the database find a Server by name without scanning every Server. IF NOT EXISTS makes the command safe to run again.

title: Questions and answers: node, selectivity, community detection
text:
Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Q: Why does the node matter?
A: Nodes are the anchor points of every query, so a clear choice of what becomes a node shapes the whole model.

Q: What is a selectivity?
A: Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Q: Why does the selectivity matter?
A: The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

Q: What is a community detection?
A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Q: Why does the community detection matter?
A: It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the community detection?
A: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

Q: What is good practice for the community detection?
A: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

Q: What is a relationship direction?
A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Q: Why does the relationship direction matter?
A: A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship direction?
A: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

title: Cypher example: show the Device nodes whose logins is above 500 in the fraud detection graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Device nodes whose logins is above 500 in the fraud detection graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Device)
WHERE n.logins > 500
RETURN n.name AS name, n.logins AS logins
ORDER BY n.logins DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Device nodes above the threshold. An index on Device(logins) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Troubleshooting: the planner reports a cartesian product warning
text:
Symptom: In a knowledge base graph, the planner reports a cartesian product warning.

Likely cause: two patterns in the same MATCH are not connected to each other. This is easy to hit when queries start from Article nodes and follow REFERENCES relationships from Article to Article.

How to fix it: connect the patterns with a relationship or split them into separate clauses on purpose.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:
Symptom: In a e-commerce graph, a query runs out of memory.

Likely cause: a variable-length pattern has no upper bound and expands through most of the graph. This is easy to hit when queries start from Category nodes and follow REVIEWED relationships from Customer to Product.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:
A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes. Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

A team modeling fraud detection data with Account, Transaction, Device will meet the traversal as soon as they need to know which merchants receive money from many new accounts.

A frequent problem: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Recommended practice: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

text:

title: Understanding the graph projection in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: make sure a Factory named Osaka Line is linked to a Part named Motor R9, without creating duplicates

title: Cypher example: find how closely ORD-1003 and ORD-1002 are connected in the e-commerce graph

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 MEMBER_OF hops of a Person called Hiro
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 4 MEMBER_OF hops of a Person called Hiro.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Hiro'})-[:MEMBER_OF*1..4]-(b)

```

The expression *1..4 allows paths of one to 4 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Cypher example: find every Genre that can be reached from a Person in two steps, first through ACTED_IN and then through IN_GENRE
text:

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: $name})-[:ACTED_IN]->(:Movie)-[:IN_GENRE]->(c:Genre)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Genre nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'Cold Harbor' could be passed as $name.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:
An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning. Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

title: Understanding the relationship in graph databases
text:
A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties. Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

A frequent problem: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

Recommended practice: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

title: Cypher example: find which Person nodes have the most MEMBER_OF relationships to Group nodes
text:
Task: Find which Person nodes have the most MEMBER_OF relationships to Group nodes.

```cypher

RETURN a.name AS name, count(b) AS total
ORDER BY total DESC
LIMIT 5
```

The query counts the Group nodes reached from each Person, sorts the counts from high to low and keeps the top five.

text:

title: Cypher example: find how closely Ohio Plant and Osaka Line are connected in the supply chain graph
text:

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(

)

```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..4 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

text:

Q: What is a aggregation?
A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Q: Why does the aggregation matter?
A: It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?
A: A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Q: Why does the uniqueness constraint matter?
A: It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the uniqueness constraint?
A: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

Q: What is good practice for the uniqueness constraint?
A: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: Why does the transaction matter?
A: It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the transaction?
A: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

title: Understanding the aggregation in graph databases

title: Understanding the MERGE in graph databases
text:

title: Understanding the relationship direction in graph databases
text:

title: Questions and answers: path, label, graph projection
text:

A: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

Q: What is a label?
A: A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the label?
A: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

Q: What is good practice for the label?
A: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: Why does the graph projection matter?
A: It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the graph projection?
A: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

Q: What is good practice for the graph projection?
A: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the pattern matching?
A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: find how closely Gdansk Site and Pune Works are connected in the supply chain graph

title: Cypher example: find how closely Central Store and East Yard are connected in the supply chain graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Central Store and East Yard are connected in the supply chain graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Warehouse {name: 'Central Store'})-[*..4]-(b:Warehouse {name: 'East Yard'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..4 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: show the Warehouse nodes whose stock is above 1000 in the supply chain graph, highest first

```cypher
WHERE n.stock > 1000
RETURN n.name AS name, n.stock AS stock
ORDER BY n.stock DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Warehouse nodes above the threshold. An index on Warehouse(stock) can help when many nodes exist.

text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, results differ every time the import is repeated.

Likely cause: CREATE was used where MERGE was needed, so duplicates accumulate. This is easy to hit when queries start from Transaction nodes and follow AT_MERCHANT relationships from Transaction to Merchant.

How to fix it: switch to MERGE on a unique key and add a uniqueness constraint.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

text:

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 POSTED hops of a Person called Ines
text:

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Ines'})-[:POSTED*1..3]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..3 allows paths of one to 3 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

text:

title: Cypher example: find how closely reports and search are connected in the IT infrastructure graph
text:
Task: Find how closely reports and search are connected in the IT infrastructure graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Service {name: 'reports'})-[*..4]-(b:Service {name: 'search'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..4 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: find every Post that can be reached from a Person in two steps, first through FRIENDS_WITH and then through POSTED
text:


title: Understanding the transaction in graph databases
text:
A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together. It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

Consider a e-commerce model built from Customer, Product, Order. To work out what a customer might like based on similar buyers, you rely directly on the transaction.

A frequent problem: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

It is closely related to the graph projection. A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Recommended practice: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

title: Understanding the path in graph databases
text:
A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node. Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

Consider a fraud detection model built from Account, Transaction, Device. To work out which chains of transfers return to the starting account, you rely directly on the path.

A frequent problem: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

It is closely related to the relationship. A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Recommended practice: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Product named Trail shoes is linked to a Category named Fitness, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Product named Trail shoes is linked to a Category named Fitness, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Product {name: 'Trail shoes'})
MERGE (b:Category {name: 'Fitness'})
MERGE (a)-[:IN_CATEGORY]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Troubleshooting: an algorithm run fails to start
text:

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory

title: Cypher example: find every Part that can be reached from a Shipment in two steps, first through SHIPS_TO and then through STORES
text:
Task: Find every Part that can be reached from a Shipment in two steps, first through SHIPS_TO and then through STORES.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Shipment {name: $name})-[:SHIPS_TO]->(:Warehouse)-[:STORES]->(c:Part)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Part nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'Port Depot' could be passed as $name.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 CONTAINS hops of a Order called ORD-1002
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 4 CONTAINS hops of a Order called ORD-1002.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Order {name: 'ORD-1002'})-[:CONTAINS*1..4]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..4 allows paths of one to 4 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Troubleshooting: an algorithm run fails to start
text:
Symptom: In a movies graph, an algorithm run fails to start.

Likely cause: the projected graph does not fit in the memory that is available. This is easy to hit when queries start from Movie nodes and follow IN_GENRE relationships from Movie to Genre.

How to fix it: project only the needed labels and relationship types, or estimate memory before running.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Omar Haddad and Tom Reyes are connected in the movies graph

text:

A: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

A: Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the index?
A: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

Q: What is good practice for the index?
A: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

title: Questions and answers: aggregation, traversal, community detection
text:

A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Q: What is a traversal?

Q: Why does the traversal matter?

Q: What is a community detection?
A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

A: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

Q: What is good practice for the community detection?
A: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Q: What is good practice for the index?

title: Understanding the variable-length path in graph databases
text:
A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum. It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

A team modeling movies data with Person, Movie, Genre will meet the variable-length path as soon as they need to know how many movies two people have in common.

A frequent problem: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Recommended practice: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

title: Cypher example: find every Part that can be reached from a Shipment in two steps, first through SHIPS_TO and then through STORES

```cypher
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Part nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'SHP-31' could be passed as $name.

title: Understanding the relationship in graph databases
text:

A team modeling fraud detection data with Account, Transaction, Device will meet the relationship as soon as they need to know which chains of transfers return to the starting account.

A frequent problem: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

Recommended practice: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

title: Troubleshooting: an algorithm run fails to start
text:

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the transaction?

A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

A: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: Why does the relationship matter?
A: Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

title: Cypher example: show the Server nodes whose cpu_cores is above 10 in the IT infrastructure graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Server nodes whose cpu_cores is above 10 in the IT infrastructure graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Server)
WHERE n.cpu_cores > 10
RETURN n.name AS name, n.cpu_cores AS cpu_cores
ORDER BY n.cpu_cores DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Server nodes above the threshold. An index on Server(cpu_cores) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Understanding the aggregation in graph databases
text:

A frequent problem: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

Recommended practice: Aggregate as late as possible and limit the size of collected lists.

title: Cypher example: list every Category connected to a given Product through IN_CATEGORY in the e-commerce graph
text:
Task: List every Category connected to a given Product through IN_CATEGORY in the e-commerce graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Product {name: $name})-[:IN_CATEGORY]->(b:Category)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Product found by name, follows outgoing IN_CATEGORY relationships, and returns the name of each Category reached. The value of $name, for example 'Wireless mouse', is passed as a parameter.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 POSTED hops of a Person called Farid
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 2 POSTED hops of a Person called Farid.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Farid'})-[:POSTED*1..2]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Troubleshooting: an algorithm run fails to start
text:
Symptom: In a e-commerce graph, an algorithm run fails to start.

Likely cause: the projected graph does not fit in the memory that is available. This is easy to hit when queries start from Order nodes and follow CONTAINS relationships from Order to Product.

How to fix it: project only the needed labels and relationship types, or estimate memory before running.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Person named Maya Lin is linked to a Movie named Cold Harbor, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Person named Maya Lin is linked to a Movie named Cold Harbor, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Person {name: 'Maya Lin'})
MERGE (b:Movie {name: 'Cold Harbor'})
MERGE (a)-[:ACTED_IN]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:

title: Cypher example: find how closely Jonas and Farid are connected in the social network graph
text:

```cypher
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..4 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Understanding the variable-length path in graph databases
text:
A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum. It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

A frequent problem: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

title: Cypher example: find every Account that can be reached from a Account in two steps, first through SENT and then through RECEIVED_BY
text:

```cypher
MATCH (a:Account {name: $name})-[:SENT]->(:Transaction)-[:RECEIVED_BY]->(c:Account)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Account nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'ACC-205' could be passed as $name.

title: Cypher example: find how closely SHP-31 and SHP-34 are connected in the supply chain graph

```cypher
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 PRODUCES hops of a Factory called Osaka Line

title: Troubleshooting: an algorithm run fails to start
text:

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the graph projection in graph databases
text:
A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms. It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

Consider a knowledge base model built from Article, Topic, Author. To work out which tags appear together on the same article, you rely directly on the graph projection.

A frequent problem: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

Recommended practice: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In a knowledge base graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

Likely cause: the first step scans every node of a label because no index supports the filter. This is easy to hit when queries start from Article nodes and follow WROTE relationships from Author to Article.

How to fix it: create an index on the filtered property and confirm with PROFILE that the scan is gone.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the aggregation in graph databases
text:
Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists. It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

A team modeling movies data with Person, Movie, Genre will meet the aggregation as soon as they need to know how many movies two people have in common.

A frequent problem: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

It is closely related to the MERGE. MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Recommended practice: Aggregate as late as possible and limit the size of collected lists.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Product named Yoga mat is linked to a Category named Sports, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Product named Yoga mat is linked to a Category named Sports, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Product {name: 'Yoga mat'})
MERGE (b:Category {name: 'Sports'})
MERGE (a)-[:IN_CATEGORY]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:
An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning. Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

A team modeling fraud detection data with Account, Transaction, Device will meet the index as soon as they need to know which accounts share a device.

A frequent problem: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

title: Understanding the variable-length path in graph databases

title: Cypher example: find how closely Osaka Line and Pune Works are connected in the supply chain graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Osaka Line and Pune Works are connected in the supply chain graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Factory {name: 'Osaka Line'})-[*..5]-(b:Factory {name: 'Pune Works'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

text:

A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query plan?
A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

Q: What is a property?

Q: What is good practice for the property?
A: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

Q: Why does the path matter?

A: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Transaction {name: $name})-[:AT_MERCHANT]->(b:Merchant)
```

title: Cypher example: show the Person nodes whose born is above 250 in the movies graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Person nodes whose born is above 250 in the movies graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Person)
WHERE n.born > 250
RETURN n.name AS name, n.born AS born
ORDER BY n.born DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Person nodes above the threshold. An index on Person(born) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Troubleshooting: an algorithm run fails to start
text:
Symptom: In a social network graph, an algorithm run fails to start.

Likely cause: the projected graph does not fit in the memory that is available. This is easy to hit when queries start from Post nodes and follow FRIENDS_WITH relationships from Person to Person.

How to fix it: project only the needed labels and relationship types, or estimate memory before running.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find every Server that can be reached from a Team in two steps, first through OWNS and then through RUNS_ON
text:
Task: Find every Server that can be reached from a Team in two steps, first through OWNS and then through RUNS_ON.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Team {name: $name})-[:OWNS]->(:Service)-[:RUNS_ON]->(c:Server)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Server nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'notifier' could be passed as $name.

title: Cypher example: list every Product connected to a given Order through CONTAINS in the e-commerce graph
text:
Task: List every Product connected to a given Order through CONTAINS in the e-commerce graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Order {name: $name})-[:CONTAINS]->(b:Product)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Order found by name, follows outgoing CONTAINS relationships, and returns the name of each Product reached. The value of $name, for example 'ORD-1004', is passed as a parameter.

title: Questions and answers: query plan, uniqueness constraint, shortest path
text:
Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

A: It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

A: It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

title: Cypher example: add a new Customer and connect it to a Order with a PLACED relationship

title: Troubleshooting: the planner reports a cartesian product warning
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, the planner reports a cartesian product warning.

Likely cause: two patterns in the same MATCH are not connected to each other. This is easy to hit when queries start from Team nodes and follow RUNS_ON relationships from Service to Server.

title: Questions and answers: full-text index, query plan, PageRank
text:
Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the full-text index?
A: Using a regular index for substring search gives poor results and slow scans.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query plan?
A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: What is good practice for the PageRank?
A: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the transaction?
A: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Q: What is good practice for the variable-length path?
A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Person named Farid is linked to a Person named Hiro, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Person named Farid is linked to a Person named Hiro, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Person {name: 'Farid'})
MERGE (b:Person {name: 'Hiro'})

```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

A: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Cypher example: show the Person nodes whose age is above 10 in the social network graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Person nodes whose age is above 10 in the social network graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Person)
WHERE n.age > 10
RETURN n.name AS name, n.age AS age
ORDER BY n.age DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Person nodes above the threshold. An index on Person(age) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Modeling a movies domain as a graph
text:
Goal: represent movies data so that connection questions are fast to answer.

Node labels: Person, Movie, Genre.

Properties:
- Person: name, born
- Movie: name, year
- Genre: name, titles

Relationships:
- (:Person)-[:ACTED_IN]->(:Movie)
- (:Person)-[:DIRECTED]->(:Movie)
- (:Movie)-[:IN_GENRE]->(:Genre)

Questions this model answers:

- Which genres a given actor appears in most
- How many movies two people have in common

Suggested setup: create a uniqueness constraint on the name of each label and an index on any property used in filters. A relational design can also store this data, but each extra hop in these questions would need another join.

title: Troubleshooting: an algorithm run fails to start
text:
Symptom: In a e-commerce graph, an algorithm run fails to start.

Likely cause: the projected graph does not fit in the memory that is available. This is easy to hit when queries start from Product nodes and follow CONTAINS relationships from Order to Product.

How to fix it: project only the needed labels and relationship types, or estimate memory before running.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find how closely ACC-201 and ACC-206 are connected in the fraud detection graph
text:
Task: Find how closely ACC-201 and ACC-206 are connected in the fraud detection graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Account {name: 'ACC-201'})-[*..4]-(b:Account {name: 'ACC-206'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..4 stops the search from growing without limit.

Q: What is a traversal?

Q: What is a query parameter?

Q: What is a path?

title: Questions and answers: pattern matching, aggregation, uniqueness constraint
text:

A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

A: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

Q: What is a aggregation?
A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the aggregation?
A: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?
A: A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 REVIEWED hops of a Customer called Amara
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 3 REVIEWED hops of a Customer called Amara.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Customer {name: 'Amara'})-[:REVIEWED*1..3]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..3 allows paths of one to 3 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.


title: Cypher example: find how closely Port Depot and Port Depot are connected in the supply chain graph

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, results differ every time the import is repeated.

Likely cause: CREATE was used where MERGE was needed, so duplicates accumulate. This is easy to hit when queries start from Device nodes and follow SENT relationships from Account to Transaction.

How to fix it: switch to MERGE on a unique key and add a uniqueness constraint.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Troubleshooting: the planner reports a cartesian product warning
text:
Symptom: In a social network graph, the planner reports a cartesian product warning.

Likely cause: two patterns in the same MATCH are not connected to each other. This is easy to hit when queries start from Group nodes and follow MEMBER_OF relationships from Person to Group.

How to fix it: connect the patterns with a relationship or split them into separate clauses on purpose.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: find every Database that can be reached from a Team in two steps, first through OWNS and then through USES
text:
Task: Find every Database that can be reached from a Team in two steps, first through OWNS and then through USES.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Team {name: $name})-[:OWNS]->(:Service)-[:USES]->(c:Database)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Database nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'Payments' could be passed as $name.

title: Understanding the MERGE in graph databases
text:
MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat. It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

A frequent problem: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 PRODUCES hops of a Factory called Ohio Plant
text:

```cypher
MATCH (a:Factory {name: 'Ohio Plant'})-[:PRODUCES*1..3]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..3 allows paths of one to 3 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Cypher example: find how closely SHP-33 and SHP-31 are connected in the supply chain graph
text:
Task: Find how closely SHP-33 and SHP-31 are connected in the supply chain graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Shipment {name: 'SHP-33'})-[*..5]-(b:Shipment {name: 'SHP-31'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Questions and answers: traversal, variable-length path, node
text:
Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: Why does the traversal matter?
A: Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Q: What is good practice for the variable-length path?
A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the node?
A: A common mistake is storing a repeating group of values inside one node instead of giving each its own node.

Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: Why does the full-text index matter?
A: It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

Q: What is good practice for the full-text index?
A: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: Why does the shortest path matter?
A: It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

Q: What is good practice for the shortest path?
A: Set a maximum depth and check that both endpoints are indexed.

title: Questions and answers: community detection, traversal, transaction
text:

A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Q: Why does the community detection matter?
A: It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

Q: What is good practice for the community detection?
A: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: Why does the traversal matter?
A: Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

A: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Q: What is good practice for the traversal?
A: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: Why does the transaction matter?
A: It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

A: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

A: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What is good practice for the supernode?
A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

Q: What is a pattern matching?

A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In a supply chain graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

Likely cause: the first step scans every node of a label because no index supports the filter. This is easy to hit when queries start from Factory nodes and follow PRODUCES relationships from Factory to Part.

How to fix it: create an index on the filtered property and confirm with PROFILE that the scan is gone.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Security basics and Index tuning are connected in the knowledge base graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Security basics and Index tuning are connected in the knowledge base graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Article {name: 'Security basics'})-[*..5]-(b:Article {name: 'Index tuning'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: show the Tag nodes whose uses is above 500 in the knowledge base graph, highest first
text:

```cypher
MATCH (n:Tag)
WHERE n.uses > 500
RETURN n.name AS name, n.uses AS uses
ORDER BY n.uses DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Tag nodes above the threshold. An index on Tag(uses) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Questions and answers: path, relationship, community detection
text:
Q: What is a path?
A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: Why does the path matter?
A: Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

Q: What is good practice for the path?
A: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: Why does the relationship matter?
A: Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

Q: What is good practice for the relationship?
A: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

Q: What is a community detection?
A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the community detection?
A: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the pattern matching?
A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Q: What is good practice for the variable-length path?
A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

title: Understanding the transaction in graph databases
text:
A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together. It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

Consider a fraud detection model built from Account, Transaction, Device. To work out which accounts share a device, you rely directly on the transaction.

It is closely related to the index. An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:
A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes. Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

A frequent problem: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

It is closely related to the query plan. A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Recommended practice: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:

title: Cypher example: make sure a Shipment named SHP-31 is linked to a Part named Gear A12, without creating duplicates

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 PLACED hops of a Customer called Yuki
text:

```cypher
MATCH (a:Customer {name: 'Yuki'})-[:PLACED*1..2]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Cypher example: show the Server nodes whose cpu_cores is above 1000 in the IT infrastructure graph, highest first
text:
