title: Cypher example: show the Part nodes whose cost is above 20 in the supply chain graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Part nodes whose cost is above 20 in the supply chain graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Part)
WHERE n.cost > 20
RETURN n.name AS name, n.cost AS cost
ORDER BY n.cost DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Part nodes above the threshold. An index on Part(cost) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Understanding the relationship direction in graph databases
text:
Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it. A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

In a movies graph with Person, Movie, Genre nodes, the idea of a relationship direction appears when you ask which genres a given actor appears in most.

A frequent problem: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

Recommended practice: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Amara and Lucas are connected in the e-commerce graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Amara and Lucas are connected in the e-commerce graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Customer {name: 'Amara'})-[*..5]-(b:Customer {name: 'Lucas'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Understanding the query plan in graph databases
text:
A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query. Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

A team modeling movies data with Person, Movie, Genre will meet the query plan as soon as they need to know which actors worked with the same director.

A frequent problem: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

Recommended practice: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Person named Ben is linked to a Person named Jonas, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Person named Ben is linked to a Person named Jonas, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Person {name: 'Ben'})
MERGE (b:Person {name: 'Jonas'})
MERGE (a)-[:FRIENDS_WITH]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Troubleshooting: the planner reports a cartesian product warning
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, the planner reports a cartesian product warning.

Likely cause: two patterns in the same MATCH are not connected to each other. This is easy to hit when queries start from Transaction nodes and follow SENT relationships from Account to Transaction.

How to fix it: connect the patterns with a relationship or split them into separate clauses on purpose.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: speed up lookups of Product nodes by name
text:
Task: Speed up lookups of Product nodes by name.

```cypher
CREATE INDEX product_name IF NOT EXISTS
FOR (n:Product) ON (n.name)
```

The index lets the database find a Product by name without scanning every Product. IF NOT EXISTS makes the command safe to run again.

title: Understanding the path in graph databases
text:
A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node. Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

title: Understanding the aggregation in graph databases
text:
Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists. It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

A team modeling movies data with Person, Movie, Genre will meet the aggregation as soon as they need to know how many movies two people have in common.

A frequent problem: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

It is closely related to the transaction. A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Recommended practice: Aggregate as late as possible and limit the size of collected lists.

text:

A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

A: It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the graph projection?
A: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

A: Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

A: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

Q: What is good practice for the index?
A: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Q: What is good practice for the variable-length path?
A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases
text:
A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels. Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

A team modeling fraud detection data with Account, Transaction, Device will meet the label as soon as they need to know which merchants receive money from many new accounts.

A frequent problem: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

It is closely related to the supernode. A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Recommended practice: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

title: Cypher example: find every Genre that can be reached from a Person in two steps, first through DIRECTED and then through IN_GENRE
text:
Task: Find every Genre that can be reached from a Person in two steps, first through DIRECTED and then through IN_GENRE.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: $name})-[:DIRECTED]->(:Movie)-[:IN_GENRE]->(c:Genre)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Genre nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'Victor Hale' could be passed as $name.

title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:
A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph. Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Consider a fraud detection model built from Account, Transaction, Device. To work out which merchants receive money from many new accounts, you rely directly on the supernode.

A frequent problem: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

It is closely related to the full-text index. A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Recommended practice: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:
A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes. Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

In a e-commerce graph with Customer, Product, Order nodes, the idea of a traversal appears when you ask what a customer might like based on similar buyers.

A frequent problem: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

It is closely related to the selectivity. Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Recommended practice: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Understanding the uniqueness constraint in graph databases
text:
A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property. It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

Consider a supply chain model built from Factory, Warehouse, Shipment. To work out which shipments carry parts from several factories, you rely directly on the uniqueness constraint.

A frequent problem: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

Recommended practice: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

title: Cypher example: add a new Person and connect it to a Movie with a DIRECTED relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Person and connect it to a Movie with a DIRECTED relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Person {name: 'Sara Cole'})-[:DIRECTED]->(b:Movie {name: 'Last Lantern'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In a movies graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 TAGGED hops of a Article called Security basics
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 2 TAGGED hops of a Article called Security basics.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Article {name: 'Security basics'})-[:TAGGED*1..2]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

text:

```cypher
MATCH (n:Movie)
WHERE n.year > 50
RETURN n.name AS name, n.year AS year
ORDER BY n.year DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Movie nodes above the threshold. An index on Movie(year) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Cypher example: find how closely ACC-205 and ACC-205 are connected in the fraud detection graph
text:

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Questions and answers: variable-length path, supernode, community detection
text:

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

title: Questions and answers: transaction, graph projection, MERGE
text:
Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: Why does the transaction matter?

Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the graph projection?
A: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: Why does the MERGE matter?
A: It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Q: Why does the index matter?
A: Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the index?
A: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

title: Understanding the property in graph databases
text:

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 TAGGED hops of a Article called Index tuning

title: Cypher example: find how closely TX-9005 and TX-9004 are connected in the fraud detection graph

```cypher
)
```

title: Understanding the aggregation in graph databases

text:

In a knowledge base graph with Article, Topic, Author nodes, the idea of a graph projection appears when you ask which articles are most referenced by others.

A frequent problem: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

It is closely related to the community detection. Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Recommended practice: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

title: Cypher example: add a new Movie and connect it to a Genre with a IN_GENRE relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Movie and connect it to a Genre with a IN_GENRE relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Movie {name: 'Last Lantern'})-[:IN_GENRE]->(b:Genre {name: 'Romance'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Understanding the uniqueness constraint in graph databases
text:
A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property. It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

Consider a movies model built from Person, Movie, Genre. To work out which genres a given actor appears in most, you rely directly on the uniqueness constraint.

A frequent problem: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

It is closely related to the PageRank. PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Recommended practice: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

title: Questions and answers: node, path, label
text:
Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Q: Why does the node matter?
A: Nodes are the anchor points of every query, so a clear choice of what becomes a node shapes the whole model.

Q: What is good practice for the node?
A: Give every node at least one label and a stable identifying property.

Q: What is a path?
A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: What is good practice for the path?
A: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

Q: What is a label?
A: A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Q: Why does the label matter?
A: Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the label?
A: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: Why does the MERGE matter?
A: It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the MERGE?
A: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

Q: What is good practice for the MERGE?
A: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

title: Understanding the variable-length path in graph databases
text:
A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum. It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

A team modeling social network data with Person, Post, Group will meet the variable-length path as soon as they need to know which groups a user's friends have joined.

A frequent problem: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Recommended practice: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

title: Understanding the query plan in graph databases
text:
A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query. Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Consider a social network model built from Person, Post, Group. To work out which posts are liked by the most people, you rely directly on the query plan.

A frequent problem: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

It is closely related to the supernode. A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Recommended practice: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:
A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes. Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

A team modeling movies data with Person, Movie, Genre will meet the traversal as soon as they need to know which genres a given actor appears in most.

A frequent problem: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

It is closely related to the uniqueness constraint. A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Recommended practice: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Questions and answers: transaction, community detection, shortest path
text:
Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the transaction?
A: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

Q: What is good practice for the transaction?
A: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

Q: What is a community detection?
A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Q: Why does the community detection matter?
A: It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

Q: What is good practice for the community detection?
A: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: Why does the shortest path matter?
A: It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is a property?
A: A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the property?
A: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

Q: What is good practice for the property?
A: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

title: Questions and answers: pattern matching, query plan, PageRank
text:
Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the pattern matching matter?
A: It lets you express a multi-hop question in a single line instead of a chain of joins.

Q: What is a query plan?

Q: Why does the query plan matter?

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: What is good practice for the PageRank?
A: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Q: Why does the index matter?
A: Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the index?
A: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

Q: What is good practice for the index?
A: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

title: Troubleshooting: an import fails with a constraint violation
text:

title: Cypher example: find every Transaction that can be reached from a Transaction in two steps, first through RECEIVED_BY and then through SENT
text:
Task: Find every Transaction that can be reached from a Transaction in two steps, first through RECEIVED_BY and then through SENT.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Transaction {name: $name})-[:RECEIVED_BY]->(:Account)-[:SENT]->(c:Transaction)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Transaction nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'TX-9004' could be passed as $name.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 IN_GENRE hops of a Movie called Iron Tide
text:

text:

title: Questions and answers: aggregation, supernode, query parameter
text:
Q: What is a aggregation?
A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Q: Why does the aggregation matter?
A: It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

Q: What is good practice for the aggregation?
A: Aggregate as late as possible and limit the size of collected lists.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

A: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

Q: What is good practice for the supernode?
A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

A: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

Q: What is good practice for the query parameter?
A: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

text:

title: Troubleshooting: one query is much slower for some start nodes than others
text:

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 PLACED hops of a Customer called Noah
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 4 PLACED hops of a Customer called Noah.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Customer {name: 'Noah'})-[:PLACED*1..4]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..4 allows paths of one to 4 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

Likely cause: the first step scans every node of a label because no index supports the filter. This is easy to hit when queries start from Merchant nodes and follow RECEIVED_BY relationships from Transaction to Account.

How to fix it: create an index on the filtered property and confirm with PROFILE that the scan is gone.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Questions and answers: shortest path, relationship, property
text:
Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: Why does the relationship matter?
A: Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

Q: What is a property?
A: A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the property?
A: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

Q: What is a LOAD CSV?
A: LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the LOAD CSV matter?
A: It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the LOAD CSV?
A: Running it without a constraint and without batching makes the import slow and error-prone.

Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Q: Why does the index matter?
A: Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

title: Cypher example: show the Person nodes whose age is above 20 in the social network graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Person nodes whose age is above 20 in the social network graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Person)
WHERE n.age > 20
RETURN n.name AS name, n.age AS age
ORDER BY n.age DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Person nodes above the threshold. An index on Person(age) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Understanding the community detection in graph databases
text:
Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest. It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

In a knowledge base graph with Article, Topic, Author nodes, the idea of a community detection appears when you ask which topics an author covers.

A frequent problem: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

Recommended practice: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Espresso maker and Espresso maker are connected in the e-commerce graph
text:

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(

)

```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:

Recommended practice: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Account named ACC-201 is linked to a Device named DEV-B2, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Account named ACC-201 is linked to a Device named DEV-B2, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Account {name: 'ACC-201'})
MERGE (b:Device {name: 'DEV-B2'})
MERGE (a)-[:USED_DEVICE]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Understanding the PageRank in graph databases
text:
PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them. It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

A frequent problem: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Recommended practice: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

text:

title: Cypher example: find every Product that can be reached from a Customer in two steps, first through PLACED and then through CONTAINS

title: Understanding the pattern matching in graph databases
text:

A frequent problem: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:

The pattern starts from one Shipment found by name, follows outgoing CONTAINS_PART relationships, and returns the name of each Part reached. The value of $name, for example 'SHP-33', is passed as a parameter.

title: Understanding the LOAD CSV in graph databases
text:
LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships. It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

In a movies graph with Person, Movie, Genre nodes, the idea of a LOAD CSV appears when you ask which actors worked with the same director.

A frequent problem: Running it without a constraint and without batching makes the import slow and error-prone.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 PLACED hops of a Customer called Marcus
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 4 PLACED hops of a Customer called Marcus.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Customer {name: 'Marcus'})-[:PLACED*1..4]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..4 allows paths of one to 4 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Questions and answers: index, graph projection, LOAD CSV
text:
Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the index?
A: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

Q: What is good practice for the index?
A: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: Why does the graph projection matter?
A: It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

Q: What is good practice for the graph projection?
A: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

Q: What is a LOAD CSV?
A: LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the LOAD CSV matter?
A: It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

Q: What is good practice for the LOAD CSV?
A: Create constraints first and process the file in batches.

Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is good practice for the shortest path?
A: Set a maximum depth and check that both endpoints are indexed.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Q: What is good practice for the variable-length path?
A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

title: Understanding the shortest path in graph databases
text:
A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships. It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

A team modeling IT infrastructure data with Server, Service, Database will meet the shortest path as soon as they need to know which team owns the services that depend on a given database.

A frequent problem: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Recommended practice: Set a maximum depth and check that both endpoints are indexed.

title: Understanding the relationship direction in graph databases
text:
Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it. A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

Consider a fraud detection model built from Account, Transaction, Device. To work out which accounts share a device, you rely directly on the relationship direction.

A frequent problem: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

It is closely related to the query parameter. A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Recommended practice: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 IN_GENRE hops of a Movie called Paper Moon
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 2 IN_GENRE hops of a Movie called Paper Moon.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Movie {name: 'Paper Moon'})-[:IN_GENRE*1..2]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

Likely cause: a large transaction holds locks on nodes that other writers need. This is easy to hit when queries start from Server nodes and follow USES relationships from Service to Database.

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Questions and answers: path, relationship, variable-length path
text:

A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the path?
A: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

Q: What is good practice for the path?
A: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: Why does the relationship matter?
A: Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: What is good practice for the variable-length path?
A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the full-text index?
A: Using a regular index for substring search gives poor results and slow scans.

title: Cypher example: add a new Article and connect it to a Tag with a TAGGED relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Article and connect it to a Tag with a TAGGED relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Article {name: 'Getting started'})-[:TAGGED]->(b:Tag {name: 'advanced'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Understanding the pattern matching in graph databases
text:
Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships. It lets you express a multi-hop question in a single line instead of a chain of joins.

Consider a movies model built from Person, Movie, Genre. To work out which genres a given actor appears in most, you rely directly on the pattern matching.

A frequent problem: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

It is closely related to the graph projection. A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Recommended practice: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

title: Understanding the uniqueness constraint in graph databases
text:
A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property. It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

In a social network graph with Person, Post, Group nodes, the idea of a uniqueness constraint appears when you ask which posts are liked by the most people.

A frequent problem: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

Recommended practice: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:

A team modeling knowledge base data with Article, Topic, Author will meet the traversal as soon as they need to know which articles are most referenced by others.

A frequent problem: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Recommended practice: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Understanding the MERGE in graph databases

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:

title: Cypher example: show the Person nodes whose age is above 500 in the social network graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Person nodes whose age is above 500 in the social network graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Person)
WHERE n.age > 500
RETURN n.name AS name, n.age AS age
ORDER BY n.age DESC
LIMIT 10
```

title: Cypher example: find how closely ORD-1002 and ORD-1004 are connected in the e-commerce graph
text:
Task: Find how closely ORD-1002 and ORD-1004 are connected in the e-commerce graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Order {name: 'ORD-1002'})-[*..6]-(b:Order {name: 'ORD-1004'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Understanding the selectivity in graph databases
text:
Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few. The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

text:

A frequent problem: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

It is closely related to the aggregation. Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Recommended practice: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 RECEIVED_BY hops of a Transaction called TX-9002
text:

title: Understanding the query plan in graph databases
text:

title: Understanding the community detection in graph databases
text:

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Person {name: 'Asha'})-[*..6]-(b:Person {name: 'Carla'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Understanding the query parameter in graph databases
text:
A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text. Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

In a social network graph with Person, Post, Group nodes, the idea of a query parameter appears when you ask which groups a user's friends have joined.

A frequent problem: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

It is closely related to the selectivity. Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Recommended practice: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

title: Questions and answers: path, transaction, query plan
text:
Q: What is a path?
A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the path?
A: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

Q: What is good practice for the path?
A: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: Why does the transaction matter?
A: It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the transaction?
A: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

Q: What is good practice for the transaction?
A: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Q: What is good practice for the PageRank?
A: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

Q: What is a property?
A: A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the property?
A: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

Q: What is good practice for the property?
A: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

title: Understanding the MERGE in graph databases
text:
MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat. It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

In a fraud detection graph with Account, Transaction, Device nodes, the idea of a MERGE appears when you ask which accounts share a device.

A frequent problem: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

It is closely related to the relationship direction. Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Recommended practice: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

title: Understanding the relationship direction in graph databases
text:
Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it. A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

A team modeling social network data with Person, Post, Group will meet the relationship direction as soon as they need to know which posts are liked by the most people.

A frequent problem: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

It is closely related to the variable-length path. A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Recommended practice: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

title: Questions and answers: traversal, pattern matching, relationship direction
text:
Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the traversal?
A: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Q: What is good practice for the traversal?
A: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the pattern matching?
A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

Q: What is a relationship direction?
A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Q: Why does the relationship direction matter?
A: A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship direction?
A: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the supernode?
A: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

Q: What is good practice for the supernode?
A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 ACTED_IN hops of a Person called Sara Cole
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 3 ACTED_IN hops of a Person called Sara Cole.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Sara Cole'})-[:ACTED_IN*1..3]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..3 allows paths of one to 3 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Person named Sara Cole is linked to a Movie named Night Train, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Person named Sara Cole is linked to a Movie named Night Train, without creating duplicates.


Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:
Symptom: In a movies graph, results differ every time the import is repeated.

Likely cause: CREATE was used where MERGE was needed, so duplicates accumulate. This is easy to hit when queries start from Movie nodes and follow ACTED_IN relationships from Person to Movie.

How to fix it: switch to MERGE on a unique key and add a uniqueness constraint.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Troubleshooting: an import fails with a constraint violation
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, an import fails with a constraint violation.

How to fix it: deduplicate the input or use MERGE on the unique key.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:

title: Understanding the query plan in graph databases
text:

title: Understanding the selectivity in graph databases
text:
Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few. The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

In a supply chain graph with Factory, Warehouse, Shipment nodes, the idea of a selectivity appears when you ask which parts depend on a single factory.

A frequent problem: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

Recommended practice: Anchor queries on unique or nearly unique properties.

title: Understanding the relationship direction in graph databases
text:
Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it. A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

In an IT infrastructure graph with Server, Service, Database nodes, the idea of a relationship direction appears when you ask which services are affected if a server fails.

A frequent problem: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

It is closely related to the relationship. A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Recommended practice: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

title: Cypher example: find which Article nodes have the most TAGGED relationships to Tag nodes
text:
Task: Find which Article nodes have the most TAGGED relationships to Tag nodes.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Article)-[:TAGGED]->(b:Tag)
RETURN a.name AS name, count(b) AS total
ORDER BY total DESC
LIMIT 5
```

The query counts the Tag nodes reached from each Article, sorts the counts from high to low and keeps the top five.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases
text:
A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels. Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

Consider a social network model built from Person, Post, Group. To work out which groups a user's friends have joined, you rely directly on the label.

A frequent problem: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

title: Understanding the community detection in graph databases
text:
Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest. It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

Consider a e-commerce model built from Customer, Product, Order. To work out which products are often bought together, you rely directly on the community detection.

A frequent problem: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

It is closely related to the pattern matching. Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Recommended practice: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, results differ every time the import is repeated.

Likely cause: CREATE was used where MERGE was needed, so duplicates accumulate. This is easy to hit when queries start from Merchant nodes and follow USED_DEVICE relationships from Account to Device.

How to fix it: switch to MERGE on a unique key and add a uniqueness constraint.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Questions and answers: uniqueness constraint, transaction, full-text index
text:
Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?
A: A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the uniqueness constraint?
A: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

Q: What is good practice for the uniqueness constraint?
A: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: Why does the full-text index matter?
A: It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the full-text index?
A: Using a regular index for substring search gives poor results and slow scans.

Q: What is good practice for the full-text index?
A: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the supernode?
A: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

Q: What is good practice for the supernode?
A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Questions and answers: query parameter, PageRank, MERGE
text:
Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Q: What is good practice for the query parameter?
A: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: Why does the MERGE matter?
A: It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the MERGE?
A: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

title: Cypher example: show the Part nodes whose cost is above 500 in the supply chain graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Part nodes whose cost is above 500 in the supply chain graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Part)
WHERE n.cost > 500
RETURN n.name AS name, n.cost AS cost
ORDER BY n.cost DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Part nodes above the threshold. An index on Part(cost) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:
An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning. Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

A frequent problem: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

It is closely related to the supernode. A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Recommended practice: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

title: Understanding the graph projection in graph databases
text:
A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms. It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

Consider a e-commerce model built from Customer, Product, Order. To work out which products are often bought together, you rely directly on the graph projection.

A frequent problem: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

Recommended practice: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

title: Understanding the transaction in graph databases
text:
A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together. It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

A team modeling e-commerce data with Customer, Product, Order will meet the transaction as soon as they need to know what a customer might like based on similar buyers.

A frequent problem: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

Recommended practice: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

title: Cypher example: speed up lookups of Article nodes by name
text:
Task: Speed up lookups of Article nodes by name.

```cypher
CREATE INDEX article_name IF NOT EXISTS
FOR (n:Article) ON (n.name)
```

The index lets the database find a Article by name without scanning every Article. IF NOT EXISTS makes the command safe to run again.

```cypher
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 RECEIVED_BY hops of a Transaction called TX-9001
text:

text:

title: Cypher example: make sure a Person named Ines is linked to a Post named Travel diary, without creating duplicates

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Understanding the selectivity in graph databases
text:
Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few. The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

title: Understanding the property in graph databases
text:

A frequent problem: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

title: Understanding the PageRank in graph databases
text:

Consider a fraud detection model built from Account, Transaction, Device. To work out which accounts share a device, you rely directly on the PageRank.

A frequent problem: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Recommended practice: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases
text:

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:
Symptom: In a supply chain graph, results differ every time the import is repeated.

Likely cause: CREATE was used where MERGE was needed, so duplicates accumulate. This is easy to hit when queries start from Warehouse nodes and follow CONTAINS_PART relationships from Shipment to Part.

How to fix it: switch to MERGE on a unique key and add a uniqueness constraint.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 RECEIVED_BY hops of a Transaction called TX-9001
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 2 RECEIVED_BY hops of a Transaction called TX-9001.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Transaction {name: 'TX-9001'})-[:RECEIVED_BY*1..2]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Jonas and Grace are connected in the social network graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Jonas and Grace are connected in the social network graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Person {name: 'Jonas'})-[*..6]-(b:Person {name: 'Grace'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:

Recommended practice: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Cypher example: find how closely S. Okafor and M. Costa are connected in the knowledge base graph
text:

title: Questions and answers: query parameter, variable-length path, MERGE
text:
Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query parameter?
A: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

Q: What is good practice for the query parameter?
A: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Q: What is good practice for the variable-length path?
A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the MERGE?
A: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

Q: What is good practice for the MERGE?
A: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In a social network graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

Likely cause: the first step scans every node of a label because no index supports the filter. This is easy to hit when queries start from Group nodes and follow MEMBER_OF relationships from Person to Group.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find every Device that can be reached from a Transaction in two steps, first through RECEIVED_BY and then through USED_DEVICE
text:
Task: Find every Device that can be reached from a Transaction in two steps, first through RECEIVED_BY and then through USED_DEVICE.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Transaction {name: $name})-[:RECEIVED_BY]->(:Account)-[:USED_DEVICE]->(c:Device)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Device nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'ACC-205' could be passed as $name.

title: Understanding the relationship in graph databases
text:
A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties. Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

A team modeling movies data with Person, Movie, Genre will meet the relationship as soon as they need to know which genres a given actor appears in most.

A frequent problem: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

Recommended practice: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

title: Understanding the transaction in graph databases

title: Cypher example: make sure a Service named notifier is linked to a Database named users-db, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Service named notifier is linked to a Database named users-db, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Service {name: 'notifier'})
MERGE (b:Database {name: 'users-db'})
MERGE (a)-[:USES]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Cypher example: list every Person connected to a given Person through FRIENDS_WITH in the social network graph
text:
Task: List every Person connected to a given Person through FRIENDS_WITH in the social network graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: $name})-[:FRIENDS_WITH]->(b:Person)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Person found by name, follows outgoing FRIENDS_WITH relationships, and returns the name of each Person reached. The value of $name, for example 'Farid', is passed as a parameter.

title: Questions and answers: index, shortest path, traversal
text:
Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Q: Why does the index matter?
A: Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the index?
A: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

Q: What is good practice for the index?
A: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: Why does the shortest path matter?
A: It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: Why does the traversal matter?
A: Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the traversal?
A: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

A: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Cypher example: show the Warehouse nodes whose stock is above 500 in the supply chain graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Warehouse nodes whose stock is above 500 in the supply chain graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Warehouse)
WHERE n.stock > 500
RETURN n.name AS name, n.stock AS stock
ORDER BY n.stock DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Warehouse nodes above the threshold. An index on Warehouse(stock) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Cold Harbor and Paper Moon are connected in the movies graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Cold Harbor and Paper Moon are connected in the movies graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Movie {name: 'Cold Harbor'})-[*..4]-(b:Movie {name: 'Paper Moon'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..4 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Understanding the pattern matching in graph databases
text:
Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships. It lets you express a multi-hop question in a single line instead of a chain of joins.

In a knowledge base graph with Article, Topic, Author nodes, the idea of a pattern matching appears when you ask which articles are most referenced by others.

A frequent problem: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

It is closely related to the node. A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Recommended practice: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

title: Troubleshooting: an import fails with a constraint violation
text:
Symptom: In a movies graph, an import fails with a constraint violation.

Likely cause: the file contains two rows with the same value for a unique property. This is easy to hit when queries start from Genre nodes and follow DIRECTED relationships from Person to Movie.

How to fix it: deduplicate the input or use MERGE on the unique key.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the selectivity in graph databases
text:
Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few. The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

Consider a fraud detection model built from Account, Transaction, Device. To work out which merchants receive money from many new accounts, you rely directly on the selectivity.

A frequent problem: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

It is closely related to the variable-length path. A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Recommended practice: Anchor queries on unique or nearly unique properties.

title: Cypher example: add a new Product and connect it to a Category with a IN_CATEGORY relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Product and connect it to a Category with a IN_CATEGORY relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Product {name: 'Notebook set'})-[:IN_CATEGORY]->(b:Category {name: 'Kitchen'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 ACTED_IN hops of a Person called Lena Park
text:

title: Questions and answers: PageRank, relationship direction, variable-length path
text:

A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: What is a relationship direction?
A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:
Symptom: In a knowledge base graph, a query runs out of memory.

Likely cause: a variable-length pattern has no upper bound and expands through most of the graph. This is easy to hit when queries start from Topic nodes and follow ABOUT relationships from Article to Topic.

How to fix it: set a maximum depth, filter early and return only the properties you need.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find how closely auth-api and billing are connected in the IT infrastructure graph
text:
Task: Find how closely auth-api and billing are connected in the IT infrastructure graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Service {name: 'auth-api'})-[*..5]-(b:Service {name: 'billing'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Understanding the path in graph databases
text:
A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node. Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

In a e-commerce graph with Customer, Product, Order nodes, the idea of a path appears when you ask what a customer might like based on similar buyers.

A frequent problem: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

It is closely related to the uniqueness constraint. A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Recommended practice: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

title: Understanding the pattern matching in graph databases
text:
Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships. It lets you express a multi-hop question in a single line instead of a chain of joins.

Consider a supply chain model built from Factory, Warehouse, Shipment. To work out which shipments carry parts from several factories, you rely directly on the pattern matching.

A frequent problem: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

It is closely related to the label. A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Recommended practice: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

title: Questions and answers: shortest path, supernode, traversal
text:
Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the traversal?
A: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Q: What is good practice for the traversal?
A: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the transaction?
A: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

Q: What is good practice for the transaction?
A: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: What is good practice for the graph projection?
A: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

title: Questions and answers: uniqueness constraint, property, index
text:
Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?
A: A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Q: Why does the uniqueness constraint matter?
A: It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the uniqueness constraint?
A: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

Q: What is good practice for the uniqueness constraint?
A: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

Q: What is a property?
A: A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Q: Why does the property matter?
A: Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the property?
A: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Q: Why does the index matter?
A: Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the index?
A: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Service named notifier is linked to a Server named srv-edge-01, without creating duplicates

A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

A: It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: Why does the traversal matter?
A: Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the traversal?
A: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Q: What is good practice for the traversal?
A: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Q: What is good practice for the variable-length path?
A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

title: Cypher example: list every Post connected to a given Person through LIKES in the social network graph
text:
Task: List every Post connected to a given Person through LIKES in the social network graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: $name})-[:LIKES]->(b:Post)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Person found by name, follows outgoing LIKES relationships, and returns the name of each Post reached. The value of $name, for example 'Carla', is passed as a parameter.

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:
Symptom: In a social network graph, results differ every time the import is repeated.

Likely cause: CREATE was used where MERGE was needed, so duplicates accumulate. This is easy to hit when queries start from Post nodes and follow LIKES relationships from Person to Post.

How to fix it: switch to MERGE on a unique key and add a uniqueness constraint.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases
text:
A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels. Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

In a e-commerce graph with Customer, Product, Order nodes, the idea of a label appears when you ask what a customer might like based on similar buyers.

A frequent problem: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

It is closely related to the path. A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Recommended practice: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:
