A team modeling knowledge base data with Article, Topic, Author will meet the index as soon as they need to know which articles are most referenced by others.

Recommended practice: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

title: Questions and answers: relationship, traversal, supernode
text:
Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

A: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

Q: What is good practice for the relationship?
A: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

A: Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

Q: What is good practice for the traversal?
A: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the supernode?
A: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

Q: What is good practice for the supernode?
A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the transaction?
A: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

A: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

title: Understanding the LOAD CSV in graph databases

title: Cypher example: find every Article that can be reached from a Article in two steps, first through REFERENCES and then through REFERENCES
text:
Task: Find every Article that can be reached from a Article in two steps, first through REFERENCES and then through REFERENCES.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Article {name: $name})-[:REFERENCES]->(:Article)-[:REFERENCES]->(c:Article)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Article nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'M. Costa' could be passed as $name.

title: Cypher example: find how closely TX-9002 and TX-9004 are connected in the fraud detection graph
text:
Task: Find how closely TX-9002 and TX-9004 are connected in the fraud detection graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Transaction {name: 'TX-9002'})-[*..4]-(b:Transaction {name: 'TX-9004'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..4 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:

title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:
A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph. Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

In a e-commerce graph with Customer, Product, Order nodes, the idea of a supernode appears when you ask what a customer might like based on similar buyers.

A frequent problem: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

Recommended practice: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

Q: What is a selectivity?

text:

title: Cypher example: find every Database that can be reached from a Team in two steps, first through OWNS and then through USES
text:

title: Cypher example: find how closely Ohio Plant and Pune Works are connected in the supply chain graph

```cypher
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 USED_DEVICE hops of a Account called ACC-201

text:

title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:

title: Troubleshooting: one query is much slower for some start nodes than others
text:

title: Cypher example: add a new Person and connect it to a Movie with a DIRECTED relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Person and connect it to a Movie with a DIRECTED relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Person {name: 'Maya Lin'})-[:DIRECTED]->(b:Movie {name: 'Night Train'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases

title: Understanding the shortest path in graph databases

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:

title: Understanding the query plan in graph databases
text:

A frequent problem: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

title: Cypher example: find every Database that can be reached from a Team in two steps, first through OWNS and then through USES
text:
Task: Find every Database that can be reached from a Team in two steps, first through OWNS and then through USES.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Team {name: $name})-[:OWNS]->(:Service)-[:USES]->(c:Database)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Database nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'reports' could be passed as $name.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Team named Data is linked to a Service named auth-api, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Team named Data is linked to a Service named auth-api, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Team {name: 'Data'})
MERGE (b:Service {name: 'auth-api'})
MERGE (a)-[:OWNS]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the property?
A: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

Q: What is good practice for the property?
A: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 REVIEWED hops of a Customer called Fatima
text:

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

Likely cause: a large transaction holds locks on nodes that other writers need. This is easy to hit when queries start from Team nodes and follow DEPENDS_ON relationships from Service to Service.

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the community detection in graph databases
text:
Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest. It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

A team modeling IT infrastructure data with Server, Service, Database will meet the community detection as soon as they need to know which team owns the services that depend on a given database.

A frequent problem: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

It is closely related to the LOAD CSV. LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Recommended practice: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Understanding the property in graph databases
text:
A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price. Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

A team modeling social network data with Person, Post, Group will meet the property as soon as they need to know who are the friends of friends of a user.

A frequent problem: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

It is closely related to the variable-length path. A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:
A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes. Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

In a fraud detection graph with Account, Transaction, Device nodes, the idea of a traversal appears when you ask which chains of transfers return to the starting account.

A frequent problem: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

It is closely related to the label. A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Recommended practice: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In a social network graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

Likely cause: the first step scans every node of a label because no index supports the filter. This is easy to hit when queries start from Post nodes and follow FRIENDS_WITH relationships from Person to Person.

How to fix it: create an index on the filtered property and confirm with PROFILE that the scan is gone.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Troubleshooting: an algorithm run fails to start
text:
Symptom: In a knowledge base graph, an algorithm run fails to start.

Likely cause: the projected graph does not fit in the memory that is available. This is easy to hit when queries start from Article nodes and follow WROTE relationships from Author to Article.

How to fix it: project only the needed labels and relationship types, or estimate memory before running.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Person named Grace is linked to a Person named Elena, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Person named Grace is linked to a Person named Elena, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Person {name: 'Grace'})
MERGE (b:Person {name: 'Elena'})
MERGE (a)-[:FRIENDS_WITH]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Troubleshooting: the planner reports a cartesian product warning

title: Modeling a e-commerce domain as a graph
text:
Goal: represent e-commerce data so that connection questions are fast to answer.

Node labels: Customer, Product, Order, Category.

Properties:
- Customer: name, age
- Product: name, price
- Order: name, total
- Category: name, items

Relationships:
- (:Customer)-[:PLACED]->(:Order)
- (:Order)-[:CONTAINS]->(:Product)
- (:Product)-[:IN_CATEGORY]->(:Category)
- (:Customer)-[:REVIEWED]->(:Product)

Questions this model answers:
- Which products are often bought together
- What a customer might like based on similar buyers
- Which categories drive the most repeat orders

Suggested setup: create a uniqueness constraint on the name of each label and an index on any property used in filters. A relational design can also store this data, but each extra hop in these questions would need another join.

text:


The constraint rejects a second Factory with the same name and also provides an index for lookups.

title: Troubleshooting: an algorithm run fails to start
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, an algorithm run fails to start.

Likely cause: the projected graph does not fit in the memory that is available. This is easy to hit when queries start from Merchant nodes and follow SENT relationships from Account to Transaction.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Service {name: $name})-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(:Service)-[:USES]->(c:Database)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Database nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'gateway' could be passed as $name.

title: Questions and answers: query parameter, selectivity, relationship direction
text:
Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query parameter?
A: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

Q: What is good practice for the query parameter?
A: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

Q: What is a selectivity?
A: Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Q: Why does the selectivity matter?
A: The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the selectivity?
A: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

Q: What is a relationship direction?
A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Q: What is good practice for the relationship direction?
A: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

title: Questions and answers: node, variable-length path, query parameter
text:

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the node?

Q: What is good practice for the node?

A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

title: Understanding the graph projection in graph databases
text:
A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms. It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

In an IT infrastructure graph with Server, Service, Database nodes, the idea of a graph projection appears when you ask which services are affected if a server fails.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In a e-commerce graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

Likely cause: a large transaction holds locks on nodes that other writers need. This is easy to hit when queries start from Product nodes and follow CONTAINS relationships from Order to Product.

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the aggregation in graph databases
text:
Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists. It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

In a movies graph with Person, Movie, Genre nodes, the idea of a aggregation appears when you ask which actors worked with the same director.

A frequent problem: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

Recommended practice: Aggregate as late as possible and limit the size of collected lists.

title: Troubleshooting: the planner reports a cartesian product warning
text:

How to fix it: connect the patterns with a relationship or split them into separate clauses on purpose.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:
A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph. Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Consider a knowledge base model built from Article, Topic, Author. To work out which topics an author covers, you rely directly on the supernode.

A frequent problem: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

It is closely related to the shortest path. A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Recommended practice: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Cypher example: add a new Account and connect it to a Device with a USED_DEVICE relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Account and connect it to a Device with a USED_DEVICE relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Account {name: 'ACC-206'})-[:USED_DEVICE]->(b:Device {name: 'DEV-C3'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

Likely cause: the first step scans every node of a label because no index supports the filter. This is easy to hit when queries start from Merchant nodes and follow AT_MERCHANT relationships from Transaction to Merchant.

How to fix it: create an index on the filtered property and confirm with PROFILE that the scan is gone.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Questions and answers: node, MERGE, shortest path
text:
Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Q: Why does the node matter?
A: Nodes are the anchor points of every query, so a clear choice of what becomes a node shapes the whole model.

Q: What is good practice for the node?
A: Give every node at least one label and a stable identifying property.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: Why does the MERGE matter?
A: It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is good practice for the shortest path?
A: Set a maximum depth and check that both endpoints are indexed.

Q: What is a label?
A: A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the label?
A: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: Why does the graph projection matter?
A: It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the graph projection?
A: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

Q: What is good practice for the graph projection?
A: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:
An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning. Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

In an IT infrastructure graph with Server, Service, Database nodes, the idea of a index appears when you ask which team owns the services that depend on a given database.

A frequent problem: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

It is closely related to the shortest path. A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Recommended practice: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

title: Understanding the uniqueness constraint in graph databases
text:
A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property. It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

In a e-commerce graph with Customer, Product, Order nodes, the idea of a uniqueness constraint appears when you ask what a customer might like based on similar buyers.

A frequent problem: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

It is closely related to the MERGE. MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Recommended practice: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

title: Questions and answers: variable-length path, uniqueness constraint, path
text:
Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What is good practice for the variable-length path?
A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?
A: A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Q: Why does the uniqueness constraint matter?
A: It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the uniqueness constraint?
A: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

Q: What is a path?
A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the path?
A: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

title: Questions and answers: query plan, community detection, node
text:
Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

Q: What is a community detection?
A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Q: Why does the community detection matter?
A: It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Q: Why does the node matter?
A: Nodes are the anchor points of every query, so a clear choice of what becomes a node shapes the whole model.

title: Questions and answers: query parameter, pattern matching, property
text:
Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query parameter?
A: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the pattern matching matter?
A: It lets you express a multi-hop question in a single line instead of a chain of joins.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the pattern matching?
A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

Q: What is good practice for the pattern matching?
A: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

Q: What is a property?
A: A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

title: Understanding the relationship in graph databases
text:
A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties. Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

In a knowledge base graph with Article, Topic, Author nodes, the idea of a relationship appears when you ask which topics an author covers.

A frequent problem: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

It is closely related to the shortest path. A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Recommended practice: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

title: Cypher example: find every Topic that can be reached from a Article in two steps, first through REFERENCES and then through ABOUT
text:
Task: Find every Topic that can be reached from a Article in two steps, first through REFERENCES and then through ABOUT.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Article {name: $name})-[:REFERENCES]->(:Article)-[:ABOUT]->(c:Topic)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Topic nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'L. Weber' could be passed as $name.

title: Questions and answers: MERGE, traversal, supernode
text:
Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the MERGE?
A: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

Q: What is good practice for the MERGE?
A: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the traversal?
A: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the supernode?
A: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

Q: What is good practice for the supernode?
A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

Q: What is a relationship direction?
A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship direction?
A: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

title: Understanding the shortest path in graph databases
text:
A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships. It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

A team modeling IT infrastructure data with Server, Service, Database will meet the shortest path as soon as they need to know which team owns the services that depend on a given database.

A frequent problem: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

title: Understanding the PageRank in graph databases
text:
PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them. It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

A team modeling social network data with Person, Post, Group will meet the PageRank as soon as they need to know who are the friends of friends of a user.

A frequent problem: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Recommended practice: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

title: Understanding the transaction in graph databases
text:
A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together. It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

A team modeling e-commerce data with Customer, Product, Order will meet the transaction as soon as they need to know which products are often bought together.

A frequent problem: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

Recommended practice: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Getting started and Security basics are connected in the knowledge base graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Getting started and Security basics are connected in the knowledge base graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Article {name: 'Getting started'})-[*..6]-(b:Article {name: 'Security basics'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 SHIPS_TO hops of a Shipment called SHP-33
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 2 SHIPS_TO hops of a Shipment called SHP-33.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Shipment {name: 'SHP-33'})-[:SHIPS_TO*1..2]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Author named S. Okafor is linked to a Article named Getting started, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Author named S. Okafor is linked to a Article named Getting started, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Author {name: 'S. Okafor'})
MERGE (b:Article {name: 'Getting started'})
MERGE (a)-[:WROTE]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Understanding the full-text index in graph databases
text:
A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking. It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

A team modeling e-commerce data with Customer, Product, Order will meet the full-text index as soon as they need to know which products are often bought together.

A frequent problem: Using a regular index for substring search gives poor results and slow scans.

Recommended practice: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

title: Cypher example: list every Database connected to a given Service through USES in the IT infrastructure graph
text:
Task: List every Database connected to a given Service through USES in the IT infrastructure graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Service {name: $name})-[:USES]->(b:Database)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Service found by name, follows outgoing USES relationships, and returns the name of each Database reached. The value of $name, for example 'search', is passed as a parameter.

title: Understanding the pattern matching in graph databases
text:

title: Understanding the MERGE in graph databases
text:

title: Understanding the shortest path in graph databases

title: Cypher example: make sure a Shipment named SHP-33 is linked to a Part named Motor R9, without creating duplicates

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 RUNS_ON hops of a Service called billing
text:

```cypher
MATCH (a:Service {name: 'billing'})-[:RUNS_ON*1..2]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

title: Understanding the graph projection in graph databases

title: Questions and answers: node, traversal, variable-length path
text:

Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

A: Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

Q: What is good practice for the traversal?
A: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?

A: Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

A: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

Q: What is good practice for the property?
A: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

title: Understanding the query plan in graph databases
text:

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, a query runs out of memory.

Likely cause: a variable-length pattern has no upper bound and expands through most of the graph. This is easy to hit when queries start from Service nodes and follow OWNS relationships from Team to Service.

How to fix it: set a maximum depth, filter early and return only the properties you need.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find how closely ACC-206 and ACC-202 are connected in the fraud detection graph
text:

```cypher
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

text:

title: Questions and answers: selectivity, transaction, traversal
text:

Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

text:

title: Understanding the transaction in graph databases
text:
A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together. It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

A team modeling supply chain data with Factory, Warehouse, Shipment will meet the transaction as soon as they need to know how a delay at one warehouse affects shipments.

A frequent problem: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

It is closely related to the supernode. A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Recommended practice: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

title: Understanding the PageRank in graph databases
text:
PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them. It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Consider a movies model built from Person, Movie, Genre. To work out how many movies two people have in common, you rely directly on the PageRank.

A frequent problem: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

It is closely related to the traversal. A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Recommended practice: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

title: Understanding the selectivity in graph databases
text:
Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few. The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

In a e-commerce graph with Customer, Product, Order nodes, the idea of a selectivity appears when you ask which categories drive the most repeat orders.

A frequent problem: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

It is closely related to the PageRank. PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Recommended practice: Anchor queries on unique or nearly unique properties.

title: Understanding the query plan in graph databases
text:
A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query. Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

A team modeling supply chain data with Factory, Warehouse, Shipment will meet the query plan as soon as they need to know which parts depend on a single factory.

A frequent problem: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

It is closely related to the transaction. A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Recommended practice: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

title: Understanding the pattern matching in graph databases

title: Troubleshooting: an algorithm run fails to start
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, an algorithm run fails to start.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:

title: Questions and answers: index, node, relationship
text:

A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Q: Why does the index matter?
A: Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the index?
A: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

Q: What is good practice for the index?
A: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship?
A: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

Q: What is a aggregation?
A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

A: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

Q: What is a supernode?

text:

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

Likely cause: the first step scans every node of a label because no index supports the filter. This is easy to hit when queries start from Account nodes and follow USED_DEVICE relationships from Account to Device.

How to fix it: create an index on the filtered property and confirm with PROFILE that the scan is gone.

title: Questions and answers: supernode, graph projection, MERGE
text:

A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: Why does the graph projection matter?
A: It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the graph projection?
A: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: What is good practice for the MERGE?
A: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

Q: What is a query plan?

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

title: Understanding the query parameter in graph databases
text:
A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text. Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Consider a knowledge base model built from Article, Topic, Author. To work out which topics an author covers, you rely directly on the query parameter.

A frequent problem: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

Recommended practice: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

title: Understanding the aggregation in graph databases
text:
Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists. It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

Consider a knowledge base model built from Article, Topic, Author. To work out which topics an author covers, you rely directly on the aggregation.

A frequent problem: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

It is closely related to the selectivity. Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Recommended practice: Aggregate as late as possible and limit the size of collected lists.

title: Understanding the relationship in graph databases
text:
A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties. Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

In a knowledge base graph with Article, Topic, Author nodes, the idea of a relationship appears when you ask which articles are most referenced by others.

A frequent problem: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

Recommended practice: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

title: Understanding the uniqueness constraint in graph databases
text:
A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property. It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

Consider a e-commerce model built from Customer, Product, Order. To work out which products are often bought together, you rely directly on the uniqueness constraint.

A frequent problem: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

It is closely related to the shortest path. A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Recommended practice: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

title: Questions and answers: label, pattern matching, LOAD CSV
text:
Q: What is a label?
A: A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Q: Why does the label matter?
A: Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

Q: What is good practice for the label?
A: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the pattern matching matter?
A: It lets you express a multi-hop question in a single line instead of a chain of joins.

Q: What is good practice for the pattern matching?
A: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

Q: What is a LOAD CSV?
A: LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the LOAD CSV matter?
A: It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

Q: What is good practice for the LOAD CSV?
A: Create constraints first and process the file in batches.

title: Understanding the query plan in graph databases
text:

A team modeling knowledge base data with Article, Topic, Author will meet the query plan as soon as they need to know which articles are most referenced by others.

A frequent problem: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

Recommended practice: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

title: Understanding the graph projection in graph databases
text:
A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms. It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

In an IT infrastructure graph with Server, Service, Database nodes, the idea of a graph projection appears when you ask which team owns the services that depend on a given database.

A frequent problem: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

Recommended practice: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

title: Understanding the property in graph databases
text:
A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price. Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

text:

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: add a new Account and connect it to a Device with a USED_DEVICE relationship
text:

```cypher
CREATE (a:Account {name: 'ACC-202'})-[:USED_DEVICE]->(b:Device {name: 'DEV-B2'})
```

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows

title: Cypher example: find which Service nodes have the most USES relationships to Database nodes
text:

```cypher
MATCH (a:Service)-[:USES]->(b:Database)
RETURN a.name AS name, count(b) AS total

LIMIT 5
```

The query counts the Database nodes reached from each Service, sorts the counts from high to low and keeps the top five.

title: Understanding the aggregation in graph databases
text:
Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists. It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

Consider a supply chain model built from Factory, Warehouse, Shipment. To work out which parts depend on a single factory, you rely directly on the aggregation.

A frequent problem: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

Recommended practice: Aggregate as late as possible and limit the size of collected lists.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Transaction named TX-9003 is linked to a Account named ACC-206, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Transaction named TX-9003 is linked to a Account named ACC-206, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Transaction {name: 'TX-9003'})
MERGE (b:Account {name: 'ACC-206'})
MERGE (a)-[:RECEIVED_BY]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Cypher example: find every Device that can be reached from a Transaction in two steps, first through RECEIVED_BY and then through USED_DEVICE
text:
Task: Find every Device that can be reached from a Transaction in two steps, first through RECEIVED_BY and then through USED_DEVICE.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Transaction {name: $name})-[:RECEIVED_BY]->(:Account)-[:USED_DEVICE]->(c:Device)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Device nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'TX-9001' could be passed as $name.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In a movies graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

Likely cause: a large transaction holds locks on nodes that other writers need. This is easy to hit when queries start from Person nodes and follow DIRECTED relationships from Person to Movie.

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 IN_CATEGORY hops of a Product called Espresso maker
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 2 IN_CATEGORY hops of a Product called Espresso maker.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Product {name: 'Espresso maker'})-[:IN_CATEGORY*1..2]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Questions and answers: selectivity, index, variable-length path
text:
Q: What is a selectivity?
A: Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the selectivity?
A: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Q: Why does the index matter?
A: Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the index?
A: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

Q: What is good practice for the index?
A: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

title: Questions and answers: graph projection, relationship direction, MERGE
text:
Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: What is good practice for the graph projection?
A: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

Q: What is a relationship direction?
A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Q: Why does the relationship direction matter?
A: A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

Q: What is good practice for the relationship direction?
A: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the MERGE?
A: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

Q: What is a aggregation?
A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the aggregation?
A: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

title: Questions and answers: pattern matching, path, MERGE
text:
Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the pattern matching?
A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

Q: What is good practice for the pattern matching?
A: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

Q: What is a path?
A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: Why does the MERGE matter?
A: It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

Q: What is good practice for the MERGE?
A: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Q: What is good practice for the PageRank?
A: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

title: Questions and answers: query plan, shortest path, relationship
text:
Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: Why does the relationship matter?
A: Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship?
A: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Customer named Marcus is linked to a Order named ORD-1005, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Customer named Marcus is linked to a Order named ORD-1005, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Customer {name: 'Marcus'})
MERGE (b:Order {name: 'ORD-1005'})
MERGE (a)-[:PLACED]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Lena Park and Maya Lin are connected in the movies graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Lena Park and Maya Lin are connected in the movies graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Person {name: 'Lena Park'})-[*..4]-(b:Person {name: 'Maya Lin'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..4 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Troubleshooting: the planner reports a cartesian product warning
text:
Symptom: In a e-commerce graph, the planner reports a cartesian product warning.

Likely cause: two patterns in the same MATCH are not connected to each other. This is easy to hit when queries start from Category nodes and follow CONTAINS relationships from Order to Product.

How to fix it: connect the patterns with a relationship or split them into separate clauses on purpose.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: list every Service connected to a given Service through DEPENDS_ON in the IT infrastructure graph
text:
Task: List every Service connected to a given Service through DEPENDS_ON in the IT infrastructure graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Service {name: $name})-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(b:Service)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Service found by name, follows outgoing DEPENDS_ON relationships, and returns the name of each Service reached. The value of $name, for example 'billing', is passed as a parameter.

title: Understanding the community detection in graph databases
text:
Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest. It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

In a social network graph with Person, Post, Group nodes, the idea of a community detection appears when you ask which groups a user's friends have joined.

A frequent problem: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

Recommended practice: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Understanding the transaction in graph databases
text:
A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together. It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

In an IT infrastructure graph with Server, Service, Database nodes, the idea of a transaction appears when you ask which team owns the services that depend on a given database.

A frequent problem: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

Recommended practice: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

title: Cypher example: show the Article nodes whose views is above 10 in the knowledge base graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Article nodes whose views is above 10 in the knowledge base graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Article)
WHERE n.views > 10
RETURN n.name AS name, n.views AS views
ORDER BY n.views DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Article nodes above the threshold. An index on Article(views) can help when many nodes exist.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the transaction in graph databases
text:
A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together. It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

In a knowledge base graph with Article, Topic, Author nodes, the idea of a transaction appears when you ask which tags appear together on the same article.

A frequent problem: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

It is closely related to the variable-length path. A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Recommended practice: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, results differ every time the import is repeated.

Likely cause: CREATE was used where MERGE was needed, so duplicates accumulate. This is easy to hit when queries start from Account nodes and follow USED_DEVICE relationships from Account to Device.

How to fix it: switch to MERGE on a unique key and add a uniqueness constraint.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:
A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph. Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

In a fraud detection graph with Account, Transaction, Device nodes, the idea of a supernode appears when you ask which chains of transfers return to the starting account.

A frequent problem: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

Recommended practice: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Jonas and Elena are connected in the social network graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Jonas and Elena are connected in the social network graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Person {name: 'Jonas'})-[*..5]-(b:Person {name: 'Elena'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:
An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning. Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

Consider a knowledge base model built from Article, Topic, Author. To work out which tags appear together on the same article, you rely directly on the index.

A frequent problem: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

Recommended practice: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

title: Cypher example: list every Order connected to a given Customer through PLACED in the e-commerce graph
text:
Task: List every Order connected to a given Customer through PLACED in the e-commerce graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Customer {name: $name})-[:PLACED]->(b:Order)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Customer found by name, follows outgoing PLACED relationships, and returns the name of each Order reached. The value of $name, for example 'Yuki', is passed as a parameter.

title: Questions and answers: selectivity, PageRank, relationship
text:
Q: What is a selectivity?
A: Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Q: Why does the selectivity matter?
A: The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Q: What is good practice for the PageRank?
A: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: Why does the relationship matter?
A: Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship?
A: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the traversal?
A: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Q: What is good practice for the traversal?
A: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Cypher example: find every Server that can be reached from a Service in two steps, first through DEPENDS_ON and then through RUNS_ON
text:
Task: Find every Server that can be reached from a Service in two steps, first through DEPENDS_ON and then through RUNS_ON.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Service {name: $name})-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(:Service)-[:RUNS_ON]->(c:Server)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Server nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'gateway' could be passed as $name.

title: Cypher example: add a new Person and connect it to a Post with a LIKES relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Person and connect it to a Post with a LIKES relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Person {name: 'Grace'})-[:LIKES]->(b:Post {name: 'Book review'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Understanding the graph projection in graph databases
text:
A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms. It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

Consider a supply chain model built from Factory, Warehouse, Shipment. To work out which shipments carry parts from several factories, you rely directly on the graph projection.

A frequent problem: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

Recommended practice: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In a knowledge base graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

Likely cause: the first step scans every node of a label because no index supports the filter. This is easy to hit when queries start from Tag nodes and follow WROTE relationships from Author to Article.

How to fix it: create an index on the filtered property and confirm with PROFILE that the scan is gone.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Troubleshooting: one query is much slower for some start nodes than others
text:

Likely cause: a few nodes have a huge number of relationships. This is easy to hit when queries start from Order nodes and follow PLACED relationships from Customer to Order.

How to fix it: avoid traversing through hub nodes or filter on a relationship property before expanding.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the LOAD CSV in graph databases
text:

A frequent problem: Running it without a constraint and without batching makes the import slow and error-prone.

It is closely related to the label. A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Recommended practice: Create constraints first and process the file in batches.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Shipment named SHP-34 is linked to a Part named Gear A12, without creating duplicates

title: Cypher example: list every Movie connected to a given Person through ACTED_IN in the movies graph
text:

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: $name})-[:ACTED_IN]->(b:Movie)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Person found by name, follows outgoing ACTED_IN relationships, and returns the name of each Movie reached. The value of $name, for example 'Tom Reyes', is passed as a parameter.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:
An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning. Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

A team modeling e-commerce data with Customer, Product, Order will meet the index as soon as they need to know which products are often bought together.

A frequent problem: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

It is closely related to the shortest path. A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Recommended practice: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Service named auth-api is linked to a Server named srv-edge-01, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Service named auth-api is linked to a Server named srv-edge-01, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Service {name: 'auth-api'})
MERGE (b:Server {name: 'srv-edge-01'})
MERGE (a)-[:RUNS_ON]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In a supply chain graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

Likely cause: a large transaction holds locks on nodes that other writers need. This is easy to hit when queries start from Warehouse nodes and follow STORES relationships from Warehouse to Part.

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:
A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph. Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

A team modeling supply chain data with Factory, Warehouse, Shipment will meet the supernode as soon as they need to know how a delay at one warehouse affects shipments.

A frequent problem: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

It is closely related to the PageRank. PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Recommended practice: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Understanding the path in graph databases
text:
A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node. Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

In a movies graph with Person, Movie, Genre nodes, the idea of a path appears when you ask which genres a given actor appears in most.

A frequent problem: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

Recommended practice: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

title: Understanding the query parameter in graph databases
text:
A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text. Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

A frequent problem: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

Recommended practice: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:

title: Questions and answers: LOAD CSV, property, label
text:

A: LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the LOAD CSV matter?
A: It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

A: Create constraints first and process the file in batches.

Q: What is a property?
A: A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Q: What is a label?
A: A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Q: Why does the label matter?
A: Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

A: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

Q: What is good practice for the label?
A: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the traversal?
A: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Q: Why does the node matter?
A: Nodes are the anchor points of every query, so a clear choice of what becomes a node shapes the whole model.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the node?
A: A common mistake is storing a repeating group of values inside one node instead of giving each its own node.

Q: What is good practice for the node?
A: Give every node at least one label and a stable identifying property.

title: Understanding the PageRank in graph databases
text:

title: Understanding the community detection in graph databases
text:
Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest. It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

A frequent problem: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

Recommended practice: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 REVIEWED hops of a Customer called Lucas
text:

Consider a knowledge base model built from Article, Topic, Author. To work out which tags appear together on the same article, you rely directly on the property.

A frequent problem: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

Likely cause: a large transaction holds locks on nodes that other writers need. This is easy to hit when queries start from Transaction nodes and follow RECEIVED_BY relationships from Transaction to Account.

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Victor Hale and Nora Quinn are connected in the movies graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Victor Hale and Nora Quinn are connected in the movies graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Person {name: 'Victor Hale'})-[*..6]-(b:Person {name: 'Nora Quinn'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Questions and answers: community detection, aggregation, relationship
text:
Q: What is a community detection?
A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Q: Why does the community detection matter?
A: It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

Q: What is good practice for the community detection?
A: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

Q: What is a aggregation?
A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Q: Why does the aggregation matter?
A: It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the aggregation?
A: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

Q: What is good practice for the aggregation?
A: Aggregate as late as possible and limit the size of collected lists.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship?
A: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

Q: What is good practice for the relationship?
A: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

title: Understanding the LOAD CSV in graph databases

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 USED_DEVICE hops of a Account called ACC-203
