title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 RECEIVED_BY hops of a Transaction called TX-9004
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 4 RECEIVED_BY hops of a Transaction called TX-9004.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Transaction {name: 'TX-9004'})-[:RECEIVED_BY*1..4]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..4 allows paths of one to 4 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Understanding the property in graph databases
text:
A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price. Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

A team modeling fraud detection data with Account, Transaction, Device will meet the property as soon as they need to know which chains of transfers return to the starting account.

A frequent problem: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

Recommended practice: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

title: Cypher example: show the Tag nodes whose uses is above 1000 in the knowledge base graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Tag nodes whose uses is above 1000 in the knowledge base graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Tag)
WHERE n.uses > 1000
RETURN n.name AS name, n.uses AS uses
ORDER BY n.uses DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Tag nodes above the threshold. An index on Tag(uses) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Questions and answers: index, traversal, selectivity
text:
Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the index?
A: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: Why does the traversal matter?
A: Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the traversal?
A: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Q: What is a selectivity?
A: Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Q: Why does the selectivity matter?
A: The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the selectivity?
A: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

title: Understanding the property in graph databases
text:
A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price. Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

Consider an IT infrastructure model built from Server, Service, Database. To work out which services are affected if a server fails, you rely directly on the property.

A frequent problem: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

It is closely related to the supernode. A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Recommended practice: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:
Symptom: In a e-commerce graph, results differ every time the import is repeated.

Likely cause: CREATE was used where MERGE was needed, so duplicates accumulate. This is easy to hit when queries start from Order nodes and follow CONTAINS relationships from Order to Product.

How to fix it: switch to MERGE on a unique key and add a uniqueness constraint.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the uniqueness constraint in graph databases
text:
A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property. It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

A team modeling e-commerce data with Customer, Product, Order will meet the uniqueness constraint as soon as they need to know which products are often bought together.

A frequent problem: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

Recommended practice: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

title: Questions and answers: shortest path, supernode, selectivity
text:
Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: Why does the shortest path matter?
A: It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What is good practice for the supernode?
A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

Q: What is a selectivity?
A: Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Q: Why does the selectivity matter?
A: The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

Q: What is good practice for the selectivity?
A: Anchor queries on unique or nearly unique properties.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: Why does the relationship matter?
A: Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

Q: What is a label?
A: A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Q: Why does the label matter?
A: Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

Q: Why does the transaction matter?

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the uniqueness constraint?
A: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query plan?
A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

title: Understanding the LOAD CSV in graph databases
text:
LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships. It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

In an IT infrastructure graph with Server, Service, Database nodes, the idea of a LOAD CSV appears when you ask which services are affected if a server fails.

A frequent problem: Running it without a constraint and without batching makes the import slow and error-prone.

It is closely related to the node. A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Recommended practice: Create constraints first and process the file in batches.

title: Questions and answers: community detection, PageRank, label
text:
Q: What is a community detection?
A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Q: What is good practice for the community detection?
A: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Q: What is good practice for the PageRank?
A: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

Q: What is a label?
A: A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Q: Why does the label matter?
A: Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the label?
A: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

Q: What is good practice for the label?
A: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Q: Why does the node matter?
A: Nodes are the anchor points of every query, so a clear choice of what becomes a node shapes the whole model.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the node?
A: A common mistake is storing a repeating group of values inside one node instead of giving each its own node.

Q: What is good practice for the node?
A: Give every node at least one label and a stable identifying property.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What is good practice for the supernode?
A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Cypher example: find how closely North Hub and Central Store are connected in the supply chain graph
text:
Task: Find how closely North Hub and Central Store are connected in the supply chain graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Warehouse {name: 'North Hub'})-[*..5]-(b:Warehouse {name: 'Central Store'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: add a new Service and connect it to a Service with a DEPENDS_ON relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Service and connect it to a Service with a DEPENDS_ON relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Service {name: 'auth-api'})-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(b:Service {name: 'auth-api'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Cypher example: find every Post that can be reached from a Person in two steps, first through FRIENDS_WITH and then through POSTED
text:
Task: Find every Post that can be reached from a Person in two steps, first through FRIENDS_WITH and then through POSTED.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: $name})-[:FRIENDS_WITH]->(:Person)-[:POSTED]->(c:Post)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Post nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'Carla' could be passed as $name.

title: Questions and answers: relationship direction, full-text index, variable-length path
text:

A: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: Why does the full-text index matter?
A: It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the full-text index?
A: Using a regular index for substring search gives poor results and slow scans.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What is good practice for the variable-length path?
A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

Q: What is a traversal?

Q: What is good practice for the traversal?
A: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases
text:
A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels. Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

A team modeling fraud detection data with Account, Transaction, Device will meet the label as soon as they need to know which accounts share a device.

A frequent problem: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

It is closely related to the shortest path. A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Recommended practice: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

title: Understanding the path in graph databases
text:

Consider a e-commerce model built from Customer, Product, Order. To work out what a customer might like based on similar buyers, you rely directly on the path.

A frequent problem: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

It is closely related to the variable-length path. A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Recommended practice: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

title: Understanding the pattern matching in graph databases
text:

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:
Symptom: In a knowledge base graph, results differ every time the import is repeated.

How to fix it: switch to MERGE on a unique key and add a uniqueness constraint.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 PLACED hops of a Customer called Lucas
text:

title: Cypher example: find which Account nodes have the most USED_DEVICE relationships to Device nodes
text:

The query counts the Device nodes reached from each Account, sorts the counts from high to low and keeps the top five.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:
An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning. Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

A frequent problem: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

It is closely related to the path. A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

title: Troubleshooting: an import fails with a constraint violation
text:
Symptom: In a supply chain graph, an import fails with a constraint violation.

Likely cause: the file contains two rows with the same value for a unique property. This is easy to hit when queries start from Shipment nodes and follow CONTAINS_PART relationships from Shipment to Part.

How to fix it: deduplicate the input or use MERGE on the unique key.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Last Lantern and Night Train are connected in the movies graph

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

```cypher
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..4 allows paths of one to 4 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Cypher example: add a new Movie and connect it to a Genre with a IN_GENRE relationship

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Cypher example: find how closely ORD-1001 and ORD-1001 are connected in the e-commerce graph

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(

)

```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:
Symptom: In a movies graph, a query runs out of memory.

Likely cause: a variable-length pattern has no upper bound and expands through most of the graph. This is easy to hit when queries start from Person nodes and follow IN_GENRE relationships from Movie to Genre.

How to fix it: set a maximum depth, filter early and return only the properties you need.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 WROTE hops of a Author called R. Iyer
text:

```cypher
MATCH (a:Author {name: 'R. Iyer'})-[:WROTE*1..2]-(b)

```

The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Cypher example: find every Category that can be reached from a Customer in two steps, first through REVIEWED and then through IN_CATEGORY
text:
Task: Find every Category that can be reached from a Customer in two steps, first through REVIEWED and then through IN_CATEGORY.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Customer {name: $name})-[:REVIEWED]->(:Product)-[:IN_CATEGORY]->(c:Category)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Category nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'ORD-1005' could be passed as $name.

title: Troubleshooting: one query is much slower for some start nodes than others
text:

Likely cause: a few nodes have a huge number of relationships. This is easy to hit when queries start from Team nodes and follow DEPENDS_ON relationships from Service to Service.

How to fix it: avoid traversing through hub nodes or filter on a relationship property before expanding.

title: Questions and answers: MERGE, relationship, community detection
text:
Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: Why does the MERGE matter?
A: It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the MERGE?
A: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

Q: What is good practice for the MERGE?
A: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: Why does the relationship matter?
A: Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

Q: What is a community detection?
A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Q: Why does the community detection matter?
A: It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the community detection?
A: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

Q: What is good practice for the community detection?
A: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases
text:
A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels. Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

In a knowledge base graph with Article, Topic, Author nodes, the idea of a label appears when you ask which topics an author covers.

A frequent problem: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

It is closely related to the relationship direction. Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Recommended practice: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:
A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes. Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

A team modeling knowledge base data with Article, Topic, Author will meet the traversal as soon as they need to know which articles are most referenced by others.

A frequent problem: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

It is closely related to the aggregation. Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Recommended practice: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Understanding the relationship in graph databases
text:
A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties. Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

A team modeling IT infrastructure data with Server, Service, Database will meet the relationship as soon as they need to know which services have the longest dependency chains.

A frequent problem: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

It is closely related to the supernode. A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Recommended practice: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

title: Cypher example: show the Movie nodes whose year is above 1000 in the movies graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Movie nodes whose year is above 1000 in the movies graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Movie)
WHERE n.year > 1000
RETURN n.name AS name, n.year AS year
ORDER BY n.year DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Movie nodes above the threshold. An index on Movie(year) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Questions and answers: relationship direction, PageRank, path
text:
Q: What is a relationship direction?
A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Q: Why does the relationship direction matter?
A: A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Q: What is a path?
A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: Why does the path matter?
A: Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

Q: What is good practice for the path?
A: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Q: What is good practice for the variable-length path?
A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

title: Understanding the LOAD CSV in graph databases

A frequent problem: Running it without a constraint and without batching makes the import slow and error-prone.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 CONTAINS hops of a Order called ORD-1002
text:

```cypher
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..3 allows paths of one to 3 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Cypher example: find every Genre that can be reached from a Person in two steps, first through DIRECTED and then through IN_GENRE
text:
Task: Find every Genre that can be reached from a Person in two steps, first through DIRECTED and then through IN_GENRE.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: $name})-[:DIRECTED]->(:Movie)-[:IN_GENRE]->(c:Genre)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Genre nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'Nora Quinn' could be passed as $name.

title: Understanding the PageRank in graph databases
text:

A frequent problem: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Recommended practice: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 ACTED_IN hops of a Person called Maya Lin
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 4 ACTED_IN hops of a Person called Maya Lin.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Maya Lin'})-[:ACTED_IN*1..4]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..4 allows paths of one to 4 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Cypher example: find how closely TX-9003 and TX-9005 are connected in the fraud detection graph
text:
Task: Find how closely TX-9003 and TX-9005 are connected in the fraud detection graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(

)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:
Symptom: In a e-commerce graph, results differ every time the import is repeated.

Likely cause: CREATE was used where MERGE was needed, so duplicates accumulate. This is easy to hit when queries start from Product nodes and follow CONTAINS relationships from Order to Product.

How to fix it: switch to MERGE on a unique key and add a uniqueness constraint.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the uniqueness constraint in graph databases
text:

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the MERGE in graph databases

title: Cypher example: show the Genre nodes whose titles is above 100 in the movies graph, highest first
text:

```cypher
WHERE n.titles > 100
```

title: Understanding the query plan in graph databases
text:
A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query. Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

A team modeling fraud detection data with Account, Transaction, Device will meet the query plan as soon as they need to know which merchants receive money from many new accounts.

Recommended practice: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

title: Understanding the relationship in graph databases
text:
A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties. Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

A frequent problem: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

Recommended practice: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

title: Understanding the shortest path in graph databases
text:
A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships. It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

Consider a e-commerce model built from Customer, Product, Order. To work out what a customer might like based on similar buyers, you rely directly on the shortest path.

A frequent problem: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

It is closely related to the node. A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Recommended practice: Set a maximum depth and check that both endpoints are indexed.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Yuki and Priya are connected in the e-commerce graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Yuki and Priya are connected in the e-commerce graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Customer {name: 'Yuki'})-[*..6]-(b:Customer {name: 'Priya'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: find every Article that can be reached from a Author in two steps, first through WROTE and then through REFERENCES
text:
Task: Find every Article that can be reached from a Author in two steps, first through WROTE and then through REFERENCES.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Author {name: $name})-[:WROTE]->(:Article)-[:REFERENCES]->(c:Article)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Article nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'Data modeling 101' could be passed as $name.

title: Cypher example: add a new Service and connect it to a Server with a RUNS_ON relationship
text:

```cypher
CREATE (a:Service {name: 'auth-api'})-[:RUNS_ON]->(b:Server {name: 'srv-app-01'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Ben and Dev are connected in the social network graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Ben and Dev are connected in the social network graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Person {name: 'Ben'})-[*..5]-(b:Person {name: 'Dev'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases

title: Cypher example: show the Service nodes whose replicas is above 50 in the IT infrastructure graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Service nodes whose replicas is above 50 in the IT infrastructure graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Service)
WHERE n.replicas > 50
RETURN n.name AS name, n.replicas AS replicas
ORDER BY n.replicas DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Service nodes above the threshold. An index on Service(replicas) can help when many nodes exist.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Service {name: $name})-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(:Service)-[:USES]->(c:Database)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Database nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'auth-api' could be passed as $name.

title: Understanding the aggregation in graph databases
text:

title: Understanding the selectivity in graph databases
text:
Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few. The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

A frequent problem: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

Recommended practice: Anchor queries on unique or nearly unique properties.

title: Understanding the PageRank in graph databases
text:

A frequent problem: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

It is closely related to the traversal. A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Recommended practice: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

title: Cypher example: add a new Article and connect it to a Topic with a ABOUT relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Article and connect it to a Topic with a ABOUT relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Article {name: 'Data modeling 101'})-[:ABOUT]->(b:Topic {name: 'Modeling'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:
A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph. Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

A frequent problem: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

It is closely related to the aggregation. Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 USED_DEVICE hops of a Account called ACC-206
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 2 USED_DEVICE hops of a Account called ACC-206.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Account {name: 'ACC-206'})-[:USED_DEVICE*1..2]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Understanding the path in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: find every Genre that can be reached from a Person in two steps, first through ACTED_IN and then through IN_GENRE
text:
Task: Find every Genre that can be reached from a Person in two steps, first through ACTED_IN and then through IN_GENRE.

```cypher
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Genre nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'Sara Cole' could be passed as $name.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In a supply chain graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Questions and answers: MERGE, community detection, shortest path
text:

A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

A: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

A: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is good practice for the shortest path?
A: Set a maximum depth and check that both endpoints are indexed.

```cypher
RETURN b.name AS result
```

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 RUNS_ON hops of a Service called search
text:

```cypher
MATCH (a:Service {name: 'search'})-[:RUNS_ON*1..4]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..4 allows paths of one to 4 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Understanding the uniqueness constraint in graph databases
text:
A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property. It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

Consider a fraud detection model built from Account, Transaction, Device. To work out which merchants receive money from many new accounts, you rely directly on the uniqueness constraint.

A frequent problem: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

Recommended practice: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

text:

A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Q: Why does the aggregation matter?

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the aggregation?

Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the pattern matching?

Q: What is good practice for the pattern matching?
A: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

Q: Why does the traversal matter?

Q: What is good practice for the traversal?
A: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Understanding the PageRank in graph databases
text:
PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them. It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

In a e-commerce graph with Customer, Product, Order nodes, the idea of a PageRank appears when you ask what a customer might like based on similar buyers.

A frequent problem: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

It is closely related to the full-text index. A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Recommended practice: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

title: Understanding the property in graph databases
text:
A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price. Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

Consider a social network model built from Person, Post, Group. To work out who are the friends of friends of a user, you rely directly on the property.

A frequent problem: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

Recommended practice: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

title: Understanding the transaction in graph databases
text:
A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together. It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

Consider a knowledge base model built from Article, Topic, Author. To work out which tags appear together on the same article, you rely directly on the transaction.

A frequent problem: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

It is closely related to the LOAD CSV. LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Recommended practice: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

title: Understanding the LOAD CSV in graph databases
text:

A frequent problem: Running it without a constraint and without batching makes the import slow and error-prone.

Recommended practice: Create constraints first and process the file in batches.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: make sure a Customer named Marcus is linked to a Product named Desk lamp, without creating duplicates
text:


Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(

)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: show the Part nodes whose cost is above 250 in the supply chain graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Part nodes whose cost is above 250 in the supply chain graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Part)
WHERE n.cost > 250
RETURN n.name AS name, n.cost AS cost
ORDER BY n.cost DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Part nodes above the threshold. An index on Part(cost) can help when many nodes exist.

A team modeling movies data with Person, Movie, Genre will meet the supernode as soon as they need to know which actors worked with the same director.

A frequent problem: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

It is closely related to the full-text index. A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Recommended practice: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:
A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph. Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

A team modeling fraud detection data with Account, Transaction, Device will meet the supernode as soon as they need to know which accounts share a device.

A frequent problem: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

It is closely related to the uniqueness constraint. A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Recommended practice: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Understanding the property in graph databases
text:

In a fraud detection graph with Account, Transaction, Device nodes, the idea of a property appears when you ask which accounts share a device.

A frequent problem: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

It is closely related to the community detection. Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Recommended practice: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:

Recommended practice: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

title: Understanding the aggregation in graph databases
text:

title: Troubleshooting: an algorithm run fails to start
text:

title: Cypher example: find how closely ACC-205 and ACC-201 are connected in the fraud detection graph
text:
Task: Find how closely ACC-205 and ACC-201 are connected in the fraud detection graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 OWNS hops of a Team called Growth
text:

```cypher
MATCH (a:Team {name: 'Growth'})-[:OWNS*1..4]-(b)

RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..4 allows paths of one to 4 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Cypher example: find every Post that can be reached from a Person in two steps, first through FRIENDS_WITH and then through LIKES

title: Understanding the node in graph databases
text:
A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product. Nodes are the anchor points of every query, so a clear choice of what becomes a node shapes the whole model.

In a social network graph with Person, Post, Group nodes, the idea of a node appears when you ask which posts are liked by the most people.

A frequent problem: A common mistake is storing a repeating group of values inside one node instead of giving each its own node.

It is closely related to the MERGE. MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Recommended practice: Give every node at least one label and a stable identifying property.

title: Understanding the path in graph databases
text:
A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node. Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

In a movies graph with Person, Movie, Genre nodes, the idea of a path appears when you ask which actors worked with the same director.

A frequent problem: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

It is closely related to the full-text index. A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Recommended practice: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

title: Understanding the pattern matching in graph databases
text:
Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships. It lets you express a multi-hop question in a single line instead of a chain of joins.

Consider a supply chain model built from Factory, Warehouse, Shipment. To work out which parts depend on a single factory, you rely directly on the pattern matching.

A frequent problem: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

It is closely related to the graph projection. A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Recommended practice: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

title: Cypher example: list every Movie connected to a given Person through ACTED_IN in the movies graph
text:

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: $name})-[:ACTED_IN]->(b:Movie)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Person found by name, follows outgoing ACTED_IN relationships, and returns the name of each Movie reached. The value of $name, for example 'Victor Hale', is passed as a parameter.

title: Questions and answers: shortest path, graph projection, MERGE
text:
Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: Why does the graph projection matter?
A: It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the graph projection?
A: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

Q: What is good practice for the graph projection?
A: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: Why does the MERGE matter?
A: It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

Q: What is a selectivity?
A: Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the selectivity?
A: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

Q: What is a community detection?
A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Q: Why does the community detection matter?
A: It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the community detection?
A: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

Q: What is good practice for the community detection?
A: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:
A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph. Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

In a supply chain graph with Factory, Warehouse, Shipment nodes, the idea of a supernode appears when you ask which parts depend on a single factory.

A frequent problem: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

Recommended practice: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In a e-commerce graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

Likely cause: a large transaction holds locks on nodes that other writers need. This is easy to hit when queries start from Order nodes and follow REVIEWED relationships from Customer to Product.

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the PageRank in graph databases
text:

Recommended practice: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

title: Understanding the transaction in graph databases
text:

A frequent problem: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

It is closely related to the shortest path. A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Recommended practice: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

title: Troubleshooting: the planner reports a cartesian product warning
text:

title: Understanding the query parameter in graph databases

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 AT_MERCHANT hops of a Transaction called TX-9005

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, a query runs out of memory.

Likely cause: a variable-length pattern has no upper bound and expands through most of the graph. This is easy to hit when queries start from Service nodes and follow USES relationships from Service to Database.

How to fix it: set a maximum depth, filter early and return only the properties you need.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

text:

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 REVIEWED hops of a Customer called Yuki
text:

```cypher
MATCH (a:Customer {name: 'Yuki'})-[:REVIEWED*1..2]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Understanding the aggregation in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: find which Account nodes have the most SENT relationships to Transaction nodes

title: Understanding the community detection in graph databases
text:
Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest. It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

A team modeling e-commerce data with Customer, Product, Order will meet the community detection as soon as they need to know which categories drive the most repeat orders.

A frequent problem: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

It is closely related to the query plan. A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Recommended practice: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases
text:
A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels. Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

In a social network graph with Person, Post, Group nodes, the idea of a label appears when you ask who are the friends of friends of a user.

A frequent problem: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

It is closely related to the node. A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Recommended practice: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

title: Understanding the variable-length path in graph databases
text:
A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum. It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

A team modeling movies data with Person, Movie, Genre will meet the variable-length path as soon as they need to know which genres a given actor appears in most.

A frequent problem: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

It is closely related to the supernode. A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Recommended practice: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

title: Understanding the MERGE in graph databases
text:
MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat. It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

A team modeling IT infrastructure data with Server, Service, Database will meet the MERGE as soon as they need to know which team owns the services that depend on a given database.

A frequent problem: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

Recommended practice: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

title: Questions and answers: query parameter, MERGE, LOAD CSV
text:
Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query parameter?
A: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: Why does the MERGE matter?
A: It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the MERGE?
A: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

Q: What is a LOAD CSV?
A: LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Q: What is good practice for the LOAD CSV?
A: Create constraints first and process the file in batches.

Q: What is a relationship direction?
A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship direction?
A: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the supernode?
A: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

title: Cypher example: add a new Movie and connect it to a Genre with a IN_GENRE relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Movie and connect it to a Genre with a IN_GENRE relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Movie {name: 'Iron Tide'})-[:IN_GENRE]->(b:Genre {name: 'Drama'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Understanding the full-text index in graph databases
text:
A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking. It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

A team modeling supply chain data with Factory, Warehouse, Shipment will meet the full-text index as soon as they need to know which shipments carry parts from several factories.

A frequent problem: Using a regular index for substring search gives poor results and slow scans.

It is closely related to the query parameter. A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Recommended practice: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

title: Questions and answers: community detection, PageRank, pattern matching
text:
Q: What is a community detection?
A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the community detection?
A: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Q: What is good practice for the PageRank?
A: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the pattern matching matter?
A: It lets you express a multi-hop question in a single line instead of a chain of joins.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the pattern matching?
A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

Q: What is good practice for the pattern matching?
A: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

title: Cypher example: show the Warehouse nodes whose stock is above 20 in the supply chain graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Warehouse nodes whose stock is above 20 in the supply chain graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Warehouse)
WHERE n.stock > 20
RETURN n.name AS name, n.stock AS stock
ORDER BY n.stock DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Warehouse nodes above the threshold. An index on Warehouse(stock) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Understanding the graph projection in graph databases
text:
A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms. It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

A team modeling social network data with Person, Post, Group will meet the graph projection as soon as they need to know which posts are liked by the most people.

A frequent problem: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

It is closely related to the pattern matching. Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Recommended practice: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

title: Cypher example: list every Database connected to a given Service through USES in the IT infrastructure graph
text:
Task: List every Database connected to a given Service through USES in the IT infrastructure graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Service {name: $name})-[:USES]->(b:Database)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Service found by name, follows outgoing USES relationships, and returns the name of each Database reached. The value of $name, for example 'gateway', is passed as a parameter.

title: Questions and answers: uniqueness constraint, relationship direction, node
text:
Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?
A: A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Q: Why does the uniqueness constraint matter?
A: It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the uniqueness constraint?
A: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

Q: What is good practice for the uniqueness constraint?
A: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

Q: What is a relationship direction?
A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Q: Why does the relationship direction matter?
A: A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

Q: What is good practice for the relationship direction?
A: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Q: Why does the node matter?
A: Nodes are the anchor points of every query, so a clear choice of what becomes a node shapes the whole model.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the node?
A: A common mistake is storing a repeating group of values inside one node instead of giving each its own node.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: Why does the relationship matter?
A: Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

title: Cypher example: guarantee that every Device has a unique name
text:
Task: Guarantee that every Device has a unique name.

```cypher
CREATE CONSTRAINT device_name_unique IF NOT EXISTS
FOR (n:Device) REQUIRE n.name IS UNIQUE
```

The constraint rejects a second Device with the same name and also provides an index for lookups.

title: Cypher example: find every Category that can be reached from a Order in two steps, first through CONTAINS and then through IN_CATEGORY
text:
Task: Find every Category that can be reached from a Order in two steps, first through CONTAINS and then through IN_CATEGORY.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Order {name: $name})-[:CONTAINS]->(:Product)-[:IN_CATEGORY]->(c:Category)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Category nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'ORD-1001' could be passed as $name.

title: Troubleshooting: an import fails with a constraint violation
text:
Symptom: In a knowledge base graph, an import fails with a constraint violation.

Likely cause: the file contains two rows with the same value for a unique property. This is easy to hit when queries start from Article nodes and follow REFERENCES relationships from Article to Article.

How to fix it: deduplicate the input or use MERGE on the unique key.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the selectivity in graph databases
text:
Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few. The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

In a fraud detection graph with Account, Transaction, Device nodes, the idea of a selectivity appears when you ask which merchants receive money from many new accounts.

A frequent problem: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

It is closely related to the variable-length path. A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Recommended practice: Anchor queries on unique or nearly unique properties.

title: Cypher example: find how closely SHP-34 and SHP-31 are connected in the supply chain graph
text:
Task: Find how closely SHP-34 and SHP-31 are connected in the supply chain graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Shipment {name: 'SHP-34'})-[*..4]-(b:Shipment {name: 'SHP-31'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..4 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: show the Movie nodes whose year is above 10 in the movies graph, highest first
text:

```cypher
MATCH (n:Movie)
WHERE n.year > 10
RETURN n.name AS name, n.year AS year
ORDER BY n.year DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Movie nodes above the threshold. An index on Movie(year) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Troubleshooting: the planner reports a cartesian product warning
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, the planner reports a cartesian product warning.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Shipment {name: 'SHP-34'})-[:SHIPS_TO*1..2]-(b)
```

title: Questions and answers: selectivity, query plan, aggregation
text:
Q: What is a selectivity?
A: Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Q: Why does the selectivity matter?
A: The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the selectivity?
A: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

Q: What is good practice for the selectivity?
A: Anchor queries on unique or nearly unique properties.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query plan?
A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

Q: What is a aggregation?
A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Q: Why does the aggregation matter?
A: It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: Why does the relationship matter?
A: Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship?
A: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

Q: What is good practice for the relationship?
A: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: Why does the transaction matter?
A: It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the transaction?
A: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

Q: What is good practice for the transaction?
A: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

title: Questions and answers: path, index, MERGE
text:
Q: What is a path?
A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: Why does the path matter?
A: Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Q: Why does the index matter?
A: Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the index?
A: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the MERGE?
A: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

Q: What is good practice for the MERGE?
A: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

title: Understanding the graph projection in graph databases
text:
A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms. It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

Consider a supply chain model built from Factory, Warehouse, Shipment. To work out which shipments carry parts from several factories, you rely directly on the graph projection.

A frequent problem: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

It is closely related to the transaction. A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Recommended practice: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

title: Cypher example: add a new Customer and connect it to a Product with a REVIEWED relationship
text:

```cypher
CREATE (a:Customer {name: 'Lucas'})-[:REVIEWED]->(b:Product {name: 'Desk lamp'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Cypher example: find how closely ACC-203 and ACC-201 are connected in the fraud detection graph


shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Understanding the property in graph databases
text:
A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price. Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

Consider an IT infrastructure model built from Server, Service, Database. To work out which team owns the services that depend on a given database, you rely directly on the property.

A frequent problem: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

It is closely related to the index. An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Recommended practice: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

title: Understanding the LOAD CSV in graph databases
text:
LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships. It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

A team modeling IT infrastructure data with Server, Service, Database will meet the LOAD CSV as soon as they need to know which services have the longest dependency chains.

A frequent problem: Running it without a constraint and without batching makes the import slow and error-prone.

It is closely related to the PageRank. PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Recommended practice: Create constraints first and process the file in batches.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases
text:
A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels. Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

Consider a movies model built from Person, Movie, Genre. To work out which genres a given actor appears in most, you rely directly on the label.

A frequent problem: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

It is closely related to the graph projection. A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Recommended practice: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

title: Understanding the relationship in graph databases
text:

In a social network graph with Person, Post, Group nodes, the idea of a relationship appears when you ask which groups a user's friends have joined.

A frequent problem: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

It is closely related to the relationship direction. Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Recommended practice: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

title: Questions and answers: node, aggregation, traversal
text:
Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the node?
A: A common mistake is storing a repeating group of values inside one node instead of giving each its own node.

Q: What is a aggregation?

A: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

Q: What is a traversal?

Q: What is good practice for the traversal?
A: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Cypher example: find every Service that can be reached from a Service in two steps, first through DEPENDS_ON and then through DEPENDS_ON
text:
Task: Find every Service that can be reached from a Service in two steps, first through DEPENDS_ON and then through DEPENDS_ON.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Service {name: $name})-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(:Service)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(c:Service)

```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Service nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'billing' could be passed as $name.

title: Questions and answers: query parameter, pattern matching, MERGE
text:
Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the pattern matching matter?
A: It lets you express a multi-hop question in a single line instead of a chain of joins.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the pattern matching?
A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: Why does the MERGE matter?
A: It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

Q: What is good practice for the MERGE?
A: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

Likely cause: the first step scans every node of a label because no index supports the filter. This is easy to hit when queries start from Service nodes and follow DEPENDS_ON relationships from Service to Service.

How to fix it: create an index on the filtered property and confirm with PROFILE that the scan is gone.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Troubleshooting: one query is much slower for some start nodes than others
text:
Symptom: In a social network graph, one query is much slower for some start nodes than others.

Likely cause: a few nodes have a huge number of relationships. This is easy to hit when queries start from Person nodes and follow POSTED relationships from Person to Post.

How to fix it: avoid traversing through hub nodes or filter on a relationship property before expanding.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.
