title: Understanding the PageRank in graph databases
text:
PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them. It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Consider a knowledge base model built from Article, Topic, Author. To work out which topics an author covers, you rely directly on the PageRank.

A frequent problem: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Recommended practice: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

title: Understanding the pattern matching in graph databases
text:
Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships. It lets you express a multi-hop question in a single line instead of a chain of joins.

In an IT infrastructure graph with Server, Service, Database nodes, the idea of a pattern matching appears when you ask which services are affected if a server fails.

A frequent problem: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

It is closely related to the transaction. A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Recommended practice: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

title: Questions and answers: PageRank, full-text index, variable-length path
text:
Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: What is good practice for the full-text index?
A: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Q: What is good practice for the variable-length path?
A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

title: Understanding the shortest path in graph databases
text:
A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships. It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

In a knowledge base graph with Article, Topic, Author nodes, the idea of a shortest path appears when you ask which topics an author covers.

A frequent problem: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Recommended practice: Set a maximum depth and check that both endpoints are indexed.

title: Understanding the aggregation in graph databases
text:
Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists. It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

Consider a movies model built from Person, Movie, Genre. To work out which genres a given actor appears in most, you rely directly on the aggregation.

A frequent problem: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

It is closely related to the LOAD CSV. LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Recommended practice: Aggregate as late as possible and limit the size of collected lists.

title: Understanding the MERGE in graph databases
text:
MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat. It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

Consider an IT infrastructure model built from Server, Service, Database. To work out which services have the longest dependency chains, you rely directly on the MERGE.

A frequent problem: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

It is closely related to the relationship. A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Recommended practice: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Desk lamp and Desk lamp are connected in the e-commerce graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Desk lamp and Desk lamp are connected in the e-commerce graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Product {name: 'Desk lamp'})-[*..6]-(b:Product {name: 'Desk lamp'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Understanding the relationship in graph databases
text:
A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties. Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

In a e-commerce graph with Customer, Product, Order nodes, the idea of a relationship appears when you ask which products are often bought together.

A frequent problem: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

It is closely related to the query plan. A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Recommended practice: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

title: Questions and answers: LOAD CSV, query parameter, full-text index
text:
Q: What is a LOAD CSV?
A: LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the LOAD CSV matter?
A: It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Q: What is good practice for the query parameter?
A: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: Why does the full-text index matter?
A: It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

Q: What is a community detection?
A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Q: Why does the community detection matter?
A: It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the community detection?
A: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

Q: What is good practice for the community detection?
A: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Article named Data modeling 101 is linked to a Article named Getting started, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Article named Data modeling 101 is linked to a Article named Getting started, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Article {name: 'Data modeling 101'})
MERGE (b:Article {name: 'Getting started'})
MERGE (a)-[:REFERENCES]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Understanding the relationship direction in graph databases
text:
Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it. A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

Consider a supply chain model built from Factory, Warehouse, Shipment. To work out which parts depend on a single factory, you rely directly on the relationship direction.

A frequent problem: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

Recommended practice: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

title: Understanding the transaction in graph databases
text:
A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together. It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

In a movies graph with Person, Movie, Genre nodes, the idea of a transaction appears when you ask which genres a given actor appears in most.

A frequent problem: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

It is closely related to the selectivity. Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Recommended practice: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

title: Cypher example: show the Order nodes whose total is above 50 in the e-commerce graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Order nodes whose total is above 50 in the e-commerce graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Order)
WHERE n.total > 50
RETURN n.name AS name, n.total AS total
ORDER BY n.total DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Order nodes above the threshold. An index on Order(total) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Understanding the query plan in graph databases
text:
A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query. Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

In a e-commerce graph with Customer, Product, Order nodes, the idea of a query plan appears when you ask which categories drive the most repeat orders.

A frequent problem: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

It is closely related to the transaction. A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Recommended practice: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

title: Understanding the graph projection in graph databases
text:
A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms. It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

Consider an IT infrastructure model built from Server, Service, Database. To work out which services are affected if a server fails, you rely directly on the graph projection.

A frequent problem: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

It is closely related to the query plan. A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Recommended practice: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

Likely cause: a large transaction holds locks on nodes that other writers need. This is easy to hit when queries start from Service nodes and follow RUNS_ON relationships from Service to Server.

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In a e-commerce graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

Likely cause: the first step scans every node of a label because no index supports the filter. This is easy to hit when queries start from Customer nodes and follow REVIEWED relationships from Customer to Product.

How to fix it: create an index on the filtered property and confirm with PROFILE that the scan is gone.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Customer named Ivy is linked to a Order named ORD-1004, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Customer named Ivy is linked to a Order named ORD-1004, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Customer {name: 'Ivy'})
MERGE (b:Order {name: 'ORD-1004'})
MERGE (a)-[:PLACED]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Cypher example: list every Movie connected to a given Person through DIRECTED in the movies graph

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: $name})-[:DIRECTED]->(b:Movie)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:
A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes. Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

A team modeling supply chain data with Factory, Warehouse, Shipment will meet the traversal as soon as they need to know how a delay at one warehouse affects shipments.

A frequent problem: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Recommended practice: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Understanding the query parameter in graph databases
text:
A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text. Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

In a knowledge base graph with Article, Topic, Author nodes, the idea of a query parameter appears when you ask which tags appear together on the same article.

A frequent problem: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

It is closely related to the full-text index. A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Recommended practice: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

title: Understanding the selectivity in graph databases
text:
Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few. The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

Consider a supply chain model built from Factory, Warehouse, Shipment. To work out which shipments carry parts from several factories, you rely directly on the selectivity.

A frequent problem: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

Recommended practice: Anchor queries on unique or nearly unique properties.

title: Questions and answers: traversal, MERGE, shortest path
text:
Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: Why does the traversal matter?
A: Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the MERGE?
A: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

title: Questions and answers: pattern matching, index, transaction
text:
Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the pattern matching?
A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the index?
A: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the transaction?
A: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

Q: What is good practice for the transaction?
A: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query plan?
A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

title: Questions and answers: relationship direction, PageRank, query parameter
text:
Q: What is a relationship direction?
A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Q: Why does the relationship direction matter?
A: A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship direction?
A: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

Q: What is good practice for the relationship direction?
A: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Q: What is good practice for the PageRank?
A: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

title: Cypher example: show the Transaction nodes whose amount is above 100 in the fraud detection graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Transaction nodes whose amount is above 100 in the fraud detection graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Transaction)
WHERE n.amount > 100
RETURN n.name AS name, n.amount AS amount
ORDER BY n.amount DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Transaction nodes above the threshold. An index on Transaction(amount) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

Likely cause: a large transaction holds locks on nodes that other writers need. This is easy to hit when queries start from Server nodes and follow DEPENDS_ON relationships from Service to Service.

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:
Symptom: In a supply chain graph, results differ every time the import is repeated.

Likely cause: CREATE was used where MERGE was needed, so duplicates accumulate. This is easy to hit when queries start from Warehouse nodes and follow PRODUCES relationships from Factory to Part.

How to fix it: switch to MERGE on a unique key and add a uniqueness constraint.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Fatima and Marcus are connected in the e-commerce graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Fatima and Marcus are connected in the e-commerce graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Customer {name: 'Fatima'})-[*..4]-(b:Customer {name: 'Marcus'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..4 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Questions and answers: community detection, selectivity, transaction
text:
Q: What is a community detection?
A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Q: Why does the community detection matter?
A: It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

Q: What is good practice for the community detection?
A: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

Q: What is a selectivity?
A: Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Q: Why does the selectivity matter?
A: The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: Why does the transaction matter?
A: It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the index?
A: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: Why does the relationship matter?
A: Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship?
A: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

title: Cypher example: guarantee that every Account has a unique name
text:
Task: Guarantee that every Account has a unique name.

```cypher
CREATE CONSTRAINT account_name_unique IF NOT EXISTS
FOR (n:Account) REQUIRE n.name IS UNIQUE
```

The constraint rejects a second Account with the same name and also provides an index for lookups.

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, a query runs out of memory.

Likely cause: a variable-length pattern has no upper bound and expands through most of the graph. This is easy to hit when queries start from Account nodes and follow AT_MERCHANT relationships from Transaction to Merchant.

How to fix it: set a maximum depth, filter early and return only the properties you need.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:
An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning. Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

Consider a supply chain model built from Factory, Warehouse, Shipment. To work out which parts depend on a single factory, you rely directly on the index.

A frequent problem: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

It is closely related to the relationship. A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Recommended practice: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 AT_MERCHANT hops of a Transaction called TX-9001
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 3 AT_MERCHANT hops of a Transaction called TX-9001.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Transaction {name: 'TX-9001'})-[:AT_MERCHANT*1..3]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..3 allows paths of one to 3 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Cypher example: add a new Transaction and connect it to a Account with a RECEIVED_BY relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Transaction and connect it to a Account with a RECEIVED_BY relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Transaction {name: 'TX-9003'})-[:RECEIVED_BY]->(b:Account {name: 'ACC-204'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Cypher example: list every Database connected to a given Service through USES in the IT infrastructure graph
text:
Task: List every Database connected to a given Service through USES in the IT infrastructure graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Service {name: $name})-[:USES]->(b:Database)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Service found by name, follows outgoing USES relationships, and returns the name of each Database reached. The value of $name, for example 'notifier', is passed as a parameter.

title: Cypher example: list every Movie connected to a given Person through DIRECTED in the movies graph

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 USES hops of a Service called billing
text:

```cypher
MATCH (a:Service {name: 'billing'})-[:USES*1..2]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

title: Troubleshooting: an import fails with a constraint violation
text:

title: Understanding the query parameter in graph databases

title: Cypher example: show the Person nodes whose born is above 100 in the movies graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Person nodes whose born is above 100 in the movies graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Person)
WHERE n.born > 100
RETURN n.name AS name, n.born AS born
ORDER BY n.born DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Person nodes above the threshold. An index on Person(born) can help when many nodes exist.

text:

In an IT infrastructure graph with Server, Service, Database nodes, the idea of a LOAD CSV appears when you ask which team owns the services that depend on a given database.

title: Troubleshooting: one query is much slower for some start nodes than others
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, one query is much slower for some start nodes than others.

title: Cypher example: list every Service connected to a given Team through OWNS in the IT infrastructure graph
text:
Task: List every Service connected to a given Team through OWNS in the IT infrastructure graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Team {name: $name})-[:OWNS]->(b:Service)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Team found by name, follows outgoing OWNS relationships, and returns the name of each Service reached. The value of $name, for example 'Growth', is passed as a parameter.

title: Questions and answers: query plan, full-text index, MERGE
text:
Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query plan?
A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the full-text index?
A: Using a regular index for substring search gives poor results and slow scans.

Q: What is good practice for the full-text index?
A: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the MERGE?
A: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

Q: What is good practice for the MERGE?
A: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query parameter?
A: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

title: Understanding the aggregation in graph databases
text:
Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists. It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

Consider a social network model built from Person, Post, Group. To work out which groups a user's friends have joined, you rely directly on the aggregation.

A frequent problem: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

Recommended practice: Aggregate as late as possible and limit the size of collected lists.

title: Understanding the MERGE in graph databases
text:
MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat. It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

In a fraud detection graph with Account, Transaction, Device nodes, the idea of a MERGE appears when you ask which merchants receive money from many new accounts.

A frequent problem: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

It is closely related to the node. A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Recommended practice: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

title: Understanding the relationship in graph databases
text:
A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties. Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

In a social network graph with Person, Post, Group nodes, the idea of a relationship appears when you ask which groups a user's friends have joined.

A frequent problem: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

Recommended practice: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

title: Understanding the property in graph databases
text:
A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price. Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

In a fraud detection graph with Account, Transaction, Device nodes, the idea of a property appears when you ask which accounts share a device.

A frequent problem: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

It is closely related to the path. A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Recommended practice: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

title: Questions and answers: path, shortest path, PageRank
text:

A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: Why does the path matter?
A: Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: Why does the shortest path matter?
A: It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What is good practice for the PageRank?
A: Check that relationship direction reflects influence before trusting the ranking.

Q: What is a label?
A: A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Q: Why does the label matter?
A: Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the label?
A: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

Q: What is good practice for the label?
A: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Movie named Blue Meridian is linked to a Genre named Romance, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Movie named Blue Meridian is linked to a Genre named Romance, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Movie {name: 'Blue Meridian'})
MERGE (b:Genre {name: 'Romance'})
MERGE (a)-[:IN_GENRE]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Understanding the shortest path in graph databases
text:
A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships. It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

Consider a fraud detection model built from Account, Transaction, Device. To work out which chains of transfers return to the starting account, you rely directly on the shortest path.

A frequent problem: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

It is closely related to the query parameter. A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Recommended practice: Set a maximum depth and check that both endpoints are indexed.

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:
A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes. Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

In a knowledge base graph with Article, Topic, Author nodes, the idea of a traversal appears when you ask which topics an author covers.

A frequent problem: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Recommended practice: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:
A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph. Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

In a movies graph with Person, Movie, Genre nodes, the idea of a supernode appears when you ask which actors worked with the same director.

A frequent problem: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

Recommended practice: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Understanding the selectivity in graph databases
text:
Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few. The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

In a fraud detection graph with Account, Transaction, Device nodes, the idea of a selectivity appears when you ask which merchants receive money from many new accounts.

A frequent problem: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

It is closely related to the query plan. A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Recommended practice: Anchor queries on unique or nearly unique properties.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Priya and Marcus are connected in the e-commerce graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Priya and Marcus are connected in the e-commerce graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Customer {name: 'Priya'})-[*..5]-(b:Customer {name: 'Marcus'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Understanding the relationship direction in graph databases
text:
Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it. A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

Consider a movies model built from Person, Movie, Genre. To work out how many movies two people have in common, you rely directly on the relationship direction.

A frequent problem: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

It is closely related to the LOAD CSV. LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Recommended practice: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 PRODUCES hops of a Factory called Gdansk Site
text:


title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 REFERENCES hops of a Article called Data modeling 101

title: Understanding the transaction in graph databases

title: Cypher example: list every Order connected to a given Customer through PLACED in the e-commerce graph
text:
Task: List every Order connected to a given Customer through PLACED in the e-commerce graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Customer {name: $name})-[:PLACED]->(b:Order)

```

title: Troubleshooting: an algorithm run fails to start
text:

title: Questions and answers: transaction, path, property
text:
Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the transaction?
A: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

A: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

Q: What is a path?

A: Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

Q: What is good practice for the path?
A: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

Q: What is a property?
A: A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Q: Why does the property matter?
A: Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the property?
A: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query plan?
A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: Why does the MERGE matter?
A: It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the MERGE?
A: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

title: Questions and answers: traversal, relationship direction, property
text:
Q: What is a traversal?

Q: What is a relationship direction?

A: A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

A: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

Q: What is a property?
A: A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Q: What is good practice for the property?
A: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the node?
A: A common mistake is storing a repeating group of values inside one node instead of giving each its own node.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases
text:

title: Questions and answers: graph projection, supernode, full-text index
text:
Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

A: It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

A: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

Q: What is good practice for the supernode?
A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: Why does the full-text index matter?
A: It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

title: Understanding the relationship direction in graph databases
text:

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:
A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes. Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

title: Troubleshooting: an import fails with a constraint violation
text:

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 FRIENDS_WITH hops of a Person called Ben
text:


The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Troubleshooting: an import fails with a constraint violation
text:
Symptom: In a supply chain graph, an import fails with a constraint violation.

Likely cause: the file contains two rows with the same value for a unique property. This is easy to hit when queries start from Warehouse nodes and follow PRODUCES relationships from Factory to Part.

How to fix it: deduplicate the input or use MERGE on the unique key.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory

How to fix it: set a maximum depth, filter early and return only the properties you need.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the selectivity in graph databases
text:
Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few. The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

Consider a knowledge base model built from Article, Topic, Author. To work out which tags appear together on the same article, you rely directly on the selectivity.

A frequent problem: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

It is closely related to the pattern matching. Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Recommended practice: Anchor queries on unique or nearly unique properties.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Ohio Plant and Osaka Line are connected in the supply chain graph
text:

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(

)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:
A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph. Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Consider a fraud detection model built from Account, Transaction, Device. To work out which chains of transfers return to the starting account, you rely directly on the supernode.

A frequent problem: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

It is closely related to the query plan. A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Recommended practice: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:
A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes. Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

A frequent problem: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

It is closely related to the label. A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Recommended practice: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:
Symptom: In a social network graph, results differ every time the import is repeated.

Likely cause: CREATE was used where MERGE was needed, so duplicates accumulate. This is easy to hit when queries start from Person nodes and follow FRIENDS_WITH relationships from Person to Person.

How to fix it: switch to MERGE on a unique key and add a uniqueness constraint.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

Q: Why does the transaction matter?
A: It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Q: Why does the node matter?
A: Nodes are the anchor points of every query, so a clear choice of what becomes a node shapes the whole model.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the node?
A: A common mistake is storing a repeating group of values inside one node instead of giving each its own node.

Q: What is a aggregation?
A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Q: Why does the aggregation matter?
A: It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the aggregation?
A: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

Q: What is good practice for the aggregation?
A: Aggregate as late as possible and limit the size of collected lists.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 PLACED hops of a Customer called Noah
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 3 PLACED hops of a Customer called Noah.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Customer {name: 'Noah'})-[:PLACED*1..3]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..3 allows paths of one to 3 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Cypher example: add a new Product and connect it to a Category with a IN_CATEGORY relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Product and connect it to a Category with a IN_CATEGORY relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Product {name: 'Wireless mouse'})-[:IN_CATEGORY]->(b:Category {name: 'Office'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Understanding the property in graph databases
text:
A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price. Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

In an IT infrastructure graph with Server, Service, Database nodes, the idea of a property appears when you ask which services are affected if a server fails.

A frequent problem: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

It is closely related to the shortest path. A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Recommended practice: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:
A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes. Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

Consider a social network model built from Person, Post, Group. To work out which posts are liked by the most people, you rely directly on the traversal.

A frequent problem: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Recommended practice: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Cypher example: add a new Service and connect it to a Server with a RUNS_ON relationship
text:

```cypher
CREATE (a:Service {name: 'search'})-[:RUNS_ON]->(b:Server {name: 'srv-app-01'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Cypher example: find how closely TX-9005 and TX-9005 are connected in the fraud detection graph
text:
Task: Find how closely TX-9005 and TX-9005 are connected in the fraud detection graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Transaction {name: 'TX-9005'})-[*..4]-(b:Transaction {name: 'TX-9005'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..4 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Understanding the community detection in graph databases
text:
Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest. It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

A team modeling e-commerce data with Customer, Product, Order will meet the community detection as soon as they need to know which products are often bought together.

A frequent problem: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

Recommended practice: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, a query runs out of memory.

Likely cause: a variable-length pattern has no upper bound and expands through most of the graph. This is easy to hit when queries start from Database nodes and follow DEPENDS_ON relationships from Service to Service.

How to fix it: set a maximum depth, filter early and return only the properties you need.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Questions and answers: index, PageRank, relationship

Q: What is good practice for the relationship?
A: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: What is good practice for the full-text index?
A: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

title: Cypher example: speed up lookups of Shipment nodes by name
text:
Task: Speed up lookups of Shipment nodes by name.

```cypher
CREATE INDEX shipment_name IF NOT EXISTS
FOR (n:Shipment) ON (n.name)
```

The index lets the database find a Shipment by name without scanning every Shipment. IF NOT EXISTS makes the command safe to run again.

title: Cypher example: show the Transaction nodes whose amount is above 250 in the fraud detection graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Transaction nodes whose amount is above 250 in the fraud detection graph, highest first.

```cypher
WHERE n.amount > 250
RETURN n.name AS name, n.amount AS amount
ORDER BY n.amount DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Transaction nodes above the threshold. An index on Transaction(amount) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Understanding the LOAD CSV in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: add a new Person and connect it to a Group with a MEMBER_OF relationship

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In a social network graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

Likely cause: the first step scans every node of a label because no index supports the filter. This is easy to hit when queries start from Group nodes and follow POSTED relationships from Person to Post.

How to fix it: create an index on the filtered property and confirm with PROFILE that the scan is gone.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the variable-length path in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: make sure a Person named Lena Park is linked to a Movie named Paper Moon, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Person named Lena Park is linked to a Movie named Paper Moon, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Person {name: 'Lena Park'})
MERGE (b:Movie {name: 'Paper Moon'})
MERGE (a)-[:DIRECTED]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Understanding the graph projection in graph databases
text:

A frequent problem: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

Recommended practice: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases

title: Cypher example: find how closely Grace and Jonas are connected in the social network graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Grace and Jonas are connected in the social network graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Person {name: 'Grace'})-[*..6]-(b:Person {name: 'Jonas'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Person named Jonas is linked to a Post named Chess puzzle, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Person named Jonas is linked to a Post named Chess puzzle, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Person {name: 'Jonas'})
MERGE (b:Post {name: 'Chess puzzle'})
MERGE (a)-[:POSTED]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 MEMBER_OF hops of a Person called Jonas
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 2 MEMBER_OF hops of a Person called Jonas.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Jonas'})-[:MEMBER_OF*1..2]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..2 allows paths of one to 2 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, a query runs out of memory.

Likely cause: a variable-length pattern has no upper bound and expands through most of the graph. This is easy to hit when queries start from Device nodes and follow RECEIVED_BY relationships from Transaction to Account.

How to fix it: set a maximum depth, filter early and return only the properties you need.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 2 RUNS_ON hops of a Service called auth-api
text:

title: Understanding the index in graph databases

title: Cypher example: make sure a Factory named Osaka Line is linked to a Part named Bracket M2, without creating duplicates

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Troubleshooting: an import fails with a constraint violation
text:
Symptom: In a e-commerce graph, an import fails with a constraint violation.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

text:
Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: Why does the traversal matter?
A: Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

Q: What is good practice for the traversal?
A: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

Q: What is a selectivity?
A: Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the selectivity?
A: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

Q: What is good practice for the selectivity?
A: Anchor queries on unique or nearly unique properties.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: What is good practice for the relationship?
A: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

Q: What is a LOAD CSV?
A: LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the LOAD CSV matter?
A: It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

Q: What is good practice for the LOAD CSV?
A: Create constraints first and process the file in batches.

Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the node?
A: A common mistake is storing a repeating group of values inside one node instead of giving each its own node.

Q: What is good practice for the node?
A: Give every node at least one label and a stable identifying property.

title: Cypher example: guarantee that every Product has a unique name
text:

```cypher
CREATE CONSTRAINT product_name_unique IF NOT EXISTS
FOR (n:Product) REQUIRE n.name IS UNIQUE
```

The constraint rejects a second Product with the same name and also provides an index for lookups.

title: Questions and answers: shortest path, variable-length path, relationship
text:
Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: Why does the shortest path matter?
A: It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is good practice for the shortest path?
A: Set a maximum depth and check that both endpoints are indexed.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: Why does the relationship matter?
A: Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

Q: What is a selectivity?
A: Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Q: Why does the selectivity matter?
A: The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the selectivity?
A: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

title: Understanding the variable-length path in graph databases
text:
A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum. It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Consider a social network model built from Person, Post, Group. To work out who are the friends of friends of a user, you rely directly on the variable-length path.

A frequent problem: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

It is closely related to the node. A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

title: Cypher example: add a new Person and connect it to a Post with a POSTED relationship
text:

```cypher
CREATE (a:Person {name: 'Ines'})-[:POSTED]->(b:Post {name: 'Chess puzzle'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

text:

title: Troubleshooting: an import fails with a constraint violation
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, an import fails with a constraint violation.

Likely cause: the file contains two rows with the same value for a unique property. This is easy to hit when queries start from Merchant nodes and follow SENT relationships from Account to Transaction.

How to fix it: deduplicate the input or use MERGE on the unique key.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the uniqueness constraint in graph databases
text:
A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property. It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

A team modeling social network data with Person, Post, Group will meet the uniqueness constraint as soon as they need to know which groups a user's friends have joined.

A frequent problem: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

It is closely related to the query plan. A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Recommended practice: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Farid and Farid are connected in the social network graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Farid and Farid are connected in the social network graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Person {name: 'Farid'})-[*..4]-(b:Person {name: 'Farid'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..4 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 MEMBER_OF hops of a Person called Jonas
text:

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Jonas'})-[:MEMBER_OF*1..4]-(b)
```

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Account {name: 'ACC-203'})-[*..4]-(b:Account {name: 'ACC-201'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..4 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Questions and answers: path, full-text index, query parameter
text:
Q: What is a path?
A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: What is good practice for the path?
A: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the full-text index?
A: Using a regular index for substring search gives poor results and slow scans.

Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query parameter?
A: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

Q: What is good practice for the query parameter?
A: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

title: Cypher example: find every Tag that can be reached from a Author in two steps, first through WROTE and then through TAGGED
text:
Task: Find every Tag that can be reached from a Author in two steps, first through WROTE and then through TAGGED.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Author {name: $name})-[:WROTE]->(:Article)-[:TAGGED]->(c:Tag)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Tag nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'S. Okafor' could be passed as $name.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases
text:
A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels. Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

In a movies graph with Person, Movie, Genre nodes, the idea of a label appears when you ask which genres a given actor appears in most.

A frequent problem: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

Recommended practice: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

title: Questions and answers: traversal, selectivity, index
text:
Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: Why does the traversal matter?
A: Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

Q: What is good practice for the traversal?
A: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

Q: What is a selectivity?
A: Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Q: Why does the selectivity matter?
A: The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

Q: What is good practice for the selectivity?
A: Anchor queries on unique or nearly unique properties.

Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

title: Troubleshooting: an import fails with a constraint violation
text:
Symptom: In a supply chain graph, an import fails with a constraint violation.

Likely cause: the file contains two rows with the same value for a unique property. This is easy to hit when queries start from Warehouse nodes and follow SHIPS_TO relationships from Shipment to Warehouse.

How to fix it: deduplicate the input or use MERGE on the unique key.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the LOAD CSV in graph databases
text:
LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships. It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

Consider a movies model built from Person, Movie, Genre. To work out how many movies two people have in common, you rely directly on the LOAD CSV.

A frequent problem: Running it without a constraint and without batching makes the import slow and error-prone.

Recommended practice: Create constraints first and process the file in batches.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Movie named Night Train is linked to a Genre named Comedy, without creating duplicates

```cypher
MERGE (a:Movie {name: 'Night Train'})
```

title: Understanding the relationship direction in graph databases
text:
Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it. A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

A team modeling IT infrastructure data with Server, Service, Database will meet the relationship direction as soon as they need to know which services are affected if a server fails.

A frequent problem: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

It is closely related to the selectivity. Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Recommended practice: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

title: Understanding the relationship in graph databases
text:
A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties. Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

Consider a supply chain model built from Factory, Warehouse, Shipment. To work out which shipments carry parts from several factories, you rely directly on the relationship.

A frequent problem: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

It is closely related to the traversal. A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Recommended practice: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

title: Questions and answers: variable-length path, property, selectivity
text:
Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What is good practice for the variable-length path?
A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

Q: What is a property?
A: A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the property?
A: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

Q: What is good practice for the property?
A: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

Q: What is a selectivity?
A: Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the selectivity?
A: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

Q: What is good practice for the selectivity?
A: Anchor queries on unique or nearly unique properties.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In a knowledge base graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

Likely cause: the first step scans every node of a label because no index supports the filter. This is easy to hit when queries start from Topic nodes and follow REFERENCES relationships from Article to Article.

How to fix it: create an index on the filtered property and confirm with PROFILE that the scan is gone.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 POSTED hops of a Person called Carla
text:

title: Questions and answers: selectivity, node, pattern matching
text:

A: It lets you express a multi-hop question in a single line instead of a chain of joins.

Q: What is good practice for the pattern matching?
A: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

title: Questions and answers: MERGE, graph projection, full-text index
text:
Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: Why does the MERGE matter?
A: It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

Q: What is good practice for the MERGE?
A: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: Why does the graph projection matter?
A: It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the graph projection?
A: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: Why does the full-text index matter?
A: It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

Q: What is good practice for the full-text index?
A: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the supernode?
A: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

Q: What is a query parameter?

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query parameter?
A: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

title: Questions and answers: query plan, variable-length path, PageRank
text:
Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Q: What is a LOAD CSV?
A: LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the LOAD CSV?
A: Running it without a constraint and without batching makes the import slow and error-prone.

title: Understanding the query parameter in graph databases
text:
A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text. Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:

title: Understanding the PageRank in graph databases
text:
PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them. It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

A frequent problem: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases

title: Cypher example: make sure a Product named Trail shoes is linked to a Category named Kitchen, without creating duplicates
text:


Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.
