title: Cypher example: find how closely Tom Reyes and Lena Park are connected in the movies graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Tom Reyes and Lena Park are connected in the movies graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Person {name: 'Tom Reyes'})-[*..4]-(b:Person {name: 'Lena Park'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..4 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Understanding the community detection in graph databases
text:
Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest. It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

In an IT infrastructure graph with Server, Service, Database nodes, the idea of a community detection appears when you ask which services have the longest dependency chains.

A frequent problem: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

It is closely related to the transaction. A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Recommended practice: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 TAGGED hops of a Article called Getting started
text:

```cypher
MATCH (a:Article {name: 'Getting started'})-[:TAGGED*1..3]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..3 allows paths of one to 3 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Questions and answers: MERGE, relationship, label
text:

Q: What is a relationship?

title: Troubleshooting: the planner reports a cartesian product warning
text:

title: Questions and answers: graph projection, full-text index, relationship direction
text:
Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the graph projection?
A: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: Why does the full-text index matter?
A: It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

Q: What is good practice for the full-text index?
A: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

Q: What is a relationship direction?
A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship direction?
A: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?
A: A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Q: Why does the uniqueness constraint matter?
A: It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the uniqueness constraint?
A: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.


Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:
An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning. Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

Consider a movies model built from Person, Movie, Genre. To work out how many movies two people have in common, you rely directly on the index.

A frequent problem: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

It is closely related to the PageRank. PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Recommended practice: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

title: Troubleshooting: an algorithm run fails to start
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, an algorithm run fails to start.

Likely cause: the projected graph does not fit in the memory that is available. This is easy to hit when queries start from Transaction nodes and follow RECEIVED_BY relationships from Transaction to Account.

How to fix it: project only the needed labels and relationship types, or estimate memory before running.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: show the Service nodes whose replicas is above 250 in the IT infrastructure graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Service nodes whose replicas is above 250 in the IT infrastructure graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Service)
WHERE n.replicas > 250
RETURN n.name AS name, n.replicas AS replicas
ORDER BY n.replicas DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Service nodes above the threshold. An index on Service(replicas) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Questions and answers: query plan, PageRank, relationship direction
text:

title: Understanding the query parameter in graph databases
text:

title: Understanding the community detection in graph databases
text:
Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest. It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 ACTED_IN hops of a Person called Omar Haddad
text:

```cypher
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..3 allows paths of one to 3 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

text:

Q: What is a query plan?

title: Troubleshooting: an import fails with a constraint violation
text:
Symptom: In a supply chain graph, an import fails with a constraint violation.

How to fix it: deduplicate the input or use MERGE on the unique key.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 SENT hops of a Account called ACC-202
text:

title: Questions and answers: supernode, transaction, path
text:
Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the supernode?
A: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

Q: What is good practice for the supernode?
A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

Q: What is a transaction?
A: A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Q: Why does the transaction matter?
A: It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

Q: What is a path?
A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: What is good practice for the path?
A: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the graph projection?
A: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

A: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

Q: What is a relationship direction?
A: Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it.

Q: Why does the relationship direction matter?
A: A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship direction?
A: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

title: Understanding the property in graph databases
text:
A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price. Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

In a movies graph with Person, Movie, Genre nodes, the idea of a property appears when you ask how many movies two people have in common.

A frequent problem: Very large values such as whole documents make nodes heavy and slow down scans.

It is closely related to the graph projection. A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Recommended practice: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

title: Understanding the PageRank in graph databases
text:
PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them. It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

In a supply chain graph with Factory, Warehouse, Shipment nodes, the idea of a PageRank appears when you ask which shipments carry parts from several factories.

A frequent problem: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

title: Questions and answers: index, query parameter, variable-length path
text:

A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

A: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query parameter?
A: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

Q: What is good practice for the query parameter?
A: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Q: What is good practice for the variable-length path?
A: Always write an explicit upper bound such as 1..4.

title: Troubleshooting: an import fails with a constraint violation
text:
Symptom: In a knowledge base graph, an import fails with a constraint violation.

Likely cause: the file contains two rows with the same value for a unique property. This is easy to hit when queries start from Tag nodes and follow TAGGED relationships from Article to Tag.

How to fix it: deduplicate the input or use MERGE on the unique key.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Person {name: 'Nora Quinn'})-[:DIRECTED]->(b:Movie {name: 'Paper Moon'})
```

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:
A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes. Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

In a social network graph with Person, Post, Group nodes, the idea of a traversal appears when you ask which groups a user's friends have joined.

A frequent problem: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

It is closely related to the query parameter. A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Recommended practice: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Cypher example: show the Author nodes whose posts is above 100 in the knowledge base graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Author nodes whose posts is above 100 in the knowledge base graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Author)
WHERE n.posts > 100
RETURN n.name AS name, n.posts AS posts
ORDER BY n.posts DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Author nodes above the threshold. An index on Author(posts) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Ben and Asha are connected in the social network graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Ben and Asha are connected in the social network graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Person {name: 'Ben'})-[*..5]-(b:Person {name: 'Asha'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Cypher example: list every Post connected to a given Person through POSTED in the social network graph
text:
Task: List every Post connected to a given Person through POSTED in the social network graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: $name})-[:POSTED]->(b:Post)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Person found by name, follows outgoing POSTED relationships, and returns the name of each Post reached. The value of $name, for example 'Asha', is passed as a parameter.

title: Questions and answers: property, supernode, query plan
text:
Q: What is a property?
A: A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Q: Why does the property matter?
A: Properties keep descriptive data next to the entity it describes and can be filtered, sorted and indexed.

Q: What is good practice for the property?
A: Keep properties small and store big files outside the database with a reference.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the supernode?
A: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

Q: What is good practice for the supernode?
A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: Why does the shortest path matter?
A: It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: Why does the graph projection matter?
A: It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the graph projection?
A: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

Q: What is good practice for the graph projection?
A: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

title: Understanding the label in graph databases
text:
A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels. Labels let a query start from a small group of nodes instead of scanning the whole graph.

In a social network graph with Person, Post, Group nodes, the idea of a label appears when you ask who are the friends of friends of a user.

A frequent problem: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

It is closely related to the pattern matching. Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Recommended practice: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

title: Understanding the pattern matching in graph databases

title: Troubleshooting: an import fails with a constraint violation
text:
Symptom: In a social network graph, an import fails with a constraint violation.

Likely cause: the file contains two rows with the same value for a unique property. This is easy to hit when queries start from Post nodes and follow POSTED relationships from Person to Post.

title: Understanding the relationship in graph databases
text:
A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties. Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

Recommended practice: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 IN_GENRE hops of a Movie called Paper Moon

title: Cypher example: show the Article nodes whose views is above 50 in the knowledge base graph, highest first

title: Understanding the uniqueness constraint in graph databases
text:

A frequent problem: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

title: Cypher example: find which Person nodes have the most DIRECTED relationships to Movie nodes

```cypher
RETURN a.name AS name, count(b) AS total

```

The query counts the Movie nodes reached from each Person, sorts the counts from high to low and keeps the top five.

title: Understanding the selectivity in graph databases
text:

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, results differ every time the import is repeated.

Likely cause: CREATE was used where MERGE was needed, so duplicates accumulate. This is easy to hit when queries start from Team nodes and follow USES relationships from Service to Database.

How to fix it: switch to MERGE on a unique key and add a uniqueness constraint.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

text:

title: Understanding the variable-length path in graph databases
text:

title: Questions and answers: community detection, graph projection, pattern matching
text:

Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the pattern matching?
A: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

Q: What is good practice for the pattern matching?
A: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

Q: What is a label?

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the label?

Q: What is a query parameter?

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query parameter?
A: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

title: Questions and answers: path, MERGE, selectivity
text:

title: Cypher example: find every Topic that can be reached from a Article in two steps, first through REFERENCES and then through ABOUT


Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Topic nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'Backup guide' could be passed as $name.

title: Questions and answers: community detection, relationship, query plan
text:

Q: What is a relationship?

A: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

Q: What is a node?

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the supernode?
A: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:

title: Cypher example: show the Movie nodes whose year is above 100 in the movies graph, highest first
text:

```cypher
MATCH (n:Movie)
WHERE n.year > 100
RETURN n.name AS name, n.year AS year
ORDER BY n.year DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Movie nodes above the threshold. An index on Movie(year) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Modeling an IT infrastructure domain as a graph
text:
Goal: represent IT infrastructure data so that connection questions are fast to answer.

Node labels: Server, Service, Database, Team.

Properties:
- Server: name, cpu_cores
- Service: name, replicas
- Database: name, size_gb
- Team: name, people

Relationships:
- (:Service)-[:RUNS_ON]->(:Server)
- (:Service)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(:Service)
- (:Service)-[:USES]->(:Database)
- (:Team)-[:OWNS]->(:Service)

- Which services are affected if a server fails
- Which services have the longest dependency chains
- Which team owns the services that depend on a given database

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 STORES hops of a Warehouse called Port Depot

title: Cypher example: find every Article that can be reached from a Article in two steps, first through REFERENCES and then through REFERENCES

title: Troubleshooting: an algorithm run fails to start
text:
Symptom: In a supply chain graph, an algorithm run fails to start.

How to fix it: project only the needed labels and relationship types, or estimate memory before running.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Questions and answers: LOAD CSV, query plan, MERGE
text:
Q: What is a LOAD CSV?
A: LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the LOAD CSV matter?
A: It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the LOAD CSV?
A: Running it without a constraint and without batching makes the import slow and error-prone.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query plan?
A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: Why does the MERGE matter?
A: It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

title: Understanding the full-text index in graph databases
text:

A team modeling fraud detection data with Account, Transaction, Device will meet the full-text index as soon as they need to know which chains of transfers return to the starting account.

A frequent problem: Using a regular index for substring search gives poor results and slow scans.

Recommended practice: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

title: Understanding the relationship in graph databases

title: Cypher example: make sure a Person named Victor Hale is linked to a Movie named Blue Meridian, without creating duplicates
text:

title: Cypher example: find every Merchant that can be reached from a Account in two steps, first through SENT and then through AT_MERCHANT
text:
Task: Find every Merchant that can be reached from a Account in two steps, first through SENT and then through AT_MERCHANT.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Account {name: $name})-[:SENT]->(:Transaction)-[:AT_MERCHANT]->(c:Merchant)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Merchant nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'ACC-202' could be passed as $name.

title: Understanding the transaction in graph databases
text:
A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together. It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

Consider a social network model built from Person, Post, Group. To work out which groups a user's friends have joined, you rely directly on the transaction.

A frequent problem: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

Recommended practice: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

title: Cypher example: find every Server that can be reached from a Team in two steps, first through OWNS and then through RUNS_ON
text:
Task: Find every Server that can be reached from a Team in two steps, first through OWNS and then through RUNS_ON.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Team {name: $name})-[:OWNS]->(:Service)-[:RUNS_ON]->(c:Server)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Server nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'Growth' could be passed as $name.

title: Understanding the relationship in graph databases
text:
A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties. Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

Consider a movies model built from Person, Movie, Genre. To work out which genres a given actor appears in most, you rely directly on the relationship.

A frequent problem: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

It is closely related to the label. A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Recommended practice: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

Likely cause: a large transaction holds locks on nodes that other writers need. This is easy to hit when queries start from Database nodes and follow DEPENDS_ON relationships from Service to Service.

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: add a new Account and connect it to a Transaction with a SENT relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Account and connect it to a Transaction with a SENT relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Account {name: 'ACC-206'})-[:SENT]->(b:Transaction {name: 'TX-9005'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Questions and answers: node, full-text index, aggregation
text:
Q: What is a node?
A: A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Q: Why does the node matter?
A: Nodes are the anchor points of every query, so a clear choice of what becomes a node shapes the whole model.

Q: What is good practice for the node?
A: Give every node at least one label and a stable identifying property.

Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: Why does the full-text index matter?
A: It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the full-text index?
A: Using a regular index for substring search gives poor results and slow scans.

Q: What is good practice for the full-text index?
A: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

Q: What is a aggregation?
A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Q: Why does the aggregation matter?
A: It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the aggregation?
A: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

Q: What is good practice for the aggregation?
A: Aggregate as late as possible and limit the size of collected lists.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In a supply chain graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

Likely cause: a large transaction holds locks on nodes that other writers need. This is easy to hit when queries start from Part nodes and follow STORES relationships from Warehouse to Part.

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Questions and answers: relationship, shortest path, variable-length path
text:
Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: Why does the relationship matter?
A: Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the relationship?
A: Teams sometimes model a relationship as a node by accident and then pay for an extra hop in every query.

Q: What is good practice for the relationship?
A: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the shortest path?
A: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: Why does the supernode matter?
A: Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the supernode?
A: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

title: Questions and answers: traversal, shortest path, community detection
text:
Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the traversal?
A: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Q: What is good practice for the traversal?
A: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

Q: What is a shortest path?
A: A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Q: What is good practice for the shortest path?
A: Set a maximum depth and check that both endpoints are indexed.

Q: What is a community detection?
A: Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest.

Q: Why does the community detection matter?
A: It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the community detection?
A: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

Q: What is a LOAD CSV?
A: LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the LOAD CSV matter?
A: It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the LOAD CSV?
A: Running it without a constraint and without batching makes the import slow and error-prone.

Q: What is a MERGE?
A: MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat.

Q: What is good practice for the MERGE?
A: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

title: Cypher example: list every Article connected to a given Author through WROTE in the knowledge base graph
text:
Task: List every Article connected to a given Author through WROTE in the knowledge base graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Author {name: $name})-[:WROTE]->(b:Article)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Author found by name, follows outgoing WROTE relationships, and returns the name of each Article reached. The value of $name, for example 'M. Costa', is passed as a parameter.

title: Understanding the graph projection in graph databases
text:
A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms. It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

In an IT infrastructure graph with Server, Service, Database nodes, the idea of a graph projection appears when you ask which services are affected if a server fails.

Recommended practice: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

title: Understanding the selectivity in graph databases
text:
Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few. The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

A team modeling knowledge base data with Article, Topic, Author will meet the selectivity as soon as they need to know which tags appear together on the same article.

A frequent problem: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

Recommended practice: Anchor queries on unique or nearly unique properties.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 STORES hops of a Warehouse called North Hub
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 3 STORES hops of a Warehouse called North Hub.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Warehouse {name: 'North Hub'})-[:STORES*1..3]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..3 allows paths of one to 3 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:
An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning. Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

A frequent problem: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

It is closely related to the property. A property is a named value stored on a node or a relationship, such as a name, a date or a price.

Recommended practice: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Article named Index tuning is linked to a Topic named Operations, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Article named Index tuning is linked to a Topic named Operations, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Article {name: 'Index tuning'})
MERGE (b:Topic {name: 'Operations'})
MERGE (a)-[:ABOUT]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: add a new Person and connect it to a Group with a MEMBER_OF relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Person and connect it to a Group with a MEMBER_OF relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Person {name: 'Ben'})-[:MEMBER_OF]->(b:Group {name: 'Photographers'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Cypher example: show the Team nodes whose people is above 250 in the IT infrastructure graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Team nodes whose people is above 250 in the IT infrastructure graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Team)
WHERE n.people > 250
RETURN n.name AS name, n.people AS people
ORDER BY n.people DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Team nodes above the threshold. An index on Team(people) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Questions and answers: query parameter, label, query plan
text:

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query parameter?

Q: What is good practice for the query parameter?
A: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

Q: What is a label?
A: A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the label?
A: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

Q: What is a path?
A: A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the path?
A: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

Q: What is good practice for the path?

title: Understanding the MERGE in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: find how closely Sara Cole and Omar Haddad are connected in the movies graph

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(

)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Questions and answers: aggregation, index, query plan
text:
Q: What is a aggregation?
A: Aggregation collapses many rows into summary values such as counts, sums or lists.

Q: Why does the aggregation matter?
A: It turns a set of connections into answers like how many, how much and who is top.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the aggregation?
A: Collecting very large lists into a single value can use a lot of memory.

Q: What is good practice for the aggregation?
A: Aggregate as late as possible and limit the size of collected lists.

Q: What is a index?
A: An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Q: Why does the index matter?
A: Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the index?
A: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

Q: What is good practice for the index?
A: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query plan?
A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

Q: What is a traversal?
A: A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Q: Why does the traversal matter?
A: Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the traversal?
A: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

Q: What is good practice for the traversal?
A: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Understanding the query parameter in graph databases
text:
A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text. Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Consider a fraud detection model built from Account, Transaction, Device. To work out which accounts share a device, you rely directly on the query parameter.

A frequent problem: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

It is closely related to the label. A label is a tag that groups nodes into a kind, and one node can carry several labels.

Recommended practice: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

title: Understanding the transaction in graph databases
text:
A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together. It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

Consider a e-commerce model built from Customer, Product, Order. To work out what a customer might like based on similar buyers, you rely directly on the transaction.

A frequent problem: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

Recommended practice: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

title: Questions and answers: query parameter, query plan, full-text index
text:
Q: What is a query parameter?
A: A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text.

Q: Why does the query parameter matter?
A: Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query parameter?
A: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

Q: What is good practice for the query parameter?
A: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: Why does the query plan matter?
A: Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query plan?
A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

Q: What is a full-text index?
A: A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking.

Q: Why does the full-text index matter?
A: It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the full-text index?
A: Using a regular index for substring search gives poor results and slow scans.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

title: Understanding the selectivity in graph databases
text:
Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few. The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

A team modeling fraud detection data with Account, Transaction, Device will meet the selectivity as soon as they need to know which chains of transfers return to the starting account.

A frequent problem: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

Recommended practice: Anchor queries on unique or nearly unique properties.

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:
Symptom: In a movies graph, a query runs out of memory.

Likely cause: a variable-length pattern has no upper bound and expands through most of the graph. This is easy to hit when queries start from Person nodes and follow DIRECTED relationships from Person to Movie.

How to fix it: set a maximum depth, filter early and return only the properties you need.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:
A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph. Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Consider a social network model built from Person, Post, Group. To work out which groups a user's friends have joined, you rely directly on the supernode.

A frequent problem: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

Recommended practice: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Troubleshooting: an algorithm run fails to start
text:
Symptom: In an IT infrastructure graph, an algorithm run fails to start.

Likely cause: the projected graph does not fit in the memory that is available. This is easy to hit when queries start from Team nodes and follow USES relationships from Service to Database.

How to fix it: project only the needed labels and relationship types, or estimate memory before running.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: show the Genre nodes whose titles is above 1000 in the movies graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Genre nodes whose titles is above 1000 in the movies graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Genre)
WHERE n.titles > 1000
RETURN n.name AS name, n.titles AS titles
ORDER BY n.titles DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Genre nodes above the threshold. An index on Genre(titles) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Questions and answers: uniqueness constraint, selectivity, pattern matching
text:
Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?
A: A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Q: What is good practice for the uniqueness constraint?
A: Create constraints before the first import, not after.

Q: What is a selectivity?
A: Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the selectivity?
A: Starting a query from a low-selectivity label such as a status with two values touches almost everything.

Q: What is good practice for the selectivity?
A: Anchor queries on unique or nearly unique properties.

Q: What is a pattern matching?
A: Pattern matching describes the shape of the data you want with an ASCII-art style pattern of nodes and relationships.

Q: Why does the pattern matching matter?
A: It lets you express a multi-hop question in a single line instead of a chain of joins.

Q: What is a query plan?
A: A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the query plan?
A: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

Q: What is good practice for the query plan?
A: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

title: Questions and answers: relationship, PageRank, uniqueness constraint
text:
Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: Why does the relationship matter?
A: Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

Q: What is good practice for the relationship?
A: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?
A: A uniqueness constraint guarantees that no two nodes with the same label share a value for a property.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the uniqueness constraint?
A: Loading data without the constraint first leads to duplicates that are painful to merge later.

title: Troubleshooting: an import fails with a constraint violation
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, an import fails with a constraint violation.

Likely cause: the file contains two rows with the same value for a unique property. This is easy to hit when queries start from Device nodes and follow SENT relationships from Account to Transaction.

How to fix it: deduplicate the input or use MERGE on the unique key.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 IN_CATEGORY hops of a Product called Desk lamp
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 4 IN_CATEGORY hops of a Product called Desk lamp.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Product {name: 'Desk lamp'})-[:IN_CATEGORY*1..4]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..4 allows paths of one to 4 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

text:

Q: Why does the pattern matching matter?

A: Keep one connected pattern per MATCH and use separate clauses on purpose.

title: Cypher example: add a new Warehouse and connect it to a Part with a STORES relationship
text:
Task: Add a new Warehouse and connect it to a Part with a STORES relationship.

```cypher
CREATE (a:Warehouse {name: 'Central Store'})-[:STORES]->(b:Part {name: 'Motor R9'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 3 FRIENDS_WITH hops of a Person called Ben
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 3 FRIENDS_WITH hops of a Person called Ben.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Ben'})-[:FRIENDS_WITH*1..3]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..3 allows paths of one to 3 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Cypher example: find how closely gateway and reports are connected in the IT infrastructure graph
text:
Task: Find how closely gateway and reports are connected in the IT infrastructure graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(
  (a:Service {name: 'gateway'})-[*..5]-(b:Service {name: 'reports'})
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..5 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Understanding the path in graph databases
text:
A path is an alternating sequence of nodes and relationships that connects a start node to an end node. Returning a path gives you both the endpoints and the route between them.

A team modeling fraud detection data with Account, Transaction, Device will meet the path as soon as they need to know which chains of transfers return to the starting account.

A frequent problem: Returning full paths for thousands of matches can produce huge results.

It is closely related to the node. A node is the basic entity of a property graph and stands for a thing such as a person, an account or a product.

Recommended practice: Return only the properties you need from a path, or its length.

title: Understanding the graph projection in graph databases
text:
A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms. It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

In a movies graph with Person, Movie, Genre nodes, the idea of a graph projection appears when you ask which genres a given actor appears in most.

A frequent problem: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

It is closely related to the transaction. A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together.

Recommended practice: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:

How to fix it: switch to MERGE on a unique key and add a uniqueness constraint.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Cypher example: make sure a Account named ACC-203 is linked to a Device named DEV-D4, without creating duplicates
text:
Task: Make sure a Account named ACC-203 is linked to a Device named DEV-D4, without creating duplicates.

```cypher
MERGE (a:Account {name: 'ACC-203'})
MERGE (b:Device {name: 'DEV-D4'})
MERGE (a)-[:USED_DEVICE]->(b)
```

Each MERGE matches an existing element or creates it. Running the statement again changes nothing, so the import is safe to repeat.

title: Cypher example: add a new Factory and connect it to a Part with a PRODUCES relationship
text:

```cypher
CREATE (a:Factory {name: 'Osaka Line'})-[:PRODUCES]->(b:Part {name: 'Sensor T4'})
```

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Understanding the MERGE in graph databases
text:
MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat. It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

In a knowledge base graph with Article, Topic, Author nodes, the idea of a MERGE appears when you ask which topics an author covers.

A frequent problem: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

Recommended practice: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

title: Understanding the relationship direction in graph databases
text:

In a fraud detection graph with Account, Transaction, Device nodes, the idea of a relationship direction appears when you ask which accounts share a device.

A frequent problem: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

It is closely related to the index. An index is a lookup structure on a label and property that lets the database find starting nodes without scanning.

Recommended practice: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

A team modeling IT infrastructure data with Server, Service, Database will meet the pattern matching as soon as they need to know which services are affected if a server fails.

A frequent problem: Writing two disconnected patterns in one MATCH produces a cartesian product of their results.

title: Cypher example: add a new Warehouse and connect it to a Part with a STORES relationship

CREATE adds both nodes and the relationship in one statement. Running it twice would add duplicates, which is why MERGE is often a better choice for imports.

title: Understanding the query parameter in graph databases
text:
A query parameter is a named placeholder whose value is supplied separately from the query text. Parameters let the database reuse a cached plan and protect against injection.

In a social network graph with Person, Post, Group nodes, the idea of a query parameter appears when you ask who are the friends of friends of a user.

A frequent problem: Building queries by joining strings makes every call look new and invites injection bugs.

Recommended practice: Pass every user-provided value as a parameter.

title: Cypher example: show the Shipment nodes whose weight is above 100 in the supply chain graph, highest first
text:
Task: Show the Shipment nodes whose weight is above 100 in the supply chain graph, highest first.

```cypher
MATCH (n:Shipment)
WHERE n.weight > 100
RETURN n.name AS name, n.weight AS weight
ORDER BY n.weight DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Shipment nodes above the threshold. An index on Shipment(weight) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Cypher example: find every Person that can be reached from a Person in two steps, first through FRIENDS_WITH and then through FRIENDS_WITH

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:

title: Understanding the variable-length path in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: list every Service connected to a given Service through DEPENDS_ON in the IT infrastructure graph
text:

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 STORES hops of a Warehouse called Central Store
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 4 STORES hops of a Warehouse called Central Store.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Warehouse {name: 'Central Store'})-[:STORES*1..4]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..4 allows paths of one to 4 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Wireless mouse and Desk lamp are connected in the e-commerce graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Wireless mouse and Desk lamp are connected in the e-commerce graph.

```cypher
)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated

title: Understanding the full-text index in graph databases
text:
A full-text index supports searching words inside text properties with ranking. It helps users find nodes by keywords rather than by exact value.

In a knowledge base graph with Article, Topic, Author nodes, the idea of a full-text index appears when you ask which tags appear together on the same article.

A frequent problem: Using a regular index for substring search gives poor results and slow scans.

It is closely related to the traversal. A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes.

Recommended practice: Use a full-text index for search boxes and keep exact lookups on regular indexes.

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:

How to fix it: set a maximum depth, filter early and return only the properties you need.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Questions and answers: MERGE, relationship, node
text:

title: Understanding the community detection in graph databases
text:
Community detection finds groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest. It reveals natural clusters such as customer segments, fraud rings or service domains.

Consider a movies model built from Person, Movie, Genre. To work out how many movies two people have in common, you rely directly on the community detection.

A frequent problem: Treating the output as ground truth is risky because different algorithms can split the same graph differently.

Recommended practice: Compare results from more than one algorithm and inspect a sample of groups by hand.

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: list every Post connected to a given Person through LIKES in the social network graph
text:

text:

title: Cypher example: find how closely Trail shoes and Desk lamp are connected in the e-commerce graph
text:

title: Questions and answers: selectivity, aggregation, graph projection
text:

title: Questions and answers: relationship, query plan, transaction

Q: What is a transaction?

text:
A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph. Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

Consider an IT infrastructure model built from Server, Service, Database. To work out which services have the longest dependency chains, you rely directly on the supernode.

A frequent problem: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

It is closely related to the graph projection. A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Recommended practice: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 ACTED_IN hops of a Person called Nora Quinn
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 4 ACTED_IN hops of a Person called Nora Quinn.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: 'Nora Quinn'})-[:ACTED_IN*1..4]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..4 allows paths of one to 4 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Understanding the transaction in graph databases

Q: Why does the LOAD CSV matter?

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the LOAD CSV?
A: Running it without a constraint and without batching makes the import slow and error-prone.

Q: What is good practice for the LOAD CSV?

Q: What is a relationship?

title: Troubleshooting: an algorithm run fails to start
text:
Symptom: In a fraud detection graph, an algorithm run fails to start.

Likely cause: the projected graph does not fit in the memory that is available. This is easy to hit when queries start from Device nodes and follow SENT relationships from Account to Transaction.

How to fix it: project only the needed labels and relationship types, or estimate memory before running.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the MERGE in graph databases
text:
MERGE matches a pattern if it exists and creates it if it does not, which makes a write safe to repeat. It is the standard tool for idempotent imports and for avoiding duplicates.

Consider a social network model built from Person, Post, Group. To work out which posts are liked by the most people, you rely directly on the MERGE.

A frequent problem: Merging on a pattern with many properties can create near-duplicates when one value differs.

It is closely related to the query plan. A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query.

Recommended practice: Merge on the unique key only and set the other properties afterwards.

title: Understanding the transaction in graph databases
text:
A transaction groups several changes so that they either all succeed or all fail together. It keeps the graph consistent when an update touches several nodes and relationships at once.

A team modeling IT infrastructure data with Server, Service, Database will meet the transaction as soon as they need to know which team owns the services that depend on a given database.

A frequent problem: Very large transactions hold locks and memory for a long time and can fail late.

Recommended practice: Commit in batches of a few thousand changes when loading big files.

title: Cypher example: find every Part that can be reached from a Shipment in two steps, first through SHIPS_TO and then through STORES
text:
Task: Find every Part that can be reached from a Shipment in two steps, first through SHIPS_TO and then through STORES.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Shipment {name: $name})-[:SHIPS_TO]->(:Warehouse)-[:STORES]->(c:Part)
RETURN DISTINCT c.name AS result
```

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Part nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'Pune Works' could be passed as $name.

title: Cypher example: find all nodes within 4 STORES hops of a Warehouse called North Hub
text:
Task: Find all nodes within 4 STORES hops of a Warehouse called North Hub.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Warehouse {name: 'North Hub'})-[:STORES*1..4]-(b)
WHERE a <> b
RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS result
LIMIT 25
```

The expression *1..4 allows paths of one to 4 relationships. The query ignores direction, excludes the start node and limits the output to 25 rows to keep the result small.

title: Questions and answers: aggregation, label, relationship
text:

Q: What is a label?

Q: Why does the label matter?

Q: What is a relationship?
A: A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Q: Why does the relationship matter?
A: Relationships are stored as first-class records, which is why following them stays cheap as the data grows.

A: Name relationship types with verbs in upper case and pick a direction that reads naturally.

title: Understanding the graph projection in graph databases
text:
A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms. It lets algorithms run fast without touching the stored graph.

In an IT infrastructure graph with Server, Service, Database nodes, the idea of a graph projection appears when you ask which services have the longest dependency chains.

A frequent problem: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

It is closely related to the shortest path. A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships.

Recommended practice: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:
A traversal is the act of walking from a start node along relationships to reach other nodes. Traversals answer questions about connections, which is the main reason to choose a graph database.

In a e-commerce graph with Customer, Product, Order nodes, the idea of a traversal appears when you ask which categories drive the most repeat orders.

A frequent problem: A traversal with no limit on depth can touch most of the graph and exhaust memory.

It is closely related to the relationship. A relationship connects exactly two nodes, has one type and one direction, and can carry its own properties.

Recommended practice: Bound the depth and filter early so that the traversal stays small.

title: Cypher example: find every Group that can be reached from a Person in two steps, first through FRIENDS_WITH and then through MEMBER_OF

Two relationships are chained in one pattern. DISTINCT removes repeated Group nodes that can be reached by more than one route. For example, 'Ines' could be passed as $name.

title: Understanding the selectivity in graph databases
text:
Selectivity describes how few nodes a filter keeps, where a highly selective filter keeps very few. The planner starts from the most selective part of a pattern, so good selectivity means small intermediate results.

title: Understanding the index in graph databases
text:

title: Understanding the supernode in graph databases
text:
A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph. Supernodes dominate query cost because every traversal that reaches them must consider all of their neighbors.

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:
Symptom: In a supply chain graph, results differ every time the import is repeated.

title: Cypher example: find every Topic that can be reached from a Article in two steps, first through REFERENCES and then through ABOUT

title: Cypher example: show the Part nodes whose cost is above 10 in the supply chain graph, highest first

title: Cypher example: list every Movie connected to a given Person through DIRECTED in the movies graph
text:
Task: List every Movie connected to a given Person through DIRECTED in the movies graph.

```cypher
MATCH (a:Person {name: $name})-[:DIRECTED]->(b:Movie)
RETURN b.name AS result
```

The pattern starts from one Person found by name, follows outgoing DIRECTED relationships, and returns the name of each Movie reached. The value of $name, for example 'Victor Hale', is passed as a parameter.

title: Troubleshooting: results differ every time the import is repeated
text:
Symptom: In a e-commerce graph, results differ every time the import is repeated.

Likely cause: CREATE was used where MERGE was needed, so duplicates accumulate. This is easy to hit when queries start from Customer nodes and follow IN_CATEGORY relationships from Product to Category.

How to fix it: switch to MERGE on a unique key and add a uniqueness constraint.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

title: Understanding the relationship direction in graph databases
text:
Every relationship is stored with a direction, although a query can choose to ignore it. A well-chosen direction makes patterns read like a sentence and keeps queries short.

A frequent problem: Adding a second reverse relationship for convenience doubles storage and creates inconsistencies.

Recommended practice: Store one direction and match without an arrow when the direction does not matter.

title: Understanding the shortest path in graph databases
text:
A shortest path is the connection between two nodes that uses the fewest relationships. It answers questions such as how closely two people, accounts or servers are linked.

In a movies graph with Person, Movie, Genre nodes, the idea of a shortest path appears when you ask how many movies two people have in common.

A frequent problem: Running it between nodes with no connection and no depth limit can be very expensive.

Recommended practice: Set a maximum depth and check that both endpoints are indexed.

title: Understanding the LOAD CSV in graph databases
text:
LOAD CSV reads rows from a CSV file so they can be turned into nodes and relationships. It is a simple way to bring tabular data into the graph for the first time.

Consider an IT infrastructure model built from Server, Service, Database. To work out which team owns the services that depend on a given database, you rely directly on the LOAD CSV.

A frequent problem: Running it without a constraint and without batching makes the import slow and error-prone.

Recommended practice: Create constraints first and process the file in batches.

title: Understanding the query plan in graph databases
text:

In a knowledge base graph with Article, Topic, Author nodes, the idea of a query plan appears when you ask which topics an author covers.

A frequent problem: Judging a query only by its result and not by its plan hides scans that will hurt at scale.

Recommended practice: Use EXPLAIN to see the plan and PROFILE to see the real row counts.

title: Troubleshooting: a query runs out of memory
text:

title: Understanding the traversal in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: speed up lookups of Service nodes by name
text:
Task: Speed up lookups of Service nodes by name.

```cypher
CREATE INDEX service_name IF NOT EXISTS
FOR (n:Service) ON (n.name)
```

The index lets the database find a Service by name without scanning every Service. IF NOT EXISTS makes the command safe to run again.

title: Troubleshooting: a query becomes slower as the data grows
text:
Symptom: In a supply chain graph, a query becomes slower as the data grows.

Likely cause: the first step scans every node of a label because no index supports the filter. This is easy to hit when queries start from Part nodes and follow SHIPS_TO relationships from Shipment to Warehouse.

title: Cypher example: show the Transaction nodes whose amount is above 500 in the fraud detection graph, highest first
text:

```cypher
MATCH (n:Transaction)
WHERE n.amount > 500
RETURN n.name AS name, n.amount AS amount
ORDER BY n.amount DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Transaction nodes above the threshold. An index on Transaction(amount) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Questions and answers: label, PageRank, selectivity
text:

A: Using labels for values that change often, such as a status, creates churn in the store.

Q: What is good practice for the label?
A: Use labels for stable categories and properties for values that change.

Q: What is a PageRank?
A: PageRank is an algorithm that scores nodes by how many important nodes link to them.

Q: Why does the PageRank matter?
A: It highlights influential entities such as key accounts, popular articles or critical services.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the PageRank?
A: Running it on a graph where direction has no meaning gives scores that are hard to interpret.

Q: What is a selectivity?

Q: What is a uniqueness constraint?

A: It protects data quality and also creates the index that makes MERGE and lookups fast.

Q: Why does the index matter?
A: Most slow queries are slow because the first step scans every node of a label.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the index?
A: Adding indexes on every property wastes memory and slows down writes.

Q: What is good practice for the index?
A: Index the properties you filter or match on at the start of your queries.

title: Questions and answers: supernode, graph projection, variable-length path
text:
Q: What is a supernode?
A: A supernode is a node with an unusually large number of relationships compared with the rest of the graph.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the supernode?
A: Modeling a very common value such as a country as a single hub node often creates one by accident.

A: Split hubs by a second dimension or filter on relationship properties to avoid scanning all neighbors.

Q: What is a graph projection?
A: A graph projection is an in-memory copy of selected nodes and relationships prepared for running algorithms.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the graph projection?
A: Projecting the entire database when only one part is needed wastes memory.

Q: What is good practice for the graph projection?
A: Project only the labels and relationship types the algorithm needs.

Q: What is a variable-length path?
A: A variable-length path matches a chain of relationships whose length lies between a minimum and a maximum.

Q: Why does the variable-length path matter?
A: It expresses ideas like friends within three hops without writing three separate patterns.

Q: What mistake should I avoid with the variable-length path?
A: Leaving out the upper bound allows the search to grow with the size of the graph.

title: Troubleshooting: writes time out while a long report is running
text:
Symptom: In a movies graph, writes time out while a long report is running.

Likely cause: a large transaction holds locks on nodes that other writers need. This is easy to hit when queries start from Movie nodes and follow ACTED_IN relationships from Person to Movie.

How to fix it: commit in smaller batches and run the report on a read replica when available.

How to prevent it: review the query plan of important queries with EXPLAIN before they reach production, and test them on data that is as large as the real graph.

text:
A query plan is the sequence of operations the database chooses in order to answer a query. Reading the plan shows where time is spent and whether an index is used.

title: Understanding the full-text index in graph databases
text:

title: Cypher example: show the Person nodes whose born is above 10 in the movies graph, highest first
text:

```cypher
MATCH (n:Person)
WHERE n.born > 10
RETURN n.name AS name, n.born AS born
ORDER BY n.born DESC
LIMIT 10
```

The WHERE clause keeps only Person nodes above the threshold. An index on Person(born) can help when many nodes exist.

title: Cypher example: find how closely Asha and Jonas are connected in the social network graph
text:
Task: Find how closely Asha and Jonas are connected in the social network graph.

```cypher
MATCH p = shortestPath(

)
RETURN length(p) AS hops
```

shortestPath finds the route with the fewest relationships. The bound ..6 stops the search from growing without limit.
